subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN NUCLEAR

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether the government has been invited to participate in the international discussions at Geneva announced in Washington over the week end, to be held with a view to working out a system of inspection, and control of the prohibition of atomic tests.

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN NUCLEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Leader of the Opposition for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. May I say, as I stated before the house last Monday, that we are delighted that the Russians have made this proposal to hold a meeting of experts qualified to consider matters of inspection and control in relation to nuclear tests, and I again express the hope that this action gives us some encouragement that Soviet Russia may be willing to consider larger questions of disarmament.
With respect to the hon. member's question, the answer is that we have not been invited to participate in a meeting of a group of experts, but I can assure the house that we have been in constant touch with the United States authorities on the reply to be given to the U.S.S.R. proposal and that we have expressed our approval of that reply.
It seems to me that the most important aspect of this matter is that experts from at least those countries which have conducted nuclear tests should meet together, and we are concerned lest our insistence on participation in such a conference would result in delay, having regard to the composition of such a group.
Canada, as we know, has not conducted nuclear tests and has not operated a comprehensive system for the detection of such tests conducted by other countries. Nevertheless, if we are asked to contribute experts as part of a formula for participation which would make for progress rather than delay in holding a meeting, having in mind the composition of the body of experts from both sides, I am confident Canada could provide the services of highly qualified scientists.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Labour. What is the present situation with regard to the strike affecting Canadian Pacific steamship services on the Pacific coast?

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member's question I should like to make a statement to the house on the situation which exists at the present time. As hon. members are aware, a strike of unlicensed personnel employed by the Canadian Pacific Railway

Company in its British Columbia coast steamship service took place at midnight, May 16. Ten vessels of the company were tied up, and service between Vancouver and Vancouver island was partially disrupted, services of other companies still continuing. Some 300 men are on strike and some 750 other employees of the company were indirectly affected.
Prior to the strike a board of conciliation had made recommendations in this dispute. The board consisted of Mr. F. E. Harrison, Vancouver, as chairman, and Messrs. R. A. Mahoney and Owen E. Mason, both of Vancouver, nominees of the company and union respectively.
The report of the board was received on February 14, 1958, and the chairman recommended a wage increase of 16 per cent from September 15, 1957, to September 15, 1958, with an additional increase of 9 per cent from September 15, 1958, to September 15, 1959. The nominee of the company recommended a 12 per cent increase effective September 15, 1957, to September 15, 1958, with an additional advance of 5 per cent from September 15, 1958, until the expiry of the contract. The union nominee recommended an average of 50 per cent wage increase, and a two-year contract to expire September 15, 1959.
The attitude of the parties toward the recommendations of the board is as follows. The S.I.U. on March 15 advised that it would accept the recommendations of its nominee to the board.
On May 8 the Canadian Pacific Railway Company advised me that it could not accept any recommendations of the board as forming a basis for settlement. Both parties since have made some proposals, but are still far apart.
Following the strike I brought the parties together through the west coast representative of my department but, as in their direct discussions prior to the work stoppage, no settlement resulted. The officers of the department at Vancouver are in constant touch with the parties, ready to render any assistance.
I understand that over the past week end there have been proposals made for the arbitration of the dispute which under certain conditions have been accepted by the company. We are now awaiting the reaction of the union to the proposal.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. My question is based on many rather concerned inquiries and is somewhat related to commonwealth relations. speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESTRICTIONS ON IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact that an hon. member of English origin and a minister of Irish extraction should attempt to discuss haggis is in itself a mystery, and certainly is a situation which is very likely to result in a haggle, I would think. But, in any event, Mr. Speaker, I am informed by the officers of my department that haggis itself is not prohibited entry in any way under the provisions of the Customs Act.
There are, however, other acts which it is our responsibility to administer, including the Meat and Canned Foods Act and the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. Under those acts the collector of customs is prohibited from admitting any food product into this country unless it bears a certificate issued by certain officers in the country of origin. There are
Inquiries of the Ministry also regulations laid down by the Department of National Health and Welfare with respect to the labelling of food products. Any haggis which complies with the regulations of these two acts and which bears a label authorized in accordance with regulations of the Department of National Health and Welfare is automatically admitted to this country. Those which do not, unfortunately, under the acts are barred from entry by the collector of customs. That is the haggle.

Mr. Speaker, the 1956-57 barley pool was closed on May 9 and the final accounting has now been completed by the Canadian wheat board. The surplus in the pool for distribution to producers is $7,570,416.35. Producers delivered a total of 120.6 million bushels of barley to this pool. The average final payment will be 6.28 cents per bushel. The principal grades of barley delivered to the 1956-57 pool were No. 3 Canada western, six row, No. 1 feed and No. 2 feed. speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, May 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Robert Lafreniere for an address to his Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in complimenting you, the Deputy Speaker and the deputy chairman of committees of the whole respectively on your election, and the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on their selection for that high honour, I follow a tradition which, in each of those particular achievements, affords me a great deal of personal pleasure and satisfaction.
Everyone was delighted at the election of yourself and the deputy chairman of committees of the whole house, not only because of the affection in which both of you are
[Mrs. Fairclough.l
held by this house but also because of the ability of yourself and the deputy chairman of committees, as was demonstrated in the last house in the offices you held. The high honour accorded to the seconder of the address, coming on the heels of contesting three federal elections in less than a year, was a tribute in which we all joined.
You will pardon me, Mr. Speaker, when I say that the election of the Deputy Speaker and the selection of the mover of the address gave me a particular and special delight. They are the symbols of that which some hon. gentlemen said could not be; they are the symbols of a national unity which those of us in this party have sought over many, many weary years.
Last year on October 18 the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) made a speech in this house which epitomized the struggle of some Liberals toward a certain type of vision, division. They complained then of too little unity, Mr. Speaker.
Their only complaint now can be that there is too much. What a contrast are the words of the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I quote from the English translation of his speech as recorded at page 4 of the translations for May 12, 1958, when he said:
For too many years, Mr. Speaker, a few politicians have attempted to create disruption and disunity among the people of Canada by playing on racial and religious prejudices. In the name of the province of Quebec, which I particularly represent, I wish to say to the house that we are proud of the coexistence and cohabitation of the two great races which constitute the population of our country. We of Quebec earnestly want national unity through the respect of the rights and privileges of each and every one of our citizens, whatever their race, religion or language.
Then he went on to say:
There have been differences of opinion and difficulties in the past but, to me, the last election has the same significance for all those living in the province of Quebec. That province, the province of Ontario and all the other provinces, as well as people of all nationalities, are all determined to work for the success of that great experiment which is the building up of our country.
That sentiment, Mr. Speaker, as expressed by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency is an aspiration to which all those in this party and in the constituency of Saskatoon earnestly subscribe. As to the Deputy Speaker, may I say there have been few in the history of this house coming afresh into its membership who have demonstrated their ability so convincingly in such a short time.
I was astounded the other day, Mr. Speaker, to learn that among the Liberals there still appears to be opposition to an early start on the South Saskatchewan dam. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) said in effect, as found on page 201 of Hansard

of May 19, that while they are not against such a project as the South Saskatchewan dam it has not been proved to them that such projects are economically sound and urgently needed at this particular time of recession. As recorded on page 5 of Hansard of May 12, it was said in the speech from the throne:
My ministers have made progress in arrangements for the construction of the South Saskatchewan project. Proposals will be placed before you to make possible the commencement this year of the construction of the main dam intended to create a great reservoir in the heart of the prairie in order to further the productive development of this part of Canada.
Set against the background of the speech from the throne, the only inference I can draw from the remarks of the hon. member for Gloucester is that he still wishes to delay the construction of the dam. I am sure that much will be said about this project and much will be heard from the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cooper) who has worked so hard for so many years for its construction, both in his personal capacity and as vice-president of the Saskatchewan rivers development association.
In view of what has already been said on this subject in the house during this debate I want to emphasize the nature and urgency of the project. This is a multi-purpose project. The object of its construction is to satisfy six specific and urgent needs of the people of that area, and in the satisfaction of those needs to strengthen the general economy of the country. The project will require the construction of an earth dam on the South Saskatchewan river between the towns of Elbow and Outlook. The structure will be 205 feet high with a length of 16,700 feet. Associated with the dam will be a power house having an installed capacity of 150,000 kilowatts. An auxiliary earth dam in the Qu'Appelle valley will also be necessary to prevent the escape of waters impounded by the main dam.
The irrigation development will require the installation of 500 miles of main canals and laterals as well as 12 pumping stations. With regard to the irrigation aspect of this project, I should like to point out that over 500,000 acres of good soil can be irrigated. This area is distributed over 300 miles, and will be of direct benefit to over 50,000 farmers.
Another important aspect of this project is river regulation and flood control. Mr. Speaker, the wide variation in seasonal flow of the Saskatchewan river makes power development impracticable without large storage facilities. The reservoir as it is planned will provide for almost complete regulation of the river flow, and will increase 57071-3-29
The Address-Mr. Jones the power potential of five possible downstream sites. Of particular interest to the citizens of my constituency is this fact. The Pike lake area in the vicinity of Saskatoon and the Carrot river area near The Pas in Manitoba have been subject to flooding in the past. By the creation of the South Saskatchewan river reservoir this flooding will be eliminated at Pike lake and will be materially reduced in the Carrot river area.
As to water supply, the cities of Regina and Moose Jaw are now supplied with water from Buffalo Pound lake. The government of Canada is maintaining adequate levels in this lake by pumping from the South Saskatchewan river. The presence of the dam will mean that these needs can be met by gravity flow, thus eliminating the cost of pumping. But much more important than that, by the construction of this reservoir and the regulation of the flow of water in the river, the citizens of Saskatoon, Regina and Moose Jaw will be assured of adequate water supplies.
With regard to hydroelectric power and some of the other features of the dam that particularly bear on this district, it should be noted that it is estimated that 53 per cent of the population of our province live within a radius of 125 miles of the dam, and 69 per cent within a radius of 150 miles. After full upstream development of the river basin it is calculated that 375 million kilowatt hours can be produced annually in the hydro plant. Of this amount, 50 million kilowatt hours will be required for irrigation and the balance will be available for commercial and industrial use.
I have mentioned the large percentage of the people of the province who are within the vicinity of this dam. Over two-thirds of the people of our province will be within an automobile drive of less than three hours from the sorely needed recreational facilities and the other benefits which are associated with parks, lakes and streams, and which will be created especially around the lake formed by the reservoir. This lake formed by the reservoir itself will extend a distance of 135 miles from the dam. Additional recreational benefits may be expected from the raising of the levels of lakes in that area. It is to be hoped that suitable roads will be provided to the area by the province for use during as well as after construction in order that men and materials as well as the general public may move readily to the site of the dam. Everyone desirous of reaching the dam site from Saskatoon for purposes of work, supply of materials or for pleasure will realize the importance of this suggestion.
Others vitally interested in this project will undoubtedly deal at length and in much

The Address-Mr. Jones greater detail with the benefits of the dam as it will affect employment, land values, agricultural diversification and industry, but I should like to stress now the urgency of its construction, particularly with regard to power development and stream control as well as agricultural diversification, especially in the light of the rapidly increasing size of the three cities which are chiefly affected by the first two aspects of this project that I mentioned, namely power development and stream control.
My own city of Saskatoon at present has a population of 80,000. It is estimated that the population will rise to 100,000 in five years. In an additional 20 years it is expected that the population will reach 160,000. In the light of that consideration and the industrial needs which will develop as a result of the increase in population, it is clearly evident that stream control with assured adequate supply of water is a necessity. The main dam, Mr. Speaker, will take eight years to complete. By that time what are now difficult circumstances in connection with power development and stream control will have become urgent essentials requiring immediate relief.
Before parliament met, Mr. Speaker, I heard the surprising suggestion that because of their numbers, Conservative members will not have enough to do in this parliament. With the greatest respect to those who advance this theory, I suggest that it is based on a completely incorrect notion of the duties and the responsibilities of a member of parliament. On the contrary, after reading the speech from the throne and seeing what is indicated in it, some say there are not enough Conservative members to inquire into, consider and resolve the formidable legacy of tasks which we inherited from the previous administration in addition, of course, to the projects we have in mind and the problems which will inevitably arise for consideration in the course of time.
Difficult decisions will have to be made, Mr. Speaker, in the area of national defence, balancing the security needs of this country with the need for expenditures on development and other matters. In external affairs there is the relating of foreign policy to the economic advancement of this country, a relationship which seems largely to have escaped the attention of our predecessors. In that connection also I note with interest, Mr. Speaker, the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary South that a committee look into this problem of Canada-United States affairs in order that the relationships between our two countries in connection with economic and other matters may be improved.

In agriculture there is the provision of long term credits to farmers to help them to purchase land or sufficient additional land to enable them to form economic farming units. There is the difficult problem of crop insurance and the problem of the disposal of agricultural surpluses, and the consideration of other pressing problems which beset the agricultural community and of which we have all heard.
Attention should be given to consideration of the problems relating to storage at Churchill. For example, it has been suggested that instead of pressing for more storage at Fort William, where the great lakes are frozen over for many months of the year, storage facilities might be built at some other place such as Newfoundland, where the grain could be stored and be available every day of the year for ocean shipment. During harvest time the grain could be shipped to Churchill by rail, there loaded on coastal ships and taken to Newfoundland, where it could be stored for future delivery as sales are made. I sincerely regret that the royal commission on coastal shipping neglected to study the possibility of such a development.
The topics I have mentioned are but a few of the many which come readily to mind but are, I hope, sufficient to dispel the notion that there is not enough to keep all hon. members very busy indeed-and all this in addition to all the regular duties of the members in connection with the house and its committees. The committees of the house have been greatly strengthened and have been given increased importance by the suggestions of the Prime Minister for reform.
I should like to turn for a moment to the economic wastage arising out of the failure of the present mental health facilities to make adequate provision for the effective treatment of the mentally sick. It has been asserted that there are at least as many people in this country suffering from crippling mental sickness as there are people suffering from physical sickness. In general, persons suffering from a physical ailment go to a hospital with the expectation of returning to employment and to a useful life because while there they receive treatment appropriate to their illness. What is the situation with the mentally sick? I am told that in the province of Saskatchewan the government provides $4 per day for the total care of a patient with a sick brain, and that this is comparable to the amount provided in other provinces; yet the total cost, not including doctors' bills, for the care of a patient with a sore foot is now more than $14 per day.

What is the result of this low standard of care? At the present time there are more than 70,000 persons restrained in the hopelessly overcrowded confines of the 75 mental institutions of this country. Seventy thousand persons are restrained under conditions where it is not unusual to find 75 people in a single room, sleeping in beds less than six inches apart. Living under such conditions would have a serious effect on the mental health of the most robust minded; what must it do to the mentally sick? Is this effective treatment; indeed, is effective treatment possible under such circumstances?
It has been emphatically recommended by those whose profession is the treatment of the mentally ill that, given the same standard of care as the physically ill, the mentally sick could go to the hospital with the expectation of returning to the community after treatment rather than remaining incarcerated for years or even for life. Mental sickness can be treated effectively. Much mental sickness can be treated effectively with very little hospitalization, provided the patient is afforded the same standard of care that is afforded to the physically sick. Such treatment could be provided in small hospitals or in the wards of general hospitals, and in fact much mental sickness can be treated without any hospitalization at all if adequate out-patient clinics are available.
Mental sickness, when treated effectively, changes a person from a continual drain on the taxpayer to a person who may take his productive place in life, who can pay taxes and fill his place in the community, discharging his duties and obligations. It is held by many that the present overcrowded mental institutions can never effectively perform this task; in fact the existing conditions in many cases may aggravate rather than lessen the degree of emotional disturbance.
This problem is particularly important because of the numbers involved, and also because this government might consider the advisability of encouraging the same standard of care rather than encouraging, either directly or indirectly, the perpetuation of the present type of mental institutions.
In closing my remarks on this particular subject I would like to quote from an article by Dr. D. G. McKerracher, professor of psychiatry at the University of Saskatchewan, which was published in the Canadian Journal of Public Health in October, 1957. Dr. McKerracher has a psychiatric ward in a general hospital in Saskatchewan which maintains the same standard of care for the mentally sick that is given the physically sick, and he has this astonishing thing to say:
57071-3-29J
The Address-Mr. Godin
We never refuse admission to a patient because of the degree of disturbance. We never transfer a patient to a provincial hospital because he is too disturbed. Day or night no patient is ever locked behind any door. All doors from the front entrance to the most remote area of the ward are open. Very sick patients get special nursing care, just as they do on a surgical or medical ward.
That, I think, indicates the advances that have been made in this field in recent times.
Before I resume my seat, may I say what a pleasure it is to me to be associated with the many new members of this house and in particular with those new members from Saskatchewan. I am very proud to be associated with these earnest, sincere and friendly men, and I am sure their constituents will be proud of the practical and capable manner in which they are already discharging their duties as they take up the various tasks of particular interest to their constituents and to the nation as a whole.
Many reasons have been advanced in this house for their being here in such numbers, but I want to say-and I am sure you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, when you know them better-that not the least of those reasons is their own personal capability and the resolution and determination which each one of them has, in addition to a wide and deep knowledge of the affairs of his constituency as well as of the affairs of the nation. This wider knowledge is, of course, essential if narrow regionalism is to be avoided.
Mr. Speaker, in the days ahead it would not be unexpected if hon. members from western Canada devoted a great deal of their attention to the particular problems of western agriculture and petroleum and mineral production, as well as to the establishment of a second trans-Canada highway through Saskatoon to the Yellowhead pass. The strengthening of the economy of the west adds directly to the strength of the great central provinces now in a way which was not so readily apparent in the days when many of our western necessities were purchased from abroad. Central Canada now -its labour, management and capital-therefore has a greater and more direct interest in the prosperity of the west than it has had at any time in the past. I do not need to say that as this region, along with the various other regions of this country, becomes strengthened so will the whole of Canada advance.

I know that my constituents would wish me to avail myself of this opportunity to congratulate you-and it is a pleasure for me to do so-on your unanimous election to the important post you now hold. I should like to echo the experienced remarks made by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition when they had occasion to move and second your nomination. I should like also to endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Laurier with regard to the wonderful task of impartiality and justice which you have undertaken in your own city of Toronto in supporting the drive for a bilingual high school there. May I add, with your permission, that it is well known that you have from the first aided an admirable Canadian institution, namely the Canadian alliance, in its objectives.
I should like, also, to add words of congratulation to the Deputy Speaker on his appointment; to the leader of this house and, possibly, to those ministers of the government who have once again been entrusted with the duties which they formerly performed, with a special word of congratulation to those who have been switched, and more particularly to those who have undertaken their present duties for the first time.
Before entering on the main purpose of my speech I should also like to pay tribute to a fellow citizen of mine who for 13 years has rendered many services to the Nickel Belt riding in this very house. I refer to my good friend and neighbour Mr. Leo Gauthier, formely member of parliament for Nickel Belt. Mr. Gauthier is endowed with a great deal of humour and common sense, and I know that while he was in this house he well performed the duties which the electorate had asked of him. The only sorrow I have is that my becoming a member of this house is due in some part to the misfortune of Mr. Gauthier, who is now ill. May I wish him a speedy restoration to his former good health, and express the hope that both he and his wife may enjoy many years of happiness.
May I pay tribute also to my two worthy opponents in the last campaign, Mr. Anthony Falzetta of White Fish, the Conservative standard bearer, and Mr. Harold Prescott of Capreol, the C.C.F. candidate. I should like to congratulate them for the loyal efforts they have made to explain the doctrines of their respective parties. I hasten to add,
[Mr. Godin 1

however, that I do not go along with them to the point of wishing that the result of the election had been different.
Mr. Speaker, I wish also to congratulate the hon. member for Yukon, who so well seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. His work was splendid, and I know that all hon. members were very pleased with his speech.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I would feel remiss if I failed to offer the usual congratulations to the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafre-niere) who, a few days ago, had the privilege of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. He delivered a marvelous speech; however he showed his submission and attachment to his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and to the policy of his party.
If I so congratulate him, this should not be construed as meaning that I support the policies he advocates. In fact, I have been quite surprised to hear the hon. member state in this house that he was speaking on behalf of all bilingual Canadians.
Then too, Mr. Speaker, I was very much surprised when the hon. members for Park-dale (Mr. Maloney), for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) and for Saskatoon (Mr. Jones), dealt at great length with the doctrine of the Conservative party in connection with the problem of national unity and sound Canadianism. I was amazed to hear the hon. member for Parkdale state that the Conservatives preach the same doctrine in Vancouver, Quebec or Halifax. I was still more surprised when the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, wishing to repeat in English what he had just said in French, gave a far from faithful translation of it.
Mr. Speaker, we Liberals believe that if there is a field where words should be followed by deeds, it is the field of national unity and sound Canadianism. So, we think that those hon. members could have cut down their speech by some 39 minutes if they had gone to the trouble of refuting the speech made two or three months ago in this house by their colleague, the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Small), on the matter of bilingual cheques.
We place more reliance on the doctrine of the Liberal party which a few years ago gave this country political independence when it abolished appeals to the Privy Council. We understand this doctrine even better

because the Liberal party expressed it in deeds by giving the people of Canada the family allowances despite the opposition of the former Conservative leader, the Hon. George Drew, who objected to it here in this house on racial grounds.
Mr. Speaker, all hon. members will have many opportunities to state what they really think of this great Canadian problem, and that is why I will say no more at this time. I will therefore deal now with a more important part of my speech in which I will have the opportunity of telling hon. members something new with regard to the Nickel Belt area.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, I realize it is my privilege, on behalf of my constituents, to inform this house of the many advantages which can be found in the riding of Nickel Belt, and possibly also inform the government of some of the problems which prevail there. Of course the riding of Nickel Belt forms part of the belt of Liberalism which is so well known in northern Ontario, and which extends from Pembroke to Fort William. It has a unique feature in the sense that it completely surrounds the district of Sudbury, and this is why there is so much co-operation between hon. members from the district of Sudbury and the district of Nickel Belt.
Nickel Belt, of course, is endowed with a great mining industry. We find there many mines operated by International Nickel and Falconbridge Mines. We also have a lumbering industry, though I must admit that since June last lumbering operations in our area have diminished by approximately 50 per cent. There are a great many farms in the valleys of the French river, the Veuve river and the Sudbury basin flats. I would like to pay tribute to one of the farmers in this area, Mr. Despatie, who distinguished himself a few years ago by being acclaimed the champion potato grower of the world. I offer his family my respects.
The nickel industry which is found in our riding, also in the riding of Sudbury, produces 75 per cent of the world's nickel. The population of the area is most cosmopolitan. The hon. member for Parkdale in his remarks the other day referred to the fact, which I respect very much, that the Conservative party in this house is composed of hon. members of at least five different racial origins. In my riding I may say I was supported by people of at least 40 different racial origins whose support I deeply appreciate.
The people in my area are worried about the present status of our economy and are suffering as a result of the present recession. If this government were to bring our economy back to the standard of a year ago I am
The Address-Mr. Godin convinced that it would solve approximately 80 per cent of our problems. May I refer to the fact that four mines in the Nickel Belt district have closed down within the last six months, with resultant hardship for the people in our area.
We have many fine local institutions in Nickel Belt, but there are no hospitals. There are, however, four hospitals in the immediate vicinity, the district of Sudbury. This situation is perhaps understandable, since the growth of our region necessarily took place around the metropolitan area of Sudbury, but I hope that before too long it will ibe possible to establish a hospital in the district of Nickel Belt. As hon. members may know, Canada's newest university is the University of Sudbury. I am proud to state that recently this institution purchased a $500,000 campus site in the district of Nickel Belt and in this aspect of our social life the Nickel Belt district has made an advance beyond the district of Sudbury.
As the representative of my riding and one who is interested in the subject of education I was surprised to realize that the speech from the throne contained no reference to the problem of higher education. It is well known today in Canada and possibly throughout the world that the standards of higher education in this country have not reached the levels that are merited. Canadian standards of higher education cannot be compared with those which obtain in certain unfriendly countries. I regret that the federal government is not prepared either to assist students who would like to specialize through better facilities for higher education or to assist educational institutions themselves without, of course, infringing on the autonomy of the provinces in this field granted under the British North America Act.
I urge the government to consider making contributions to the cost of establishing universities, and I trust that other opportunities will be afforded me at which time I can plead for assistance on behalf of our institution in Nickel Belt.
I am pleased to inform the house that the new federal building commenced some three years ago in the city of Sudbury has been completed and is rapidly being occupied. This building is a source of pride to all those in the area. I am also pleased to note that the project of constructing an armoury in Sudbury for the purpose of providing facilities for our militia and army is now proceeding. Some two years ago when I was a member of the planning board of that city I recall that the difficulty was in finding a proper site for the new armoury. Through the generosity of a local citizen a proper
454	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Godin site was acquired and donated for this purpose; and I intend, of course, to assist the minister with the forthcoming project in any way I can.
I am slightly embarrassed to note that one other project in Nickel Belt which would greatly assist the active tourist trade there has been forgotten by the present government. I refer to the construction of a dock on the French river. I feel it is my duty as the representative of the people of Nickel Belt to press for the completion of this project for which appropriations of money were granted some two years ago and the construction of which was to be commenced. I trust the dock will be built under a Conservative administration in the same way it would have been under a Liberal administration.
I have read the speech from the throne and listened to the many addresses that have been made in this house. I know that my constituents will be amazed and disheartened when I inform them of the slowness of operation of the government, and especially the confusion of the government in dealing with the problems at hand. I made reference earlier to the fact that we in the Nickel Belt district rely on the continued prosperity which this country has known for our own development. It is obvious to me at this time that a high degree of confusion exists within the government as to how to solve the problems confronting it. Indeed, I cannot resist observing that a marked degree of confusion exists on the part of the government in assessing one of the major problems in Canada today, recession. I wish to refer hon. members to a statement made by the Prime Minister. I trust that everyone remembers this. When the last election campaign commenced the Prime Minister, assisted by his candidates told the Canadian public that the Liberals were prophets of doom; that they were falsifying unemployment figures and that there was no such thing as unemployment in Canada. From coast to coast Canadians listened to that type of propaganda for some two weeks, until those who were without television sets and had to visit their neighbours' homes to watch television, because they had lost their jobs and their television sets were repossessed informed the Conservative group that it was not so; that the situation was not of a mere seasonal character.
Then came the greatest turnabout on the part of the Prime Minister that this country has ever seen. Then we heard these words: "It is true, my dear fellow Canadians, that there is a recession in this country at the present time, but the fault lies with the


Liberals if we did not know it". We all recall the story of the secret letter and document. The Conservatives admitted that they should have known from the Liberal group what the conditions were in this country. This, I feel, only added to the confusion, and explains why the government is not capable of solving the problem in Canada today.
This secret letter and document were apparently written by some expert on finance about April or March previous to the general election of June, 1957. If there is any remark to make about this document written by an employee of the government it may be this. I understand and I am told that many economists were asked to inform the government as to the situation. I am told that many specialists informed the government that things looked good ahead. Of course there was this one letter in which there was one single little paragraph which made reference to a possible recession.
The argument is simple, Mr. Speaker. Possibly those specialists who were asked to make a survey for the government took into consideration the forthcoming election in June. Any specialist who wished to give a proper opinion would take such a major fact into consideration and, of course, those who wrote that good times were ahead possibly had in their minds the fact-and it was easy to believe-that the Liberals would be re-elected. Of course it is also easy to believe that this one man who wrote this paragraph about the recession had made up his mind that the Conservatives would be taking over in June. He was right, and the recession came along.
There is some confusion as to the problem and also the policy. May I refer hon. members to the policy of the Conservative government to divert 15 per cent of our trade from the United States to the United Kingdom. Hon. members will recall the squeezing and wiggling the Prime Minister had to perform the other day to try to get out of the claws of the Leader of the Opposition when this problem was put to the Prime Minister. As a Canadian I must believe what the Conservatives say about themselves. I am absolutely convinced as a Canadian and as a newcomer to this house, Mr. Speaker, that it was definitely the policy of the Conservative government to divert 15 per cent of our trade from the United States to Great Britain. May I say that the confusion will be greater, now that the Prime Minister has stated or tried to state that it is no longer the policy of the Conservative government, when we see all the Conservatives vote favouring the diversion of 15 per cent of our trade from the United States to the United Kingdom.

It is obvious to all of us that the confusion can be found among the Conservative members of this house. Just a few days ago we were made aware of that confusion when the Secretary of State for External Affairs stood up in this house and said that the agreement to be signed with the United States would not be placed before this house. The very next morning, however, when questioned by the Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister denied this and said the agreement would be placed before the house for debate. Such confusion is obvious to at least the newcomers.
Very recently the hon. member for Resti-gouche-Madawaska spoke in this house, and I as a newcomer sincerely felt that the hon. member was perhaps sitting on the wrong side of the house when he made his speech. I recall that he was constantly applauded by members of the opposition. He criticized the government, and I was amazed when informed that he formed part of the government group.
Confusion is also found, Mr. Speaker, in the fact that the program laid down by this government does not contain proper remedies to deal with the unemployment in this country. In the last two weeks we have discussed two major matters, namely an extension of unemployment benefits and the provision of moneys for the construction of houses under the National Housing Act. The first measure, the extension of benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, does not bring about a solution to unemployment; this should be made clear.
Unemployment insurance was placed on the statute books by a Liberal regime. The history of this country will show how one party has done so much to protect its people from the administration of another party. It is true that some years ago unemployment insurance was introduced by the Liberal party and for many years funds have been accumulated, for what purpose? To protect the people of Canada against future possible Conservative administrations. That is what we witness in Canada in 1958. We are asked to extend the time of those benefits, and we Liberals are pleased to support the same. We are prepared to give our people all the protection they can receive against the present administration.
May I refer the house to the problems which municipalities are facing today. In making this reference I may state that there is one Canadian who is much involved in the present situation in Canada today, and he is the small home owner. Taxes in our municipalities are much too heavy. There is a reason for this. We realize that when confederation came about the problems were not
The Address-Mr. Godin what they are today. Our standard of living has greatly risen. If we have some knowledge of municipal problems we all realize that our municipalities are giving themselves, and rightly so, many services which were unknown years ago and which are now part and parcel of municipal activities. One example is the playground services for which municipalities are paying today.
Such facilities should be provided, but they are an added expense which was absolutely unknown in years gone by. In the province of Ontario there is a statute permitting the construction of arenas and community centres which permits municipalities to provide these services, but a possible informal meeting with the municipalities is not in itself a solution to the problem and there are two reasons why I so think. To provide under agreement for moneys to go from the federal government to the provinces and then also by agreement from the provinces to the municipalities is not the answer. In the first place we will only add expense to the present high cost of municipal administration.
In that regard I should like to refer to an editorial that appeared in the Sudbury Daily Star of May 24. Regardless of the political affiliation of the newspaper I subscribe to the view expressed in the editorial as it quotes the Montreal Star in these words:
Municipalities everywhere have gone about as far as they should go in the field of real estate taxation, the principal source of local government income since confederation.
If the federal government enters into an agreement with a province and the province enters into agreements with the municipalities, in every case the provincial government will only pay part of the cost of the undertaking. Therefore every time this occurs the municipality is burdened with additional expenses.
A moment ago I referred to the community centres act. As a member of the city council of Sudbury some years ago I recall people on the streets talked about this statute and wanted the city of Sudbury to build an arena coupled with an auditorium for concerts and such. Upon checking the act it was found by the members of the city council that if a municipality undertook to build an addition to an arena to provide for an auditorium the provincial government would grant the municipality $5,000. We all knew that an auditorium of the type contemplated would cost at least $150,000; therefore to comply with the request of those citizens who were asking for an auditorium would have meant that the city would have been faced with a further expenditure of $145,000.
That occurs all down the line. That is why the principle is wrong. The principle of

The Address-Mr. Godin granting municipalities money by way of provincial agreement is also wrong because the citizens of the municipality lose their autonomy. They are the ones who know what services are required. The speech from the throne makes reference to services and works. The people know what services are required, and they are definitely not the same from one municipality to another.
With higher governments dealing with the problems of small municipalities only certain types of works will be approved under the present scheme. Therefore we will see many small municipalities throughout Canada undertaking certain endeavours that possibly they would not otherwise undertake, for these municipalities will want to share in the benefits under the program proposed by the government. In my opinion the man who should decide what services are required for the community is the land owner.
There is a simple way for the federal government to return funds to the municipal rate payer, and it is not by way of provincial agreements. May I suggest that a tax deduction could be allowed from income for municipal taxation payments. This may surprise many, but I see a lot of merit in it. The other day I read an article in Le Devoir of Montreal in which it was stated that the plan to provide additional money for housing in no way solves the real situation. The real truth is that the ordinary Canadian cannot afford the type of home, the construction of which the government is trying to encourage under the National Housing Act. That is the main problem.
In this regard I am pleased to have the support of the council of Neelon and Garson, the largest municipality in my riding. I understand they have prepared a brief which is to be or has been sent to all members of the house. I suggest that the same principle could be applied that is used with regard to the medical expenses of the income taxpayer. The taxpayer is allowed to deduct from income medical expenses above a certain percentage of what he earns. I feel that we would obviate much red tape if the same principle were applied to property taxes and income tax, and at the same time we would strike at high taxation on the homes of workers and the high rate of interest which the workers cannot afford.
Under the National Housing Act a $14,000 home with a $11,000 mortgage costs a lot of money to maintain. We all realize that interest alone amounts to over $700. Then there are the taxes amounting to $500 or $600, in some cases. It is well known that a man cannot afford to own a home if it costs him more than 25 per cent of his income. If we


make the necessary calculations it is obvious that the ordinary worker earning $3,500 or $4,000 a year cannot afford a home which costs him nearly $200 a month.
Therefore I suggest that when Canadians are making out their income tax returns they should be able to attach their municipal tax and interest receipts and claim exemption over and above a certain percentage of their income. After the matter had been studied that percentage could perhaps be set at 2 per cent. Then he would be able to claim the difference between 2 per cent of his income and the amount he had paid in taxes and interest on his home.
This would obviate all the checking which might have to be done and the arrangements which might have to be made with the provinces and in turn with the municipalities under the proposed agreements. The man on the street would have in his pocket the amount of money required to meet the interest charge and taxes on his home and would be able to meet his taxes for the succeeding year. It would also help to obviate the problem faced by many of our smaller municipalities that are having great difficulties in collecting taxes. If such a procedure were implemented it is likely the taxpayers would pay their taxes promptly so they would have their receipt enabling them to make a deduction from income in the same way they are permitted for medical expenses.
I realize that this suggestion may be a surprising one, but I believe it should be adopted in order to safeguard the autonomy of our municipalities, to permit them to undertake those projects which they feel are necessary in their communities, and to provide relief to the average home owner. We all want as many Canadians as possible to own their homes. That is the object of the National Housing Act, but today only those people interested in the building and sale of homes are making use of the act because the ordinary worker cannot afford to assume the maintenance expenses which the act places upon the shoulders of the Canadian people.
I believe that if such a plan were adopted it would sufficiently reduce the tax on people owning homes. I also suggest that a ceiling might be placed on the amount they could claim, so that the person owning a $50,000 or $75,000 home would not benefit. The ceiling might be set at $500 as the greatest amount that could be claimed. This provision would have a beneficial effect if it were made to those people who require assistance, and not to those who do not.
I realize that if our Canadian people are faced with such a problem it arises mainly because of the fast Canadian growth. There

is no doubt about that fact. It is true in my riding. My riding is greatly affected especially so as a result of the difficult rocky terrain in our area. It is undoubtedly true, Mr. Speaker, that it is costlier to build services in certain municipalities than it is in others. Services such as those in connection with sewers and so on are more costly in some municipalities than in others.
Certain municipalities are located in places where local improvement costs bear heavily. By deducting in proportion as stated the government would assist in equalizing the benefits to all Canadians. Those people living in my riding and interested in the mining industry cannot very well build their homes on other soil; they must build within the mountains. They have no choice in the matter. That is where they must live. It should therefore be obvious to every one that a method of exempting the taxpayer up to a certain amount would necessarily be beneficial.

Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset to congratulate you upon your re-election as Speaker of the House of Commons.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, the distinguished and impartial manner in which you have discharged your duties in the past shows that you deserve this rare and seldom-bestowed honour of being re-elected Speaker of this house.
(Translation):
I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) on his appointment to the post of Deputy Speaker of the house.
(Text):
I should also like to congratulate the Prime Minister for the unequivocal approval his government and his party received on March 31. His popularity is such, Mr. Speaker, that even the province of Quebec, reputed to be the impregnable fortress of Liberalism, recognized in him the true representative of this new Canadian spirit of unity and equality which he has been advocating since being elected to this house.
In my own constituency of Gaspe his devotion to the well-being of every Canadian citizen made such an impression that I had the privilege of being re-elected by the sweeping majority of nearly 5,000 votes, while a year ago I had barely slipped through by 67 votes.
The Address-Mr. English (Translation):
In my constituency, as in so many others, I believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) has been rewarded for a political career entirely devoted to the promotion of the best interests of this nation.
I also congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafre-niere) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. His victory bears witness to the ascendancy of that new spirit which the Prime Minister has infused into Canadian politics and the repudiation of undesirable methods in the discussion of public affairs.
(Text):
I should also like to congratulate the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) who has espoused with such eloquence and authority the cause of the new frontiers of our immense country.
( Translation):
I should like also to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. O'Hurley) and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) on their appointment to the functions of Minister of Defence Production and Secretary of State respectively.
Mr. Speaker, if my constituency represents one of the oldest sections of Canadian territory, since Jacques Cartier landed there in 1534, it has some points of resemblance, on the other hand, with the Yukon territory. It is indeed one of the most picturesque areas of Canada. It is also, alas!, one whose immense resources are least known and developed. It can be stated, Mr. Speaker, that the Gaspe peninsula is undoubtedly, together with the maritime provinces, one of the under-developed areas of Canada.
Its population is rich in qualities and energy but poor financially, for this reason that the Gaspe peninsula has remained, for too long a time, the terra incognita of the province of Quebec. And yet it would take so little to make this area prosperous.
Similar causes result in similar effects. If the maritimes do not fully share in the country's prosperity, it is because of failure to develop their national resources, and because little was done to give them adequate means of communication. Gaspe is in the same position.
At this point I have to admit that the "electric power" of which there is no source in Gaspe itself, is now distributed throughout the peninsula, thanks to the development of resources on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. I also recognize that the province of Quebec made a generous effort to give roads to Gaspesia. But in either case the attempt is definitely inadequate. It is now up to this country's government to provide
458	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. English the auxiliary assistance expected from its new policy regarding the development of national resources.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) have already had submitted to them a project which is close to the hearts of every Gaspesian, the extension of the railway line from Matane to Ste. Anne des Monts. Construction of this line would enable an entire coastal area in Gaspe to develop abundant forest and mining resources which have so far remained untapped because of the lack of economic communications.
Mr. Speaker, I find it hard to understand why an area such as this has so long suffered neglect. For over 50 years now every succeeding government has used Gaspe as a political football, at each succeeding election.
It has always been the same thing. There has always been promise of a railway joining Matane to Ste. Anne des Monts and, later, Murdochville to Gaspe.
It will be quite impossible to develop that part of our country unless Gaspe is provided with a railway. Gaspe is one of the areas which suffers most as a result. To begin with, Mr. Speaker, it has no industries except fishing and logging. It is altogether impossible to interest industry in setting up plants in Gaspe because of the lack of railroads.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, I had always been given to understand that the railway preceded progress, instead of it being the other way round. I have already made requests in this regard; I spoke about it last session. I am taking it up today and will keep doing so as long as I have not obtained the building of this railway.
Mr. Speaker, every day I get more than 100 to 125 letters. My constituency is an extremely large one. In fact, it extends over 320 miles, just about the distance between Ottawa and Quebec. Because there is no industry in the area, and because the unfortunate people who live in my constituency cannot find work there, they write to me about their problems. And I don't blame them. I repeat what I said a moment ago; that railways are indispensable to that area. For the moment we are asking for the construction of a line approximately 47 miles long. It seems to me that that is not asking too much. Surely the people of Gaspe are entitled to ask for the construction of that line from Matane to Ste. Anne des Monts. If the line were constructed, we are convinced that we could interest businessmen in bringing industry to the area.
I have met Gaspe businessmen who would be quite willing to set up a pulp and paper


industry and newsprint industry at Ste. Anne des Monts. I have already met businessmen who would be interested to set up a chips factory. However, all such projects are out of the question for the moment since motor transportation between Ste. Anne des Monts and Matane would be far too expensive. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the present government for once will take heed of those people who, at this time, are in unfortunate circumstances. They are not asking for charity; they are simply demanding their share of the national income.
Mr. Speaker, the people of Gaspe pay taxes like those of any other area. The only difference is that they cannot benefit from the social legislation enacted by the previous government and by this government.
There is talk of making a considerable amount of money, namely $300 million, available for housing. This is of no benefit to my particular constituency. Insurance companies are not interested in lending money there for the construction of houses because they find the Gaspe peninsula too remote from large centres. The people of my constituency cannot take advantage of this beneficial legislation.
There are other excellent social laws but, when it comes to my constituency, they cannot be applied the same as elsewhere.
Let us take for example the matter of pensions to disabled persons. Well, as I said a minute ago, there are only two industries in the Gaspe peninsula: fishing and logging. If a man working in one or the other of these two industries has the misfortune of losing a leg or an arm, there is no other industry where he could, like city workers, find a job as an elevator operator or as a night watchman in a factory or somewhere else. Yet, the percentage of disabled is the same among the people of Gaspe as among city people. And the Gaspe people are told that a 25 or 30 per cent loss of capacity is insufficient to entitle them to the disability pension. On the other hand, a city worker who has got only one leg or one arm can more readily find a job in some other industry. The fisherman who has the misfortune of losing an arm or a leg can no longer practise his trade. Moreover, he can certainly not cut wood in the bush. What then is there left for him to do? Just sit down and wait until he dies. It seems to me that, for once, the voice of Gaspe should be heard and that every member in this house should co-operate to give that part of our country what these unfortunate people have been requesting for so many years.
Mr. Speaker, the implementation of that project which I have just mentioned not only would improve to a substantial degree

the commercial relationships between Gaspe and the north shore of the river, but it would prove to be a boom to the economic life of the peninsula.
The existence of a railway line in the neigbourhood of Ste. Anne des Monts would be sufficient to bring in many mining and industrial concerns which would create jobs in the Gaspe peninsula and help alleviate unemployment there. Too many Gaspesians up to now have had to go out and seek jobs in large cities or more favoured areas. If they stayed at home, they could make their peninsula one of the most prosperous areas in the country. But then they need the tools to bring about such an industrial development.
The Ste. Anne des Monts railway line would be one such tool. The construction of modern harbours at Gaspe and Chandler would be another one. I am not revealing any strategic secrets, Mr. Speaker, when I recall that, during the last war, the port of Gaspe was one of the mainstays of our military security system in Canada. I sincerely believe that if the necessary amounts are spent there, the port of Gaspe, while continuing to play that role, if ever such an eventuality arises, could be the starting point of that economic recognition of the peninsula which the whole of Canada hopes for today. A modern harbour at Gaspe would mean for the neighbourhood the installation of new industries for the development of our maritime as well as of our forest resources; it would bring to an end the decidedly tragic isolation which is at present the lot of our population.
Besides the marvellous bay of Gaspe, there is also an industrial and maritime centre, that of Chandler, which, given a little assistance, could be further extended. I know, Mr. Speaker, that, in this case also, a project for the extension of port facilities has been referred to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees). Every Gaspesian is awaiting the outcome anxiously. If Chandler were turned into a real seaport, the northern part of the Gaspe peninsula would be sure of getting all its winter suplies, local industries would benefit from better and cheaper means of transportation, the fishing industry could be extended and the construction of fishing boats could be undertaken on a larger scale. Finally, let us not forget that those are our most valuable human resources which can be used for the production of new wealth.
Three great resources can guarantee the prosperity of the Gaspe peninsula: the forest, the mines and the sea. Now then, at the present time none of those resources are properly worked or developed because the Gaspe peninsula lacks the tools of economic conquest. Let us then supply the peninsula 57071-3-301
The Address-Mr. English with those tools, and at the same time we will put an end to the complaints of courageous Canadians who are asking for the same chance that others are getting of being a powerful asset in the confederation.
All along the shore of the Gaspe peninsula there are abundant fishing grounds, but how can the rest of the country be expected to benefit by them when the peninsula does not have the communications required to reach the large markets under conditions which would allow it to meet competition.
In the interior of the Gaspe peninsula, a part of our rich forests is still undeveloped. As for the remainder, poor transport facilities prevent the farmers from selling their pulpwood and lumber at reasonable prices. Even the Chandler paper mill has to send its products to Bathurst before shipping them to their normal markets, because ships cannot put into Chandler harbour. The companies no longer let them stop there, several ships having been lost -last year.
Consequently the raw materials bound for the larger centres are transported to New Brunswick.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if a seaport were built at Chandler, it would provide jobs to local men loading and unloading ships. The setting up of a port would eliminate considerable handling costs.
As far as mines are concerned, they are still waiting for a railroad to facilitate production and marketing at a reasonable cost.
Mr. Speaker, during the last election campaign, the hon. Prime Minister aroused an immense hope in the hearts of all Canadians when he spoke of the tremendous future he is contemplating for our country. To that future, the Gaspe peninsula wishes to contribute, since its people know, as well as others, the greatness of the mission entrusted to them.
Mr. Speaker, I shall now insert a few remarks on the fisheries of the Gaspe peninsula. Our fishermen have been victimized for many years. I have always been interested in our fishermen, because, about 20 years ago, I had the great pleasure to introduce the first fisheries co-operative in my native parish of Riviere-au-Renard, following a one-year course I attended in Antigonish, Nova Scotia, in order to study the position of fishermen. If their lot has now improved, it is due to that co-operative.
I am glad to hear my western colleagues' many representations on behalf of western farmers. I approve them and I am in favour

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to join with the other hon. members who have spoken before me in congratulating you on the high honour that has been conferred on you in your re-election as Speaker of this house. I believe we are particularly fortunate in the fact that your guidance of our deliberations will be helpful and fair, as was our experience in the previous parliament.
I compliment, too, the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne in the opening of the twenty-fourth parliament. I also congratulate the Prime Minister and the government on the tremendous majority acquired through the people's mandate on March 31. Their responsibilities in the tasks ahead are heavy, and the fact that their numbers are great brings, I believe, an added burden to the task of fair and representative government.
As opposition members we too have great responsibilities, not as obstructionists but in the spirit of true Canadianism to work for Canada's continued prosperity through the deliberations of this house. We of the Liberal

party are very fortunate indeed to have as our leader the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) who is recognized throughout the world as an outstanding statesman and a loyal and devoted Canadian.
As hon. members are well aware, much of the important legislation scheduled to be brought forward this session will be a followup of legislation initiated or given earlier consideration by the former Liberal government, namely all the fine welfare measures; the completion and expansion of avenues of transportation already under way such as the St. Lawrence seaway, which is now practically an accomplished project and which Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth has graciously consented to officially open next year; airports and air travel facilities; the trans-Canada highway; equalized distribution of wealth to the provinces-and I sincerely hope that the term "equalization" will continue to hold prominence in this important matter- health insurance, the foundation of which was started a decade ago by the former Liberal government through a constructive program of hospital and health grants making it possible for the plan to be implemented in the near future.
I suggest that there appears to be no considered plan in the legislation forecast designed to bring relief for unemployment, nor has any policy been proposed to bolster Canada's failing economy at this time. In the main estimates brought down by the Minister of Finance a few days ago there were expenditures indicating an increase in practically every department of government, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration being the one exception. If the increases were extended largely to public works projects and items of relief for unemployment, then I believe it would be more constructive; but the estimates reveal no special program to relieve unemployment.
Considerable emphasis is being laid by hon. members of the government on the increased payments which the government authorized through the many welfare measures initiated by the former Liberal government. I submit that this is not building for the future; it is merely digging into the coffers of the federal treasury, the taxpayers' money. Such a policy is not constructive because it gives no indication of an effort to even maintain, much less improve, Canada's economic structure, which is the base from which these benefits were made possible. The present system is nonproductive and self-defeating. We cannot hope to maintain these benefits for Canadians except through continued increases in the national income.
All these welfare measures, including unemployment insurance, were designed by

the former Liberal government, not to provide a livelihood for Canadians but as a means of assistance to the handicapped and afflicted as well to alleviate the fear of old age dependence. As far as unemployment insurance is concerned, this was designed as a protective measure for the worker, as a provision for maintenance at such times when for one reason or another he found himself temporarily out of employment. At this time last year the reserve in the unemployment insurance fund stood at something like $300 million. It would be very interesting to know the present financial status of this fund considering the strain that has been put on it in the last several months and the consequent decrease in contributions to maintain it.
The Conservative government has been in power for almost one whole year. It has been a year of stalemate as far as Canada's economic progress is concerned. National income remained practically static last year. The forecast for the current year is that conditions will remain much the same, and as a matter of fact in the final analysis revenues may be down, as our total production is not increasing in comparison with our increasing population and general commitments.
Admitted in the speech from the throne is the fact that Canada is suffering from a situation which is both recessional and inflationary. Neither of these situations is healthy and one must ask himself where is the remedy. Recently an hon. member on the government side of the house dealt with the recession problem by quoting the increased payments that have been made through welfare measures. In his summary, however, he did not mention the great benefit of family allowances, which of course completely missed consideration when the Conservatives were authorizing increases in other benefits. This is consistent with the fact that the bill was strenuously opposed by some hon. members of the Conservative party when it was introduced in 1944, and had no place in the program set out at the Conservative national convention in 1956. Yet this benefit, which is available to all Canadian families, has provided them with approximately $4 billion since its inception in 1944.
