Taking one year's payments as a concrete example, nearly $4 million was distributed for the benefit of Canadian children in the year 1956-57. The hon. member further emphasized the proposed extension of periods for payment of unemployment insurance as another remedy. We endorse this action, of course, but will it help unemployment? In reality it does nothing to relieve the situation.
The splendid Liberal program of welfare benefits has been and is at the present time of utmost value to the Canadian people. These measures were designed by the former Liberal government with that object in mind, but they were never intended to carry the country's economy. They were made possible because of wise administration which produced increasingly greater national revenues, and I submit that this same system is still necessary for the continued well-being of our people.
The fault-as fault there must be, Mr. Speaker-lies with our present government. During the election campaign the Minister of Trade and Commerce is quoted as having made the statement that because capital investment for the year 1957-58 would equal that of the previous year we had nothing to worry about. The same situation seems to apply in the forecasts for capital investment for the current year, 1958-59. This type of figuring indicates stagnation, and bears a very close resemblance to the figures of the early thirties.
We see nothing in the legislation forecast which would encourage capital investment, either domestic or foreign. I believe it is essential to keep in mind that during our periods of progress a large part of our national income was derived from capital investment. I am afraid the extravagant promises of the last two election campaigns have rapidly dissipated the faith of prospective investors.
While Liberal policy has always been one of trade expansion, Conservative policy seems to be one of trade diversion. Certainly the suggestion of diversion of trade from our
462	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Nixon best customer, the United States, has done nothing to strengthen Canada's economic position. Apart from the fact that it has brought about retaliatory cut-backs in exports to that country, it has alienated the friendliness of our good neighbour to the south and may further be the cause of increased tariff walls which will still more adversely affect our imports. Canada is in need of this market as the most readily accessible and natural field for those products which Canadians have to sell. Trade, of course, is the keynote to progress. Great productivity can only be profitable when markets are available, and it is only by wise trade and tariff arrangements that this can be accomplished.
I should like now to refer briefly to my riding of Algoma West, which I have had the honour to represent in this house for the past 18 years. Apart from the great Algoma Steel mills and their subsidiary mining companies, which provide much of the industry in Algoma West, forest and farm products contribute considerably to the production of the area and a thriving business is carried on by commercial fishermen; but lake Superior fishermen have problems the same as any other people, Mr. Speaker. One of the problems that is causing great concern is the heavy destruction of lake trout by the sea lamprey. I sincerely trust that the Department of Fisheries will continue with the program started a few years ago in co-operation with the province to cope with this difficult and serious matter.
I might mention here, Mr. Speaker, that the Department of Public Works is already investigating another difficulty being encountered by some of those fishermen owing to the obstruction to the harbour on the Montreal river some 80 miles north of Sault Ste. Marie. The fault is a gravel bar which is continually reforming, and it is my hope that early and permanent remedies may be applied in this instance, as it is the only harbour available to commercial fishermen and other boatmen for 30 miles on either side of the Montreal river. Its present condition is not only a detriment to the financial welfare of the fishermen, but the fact that the harbour is inaccessible at the present time might easily be the cause of loss of life to the fishermen and other boatmen owing to the danger of turbulent storms on lake Superior.
Sault Ste. Marie is the largest urban centre in my riding. It was in 1622 that two French explorers, Brule and Grenolle, visited the rapids at this point and gave them the name of Sault du Gaston. It was in 1762 that a British garrison took possession of the fort. The region was under British rule until 1867, when the act of confederation created Canada.


Earlier, under French rule, Sault Ste. Marie became the central fur market of the northwest. In 1797-98 the first Sault canal was built, with a lock large enough to take the largest freight canoe. This lock still stands to remind us of the hardships of the early travellers. Preserved, too, is the old Hudson's Bay blockhouse, telling of the days when fur trading was an armed affair.
As an indication of progress, four separate locks, of proportions sufficient to accommodate ocean-going vessels, now exist in the St. Mary's river, linking lake Huron with lake Superior. Next year these canals will form part of the great St. Lawrence seaway which will continue on to the great lakes. When it is realized that more tonnage passes through the locks at Sault Ste. Marie in a season than passes in 12 months through the Panama, the Suez, the Manchester and Kiel canals combined, one can get some idea of what the opening of this river has meant to the economy of our country.
In view of the developments described I have previously taken up in person with the Department of Transport the fact that there may be need some day for an additional lock on the Canadian side of the St. Mary's river in order to accommodate the increased traffic when the St. Lawrence seaway is opened up. The time has now come to look into the development of such a project. It would create employment when jobs are urgently needed, and it would prove an asset to the navigation facilities of this busy waterway.
Additional harbour facilities are also required at the Sault. This need was recognized by the former Liberal government. A survey was made and reports are on hand in the Department of Public Works. During the past year the question has been given some consideration by the present government. A suitable site is available, and I would ask the government to recognize this as a much needed improvement and urge them to give it their immediate consideration. Also, under the former Liberal government land was purchased for the building of an airport at Sault Ste. Marie. Surveys were made and the field is now being constructed. I have every faith that the government will proceed quickly with this project.
The riding of Algoma West, and in fact the whole district of Algoma, abounds in historic sites due, no doubt, to the early settlement of this part of the country. In the Sault Ste. Marie district there are two special landmarks of historic interest, both of which are well known to the national historic sites division of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I refer in the first instance to Fort St. Joseph,

located on St. Joseph's island east of Sault Ste. Marie. In 1783 this was a fur-trading fort built by the Northwest company. In 1796 British troops took it over as a military establishment. Today parts of three buildings and the military cemetery still remain. Laid out as a park and bird sanctuary, this is of considerable interest to tourists. The main fort and the grounds are in fairly good condition, and I have recently approached the department requesting that certain items be given attention. I believe it is in the interests of our national background that such an historic landmark as Fort St. Joseph be preserved and further improved.
The other landmark is located in Sault Ste. Marie and is known there as the old stone house. Beginning with the early 1800's mention is repeatedly made of an elegant house on the north bank of the St. Mary's river, below the rapids. The house was built in 1814 by a fur trader. I understand it is the oldest house in existence north of Toronto. I could describe in some detail the workmanship and architecture which this house displays and also the part it played in the lives of the fur traders and the British settlement which followed Captain Roberts in his military campaigns in the early 1800's.
All details in connection with this house are on file in the national historic sites division. Representations have been made that the national interest is involved, and an appeal has been made to the federal government for assistance in the preservation of this historic monument to early Canadian history and culture. I hope this historic old house will receive the sponsorship of the national historic sites division, and that special consideration will be given this request by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
In closing I might say that the district of Algoma West has a tremendous attraction for tourists and sportsmen, and acts as a distributor of visitors from the United States to all parts of Canada. Sault Ste. Marie is the only port of entry to Canada from the United States between Sarnia on the east and the head of the lakes on the west, a distance of about 500 miles each way. Well maintained highways lead directly to the Sault and the stupendous new bridge built by the state of Michigan across the straits of Mackinaw, officially opened last fall, will greatly increase traffic during the coming tourist season.
It is interesting to note that within a day's drive of the Sault there is an American population of nearly 40 million people. We have every hope that an international bridge will soon be built between the Michigan Sault and the Canadian Sault, which will further facilitate travel. At the Sault there is a
The Address-Mr. MacEwan direct traffic connection with the trans-Canada highway. The lake Superior link of the highway, now under construction along the north shore of lake Superior, will go through the Michipicoten area, a very important section of my riding because of the rich iron ore potential and the natural resources of the district.
While this area has been well served for many years by the Algoma Central Railway, the linking of the district with the trans-Canada highway will mean the realization of a dream that its residents have had for many years, namely the provision of adequate motor transport facilities; and with the development of resources already in sight, plus potential discoveries, it may well prove to be the gateway to a world of new wealth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the opportunity today to take part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. During the last session of parliament I did not have the opportunity to do so. At this time I should like to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on your election as Speaker of the house. As others have said, I know from having been here during last session that you will carry on with fairness and impartiality befitting the high standing of Speaker of the House of Commons of Canada.
I should like to compliment the hon. member for Longueil (Mr. Sevigny), on his election as Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons. May I as a dour Scot from the historic Scottish county of Pictou salute the French speaking members of the house and attempt to congratulate you in French, sir. (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate you on your re-election to the office of Speaker of the House of Commons. I also congratulate my good friend the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) on his election to the office of Deputy Speaker of the house. (Text):
At this time I should like to welcome to the house two hon. members with whom I attended that honourable college by the sea, Dalhousie University, in the person of the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Creag-han), with whom I roomed for two years at law school, and the hon. member for Inver-ness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan) who has joined us at this time. I should also like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen)-who also attended the college by the sea-of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
There are a few matters I should like to discuss with regard to certain things mentioned in the speech from the throne. The

The Address-Mr. MacEwan first is the reference to a bill of rights which is to be introduced at an early date. This measure is most important so far as the freedom of all Canadians is concerned, when we see in this day and age throughout the world transgressions upon freedom in many countries. I believe it is a most important matter, and I congratulate the government on this announcement. We look forward to the introduction of the legislation.
Then there are the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Certain changes have already been made, and the speech from the throne indicates that other changes will be made at a later date. At this point I should like to refer to certain suggestions and submissions made to me by the united steelworkers of America, local 1231, of Trenton, Nova Scotia. Before I came to Ottawa they submitted a brief to me, and I should like to refer to certain parts of it. They make the suggestion that it would be a good thing if a measure were introduced to increase the amount of unemployment insurance benefits. They point out that there should be an increase of at least 40 per cent in order to make larger benefits available to the workers of Canada under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I think this is something that could be taken into consideration by the government in the amendments which will come forward at a later date. The union points out in its brief that increased benefits would probably help to make more consumer money available in Canada.
Certainly we know that the benefits are not large, the greatest amount payable at this time being $30 a week. Hon. members will realize that with the cost of living today this amount will not go too far. I draw this matter to the attention of the government as one which could be readily considered in making changes in the legislation.
The changes in the National Housing Act are welcome. In discussing the matter last year in this house I said the government might consider accepting owner labour as part of the down payment for the purpose of loans under the act. I believe one hon. member also suggested during the resolution stage of the recent amendment that owner labour could be applied to more advanced stages in the building of a house.
The area I represent contains a number of smaller towns, the largest having a population of perhaps 11,000. I do not believe the National Housing Act has been used enough by the people in the area because of the fact that there seems to be a little too much red tape in obtaining loans. I think perhaps the red tape could be cut down somewhat and that there should be more publicity as

to the act and how it works, so that more people can take advantage of this important legislation.
Another matter dealt with in the speech from the throne had to do with expansion in the construction of airports and airstrips. Certainly this will be welcomed by the people of Canada, because we are living in an age of accelerated air transport and we should keep pace with the age in which we are living.
In my work as a barrister I have had something to do with criminal law and particularly the Ticket of Leave Act. I believe the setting up of a parole board as forecast in the speech from the throne is important. The Ticket of Leave Act has certainly had its place in the matter of parole, but in my opinion there have been a number of worthy cases which could have been more fully investigated. The matter is of great importance throughout the country, and a national board to deal with parole is a most important measure.
During the debate it has been most interesting to listen to members from various parts of Canada, from the Atlantic right through to the Pacific, from Newfoundland to British Columbia. I was particularly interested in listening to members from the western provinces, especially the province of Manitoba, and learning about the various problems they brought forward. I can say that I have an interest in the province of Manitoba, as some of my own relatives went west in the early days and settled around Brandon. I believe that some of them play a part in public life in the legislature of that province. I am therefore most interested in the speeches of those members from that province.
In the county of Pictou various types of industry are represented. In fact it is a constituency which involves almost every type of work. Among other things we have a car company which manufactures freight cars for the various railways in Canada. In that regard, in the submission which was made to me by the local union and which I am sure would be concurred in by the management of Eastern Car, which is part of A. V. Roe Limited, a former Dosco subsidiary, is the suggestion that the Canadian National railways could consider a carbuilding program to help the industry. I understand there are approximately 50,000 obsolete cars used by the Canadian National Railways. I would suggest that the transport department, along with the management of the Canadian National Railways, consider a car-building program instituted for a period of five years to help the various car plants in Canada.

This car work involves not only work on freight cars; it also involves various other allied trades in the county and indeed in the province and in the Dominion of Canada. There are other plants sharing it. There is the steel works which is next door which manufactures axles, and Maritime Steel and Foundries Limited, well known for its foundry work. It involves a great deal as far as labour is concerned and, as I understand it, as far as other plants are concerned in the immediate area and throughout the province.
Also in the constituency is the Pictou shipyard of Ferguson Industries Limited. I would submit that work should be placed in that area as well as in other parts of the province, and in the Atlantic provinces generally.
Among other things, a ferry was built by Ferguson Industries Limited, Pictou, that plies between Caribou on the mainland of Nova Scotia and Wood Island, Prince Edward Island; it is known as the Lord Selkirk. If it is not in operation at the present time it will soon go into service between those two points. It means a great deal as far as transport between the mainland of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island is concerned. After considering the help given and the size of this ferry, which is very modern, which will carry some 60 cars, and is much better than the ferry which formerly plied between those two points, I would ask the Department of Transport to look into the submission that another ferry be built for the area to help out the transportation problems. Every summer we see a number of cars, particularly tourist cars, lined up at the wharf at Caribou, and this has done a great deal to emphasize the fact that we need better facilities for this area.
We also appreciate greatly the passing at the last parliament of the Atlantic provinces power bill which involves subventions on coal going out of the maritimes for power use. This is something which is extremely helpful. It will mean cheaper power for industries within our area, within the province and within the Atlantic provinces.

I will answer the hon. member for Gloucester. As far as my own area is concerned, I believe he was in there during the last election campaign or during the past year; at least he passed through. If he would travel down to Trenton he would come to the Trenton power plant, which is now being enlarged; and of course it uses the coal of independent producers such as Greenwood Coal Company at Thor-burn. It definitely uses coal; I can assure him of that fact.
The Address-Mr. MacEwan
There is another point in connection with the subvention; the fact that these power plants of course will come into being and new industries cannot be set up immediately to use the extra power which will be available. This is a matter which was brought to my attention before leaving, namely the fact that some coal mined by the independent producers-I am not referring to A. V. Roe mines but the independent producers in the county-is sent out. I refer to Greenwood Coal Company in Thorburn and the Drummond Coal Company in Westville, Nova Scotia. The amount sent out depends on the market in Halifax. Something might be done, I submit-and this suggestion has been made-in the way of freight subventions to the C.N.R. to help provide markets for these independent producers.
I believe that throughout the province there are other independent producers which this step would help out greatly. I submit that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys could perhaps bring this matter to the attention of the dominion coal board, and that it is something which should be considered along with other measures to help our coal industry.
We have our Atlantic provinces power bill which will help us to have cheaper power as far as our provinces are concerned. There is something which should be considered by the government, I submit, namely some change as far as freight rates are concerned. I know this matter has been brought to the attention of this house a good many times in the past. However, I believe that with new industry, with an abundance of cheap power, and with help in our freight rates we can progress as we should in our province and indeed in all the Atlantic provinces.
Under Industrial Estates Limited, a crown company of the province of Nova Scotia, we have been able to secure an Italian textile industry to set up in our county of Pictou this fall. I hope that others will follow suit. I hope this is only the beginning of a great economic step forward for our province.
In our county of Pictou we also have farming carried on. In the speech from the throne I note that mention is made of the fact that changes will be made in the Canadian Farm Loan Act. In the province of Nova Scotia a royal commission was set up, and it reported on the matter of loans and farming generally in the province. Among other recommendations it submitted was that there should be changes in the Canadian Farm Loan Act in order to make it possible for young farmers to get loans readily from the Canadian farm loan board.

The Address-Mr. MacEwan According to the submission to the commission by the farmers' federation of Nova Scotia, the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture, the Canadian Farm Loan Act seemed to be so framed as to help farmers perhaps in the western part of Canada in larger tracts of land. They submitted that most loans now are obtained under the Nova Scotia land settlement board, and that there should be changes in the Canadian Farm Loan Act in order to make it possible for smaller farmers to obtain loans. They must have the credit to commence their work and to set up their farms. I believe the government should take this matter into consideration.
We also have in the county fishing of various types carried on. As a result of the report of the royal commission which dealt with agriculture and fishing I hope that encouragement will be given to this industry also.
In the Atlantic area, speaking generally, we have the Atlantic provinces economic council, which is a body made up not just of politicians but of men from various types of work and various professions throughout the whole area. This APEC has been doing a good job, and I suggest that members from that area encourage them in their efforts. Among the things they have set up, of course, has been the shoe show last year in order to show the various types of shoes we produce, and also this year the food show exhibiting Atlantic products.
In my own area, if I might just mention it once more, we have the Hamilton factory which manufactures biscuits of various types. I have today received discouraging word to the effect that this plant will probably be shut down. During the last two election campaigns I visited this plant and became acquainted with its products, its workers and its management, and I must say that this is a particularly fine plant. The workers and management have always worked very well together, and I do hope that in addition to all possible efforts on my own part, every effort will be made to see that this fine little industry will not have to be closed down, as has happened in the case of some other industries, but that it will be able to continue to serve Pictou and Nova Scotia.
Among other measures mentioned in the speech from the throne is the setting up of a standing committee on veterans affairs. During the short time I have been actively engaged in politics many veterans have brought this matter to my attention, and I commend the minister and the government for having taken this most important step.
I Mr. MacEwan.]
We have heard many hon. members speak of other measures set forth in the speech from the throne, including the work to be done in the far north; and this, of course, is a step in the right direction. All these things are necessary for the future of our great country, of which, as each year advances, we as members of this House of Commons and members of the government party will be a part.
The people of Canada have given this party and this government an overwhelming majority, and I submit that it is up to the government and to each and every member of the party to see that such power is used as wisely as it should be. The people of our country have placed in the Prime Minister and the government a trust which I wholeheartedly believe has not been misplaced.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to see you in the chair this afternoon, because this gives me the opportunity to join hon. members who rose before me on all sides of the house, and tender my own congratulations. I do not see anything I could add to the praise already expressed, so I shall just say that it was amply deserved.
I also would join the other speakers in commending the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have carried out their task with great eloquence.
I also would congratulate the two new ministers from the province of Quebec, to whom I wish the best of luck in their new responsibilities, which I am sure, will end with this parliament.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago when I had occasion to speak in this house I made my remarks in English, but this afternoon I would like to make myself understood in French, because just a few minutes ago we had yet another opportunity to see that the French lessons given to some members are beginning to bear fruit and that some English speaking members are now able to say a few words in French. I hope they will not have any difficulty in following me. (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, in taking part this afternoon in the debate on the speech from the throne, I should like first of all to draw the government's attention to three questions of vital importance to the majority of the people in my constituency. I am sure these matters are also of the greatest interest to thousands of citizens in other districts of Canada.

I already had in the past the opportunity of discussing those problems right here in this house, but I think that, in view of the circumstances, it is good to turn back to them again today.
The first matter I should like to deal with concerns the shipbuilding industry. I shall deal with its present position and especially with its future. Many of us-and I would go as far as to say most of us-know that in my constituency of Levis, which I have been representing here for the last eighteen years, we have two important shipyards which, for hundreds of families in my constituency, and in other constituencies of the area, represent their sole livelihood. Incidentally it is the only heavy industry we have in the district.
The importance of keeping that industry in operation will therefore be readily appreciated. If its activities were curtailed, hundreds of men would be laid off who depend on this industry for a living and the support of their families. And if this sad situation came about, it would certainly likewise affect other districts where shipbuilding and repair are vitally important.
As we know, at the present time there are 17 major shipyards in Canada. They are located on the Atlantic coast, on the St. Lawrence in the province of Quebec, on the great lakes, and there are two or three other large ones in British Columbia. According to the latest figures I could get, at the end of March of this year those shipyards were employing over 15,000 men, and this figure of course does not include the other thousands of employees working in the industries which produce the necessary materials or machines for the building or repair of those ships.
Therefore I do not see that I should speak at great length on the necessity of keeping an industry such as this in operation at the present time in this country, either from an economic standpoint or for purposes of national defence. Hon. members who were sitting here when the last war broke out will remember how much taxpayers had to pay to put that industry back into full operation, at a time when it had slowed down, not to speak of the precious time lost, in the circumstances, in training a specialized labour force which was practically nonexistent.
It is recalled that during their peak war time activity, our shipyards were employing more than 75,000 workers. We are also proud to recall the efficient role played by our shipyards during the conflict, and their priceless contribution to the Allied victory.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, we are living in a somewhat precarious state of security,
The Address-Mr. Bourget with almost every country spending vast sums on defence, because no one knows when another conflict will break out. It is therefore necessary to remain constantly on the alert. If another war breaks out, more up-to-date arms will no doubt be used than during the last war. But nobody, I think, inside or outside this house will be able to deny that our navy will have an important part to play during a future war. The necessity of keeping up this essential industry so that it may be used without delay in case of a national emergency will therefore be conceded.
Ever since 1940, the naval shipyards in my riding have been quite busy, through contracts awarded first of all by the Department of National Defence, by the Department of Transport, and, in a lesser way, by private industry. Incidentally, I would like to point out to hon. members that, from 1949 to 1957, our two naval shipyards received contracts for an average of $16 million a year, for the construction and repair of government-owned vessels. I might also state, without any fear of contradiction that all other shipyards, whether in the Atlantic provinces, on the Pacific coast or on the great lakes, relied to a large extent on the generous help of the government in order to carry on.
Mr. Speaker, will the present government continue this precious help awarded by the federal authorities, and which, to my mind, is essential for the survival of this industry? I am no pessimist by nature, nor would I like to be one now, but judging from the statements made by some government members and the action taken by the government in the last few months, we are compelled to admit that the future of our shipyards is uncertain at present.
As a matter of fact, at the beginning of January, there were press reports to the effect that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) had stated that the government proposed to discontinue its shipbuilding program until such time as the possibility of building nuclear-propelled ships had been thoroughly considered. That policy aroused criticism in several papers and especially, of course, among shipbuilding associations. It was criticism based on serious arguments against the decision of the Minister of National Defence. One critic mentioned the opinion expressed by the Commander-in-chief of the NATO Atlantic fleet, Admiral Wright, who is said to have stated that there was a scarcity of ships and especially of submarine destroyers.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, how long it will take national defence experts to make a thorough study of the plans for the building of nuclear-propelled ships, but on the

The Address-Mr. Bourget other hand, I am sure that our shipyards will suffer through being deprived of the contracts granted them in years past by the Department of National Defence.
I hope the Department of National Defence and its experts will reconsider their decision, and that the shipbuilding program will be resumed. Even if they are not nuclear -propelled, the ships could easily be converted later on, at no great cost, according to the experts.
In the last few days, the future of our shipyards has become grimmer still. In fact, on Wednesday May 21, the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), in a statement made in this house, announced that the registration of eight ships of the Canadian National Steamships Limited had been transferred from Trinidad to Canada, and that they would shortly be put up for sale through advertisements in the press.
Needless to say, this announcement by the Minister of Transport caused much concern and disappointment among shipyard owners and employees. Indeed, these people, who relied on statements made by prominent representatives of the Conservative party, had been looking forward to a revival of the merchant navy now that the party has been returned to power.
Who does not recall, Mr. Speaker-especially those who have been here for several years-the promises made by the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green), at the time when he was accusing the previous government of having scuttled our merchant navy and was clamouring for its rebuilding? One may read on pages 7410 and 7411 of the Hansard report dated August 10, 1956 that he made the following statement in this house:
I do urge in all earnestness that the government delay no longer in adopting a policy which will put a Canadian flag deep sea fleet into being again.
And further on he said:
Canada is now in a position where she could have a modern merchant navy, and it is far more important to us now than it has ever been, particularly because of the development of the St. Lawrence seaway.
I do urge upon the minister not to be satisfied with the program he announced tonight as the great cure-all. This is only a stop-gap. I would ask him to see that his colleagues in the cabinet approve a policy which will favour the reappearance of a Canadian flag deep sea fleet.
A little later-and on a date which is not so very remote-i.e. on January 21, 1957, as appears on page 443 of Hansard, the minister said the following words:

On these four questions, the joint development of power projects, re-establishing the Canadian deep sea fleet, legislation for veterans and welfare legislation, the government as yet is offering no leadership. On these questions the speech from the throne is just one big blank.
And farther on he said:
I suggest that the government bestir itself and deal with these problems. There is no reason why these and other problems should be shelved. They should be dealt with this spring, and I can assure you-
And these are remarkable words, Mr. Speaker.
-that if they are not the new government which will take over this fall will deal with them promptly and effectively.
Besides, he was not the only one to call for a Canadian merchant navy, for if you read pages 7412 and 7413 of the official record for August 10, 1956, you will see that the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell), who represents a riding extremely interested in shipbuilding and repair, approved the remarks and wishes of his colleague.
As reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of November 13, 1957, the hon. Minister of Transport himself stated the following, in March 1955, before the Conservative women's Primrose club in Vancouver. I quote:
(Text):
In March 1955, Mr. Hees himself told a meeting of the Primrose Women's Conservative Club in Vancouver that ''do-nothing" policies of the Liberal government were "destroying" Canada's merchant marine. Mr. Hees said then, that the federal government should adopt a policy of developing and maintaining a strong nucleus of at least 50 oceangoing ships for foreign trade and to protect the country's supply lines in the event of a war.
(Translation):
As you can see from those statements, Mr. Speaker, our shipyard owners and employees were right when they were looking forward to a new era of prosperity, through the creation of the merchant navy so often promised by our friends opposite.
I am very sorry for their sake that their dream should have been shattered so soon. This serves to show up the Conservative party's swift about-face in this matter, as on many others. Indeed we now realize that when a party has to face reality and is itself responsible for solving problems, it does not always find it easy to solve them to everyone's satisfaction. As is often said among our people, Mr. Speaker, criticism is easy but art is difficult.
I trust however that the government will find some way to help that important industry survive and remain prosperous-and I

emphasize the word because our yards have been very active since the end of the last war-and I hope they will remain as prosperous as they were under a Liberal administration.
Mr. Speaker, the other matter which I would like to bring to the attention of the government, and more particularly to that of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) concerns railway employees.
For some time now many of these men have been living in uncertainty and fear following a series of lay-offs. They are wondering whether, in spite of their record of service of ten, twelve, fifteen or even eighteen years, they will not themselves be the next victims of these lay-offs in the very near future. For instance last fall, in the Levis division of my own constituency, thirty sections out of eighty were eliminated, adding forty people to the already long list of jobless.
At that time the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) and myself drew the matter to the attention of the Minister of Transport. After taking it up with the Canadian National Railways authorities the minister answered that nothing could be done. His answer, Mr. Speaker, I must admit, was in strange contrast to the speeches he made when he sat in opposition. It was in 1955, in Moncton, I think, that he stated that these layoffs were regrettable and quite unnecessary.
I must add that I feel particularly sorry for those railwaymen who lose their jobs. More than any other class of workers they find rehabilitation difficult and have a hard time finding new jobs in other industries. Having worked as specialists for years, they cannot easily obtain the same type of employment in other industries.
To be perfectly fair, Mr. Speaker, I will admit that technological changes, changes due to automation, are largely responsible for these lay-offs. On the other hand I do believe that the Minister of Transport, in co-operation with the management of the Canadian National Railways, could devise some way of keeping these men on the job.
One way in which it might be done would be for the railways to undertake themselves much of the work they farm out to private enterprise.
The time has come also, in my opinion, to implement the suggestion made by the leader of the Liberal party in favour of the immediate establishment of a National Advisory Board on Economic Development and Automation, made up of representatives of the labour, industry, agriculture and universities.
One of the essential functions of the board would be to study long term measures to
The Address-Mr. Bourget guarantee a high level of employment and to soften the impact of automation on labour, by developing rehabilitation programs to ensure a greater mobility of our labour force as well as by recommending other necessary steps.
Secondly, the board would be asked to set long term programs of investment and development to promote the continuing expansion of the Canadian economy and the maintenance of full employment.
Mr. Speaker, I humbly make this suggestion to the government for the sole purpose of being useful to my fellow-citizens.
The last point I wish to deal with today is the one which, to my mind, presents the most difficult problem at this time, namely unemployment. I do not want to speak at length on this subject because several of my colleagues have already done so. However, I should like to say a few words about it. Everybody regrets that, in a country as rich as Canada, there should still be at this time of the year more than half a million unemployed. The fine promises made by the Prime Minister and the members of his government, as well as the announcement of this famous special public works program have not solved the problem.
With respect to this special public works program, I must say, Mr. Speaker, that as far as the area of Quebec city is concerned, our unemployed have not been favoured, nor spoiled, because I had occasion to look at the estimates after they were tabled and I found no special project for the Quebec city area. I expected to find a certain amount of money earmarked for the building of a post office in Quebec city but I saw nothing for that purpose. Be that as it may, we shall have occasion to deal with this matter, because in the estimates which were tabled recently I saw no special project other than ordinary public works which were also carried out by the former administration. Like everybody I believe that it is not enough to be content with vague promises but that it is important to act and try to find the solutions required to improve the situation.
With this in mind, I should like to make another suggestion to the government.
A few days ago, when I took part in the debate on the amendments to the National Housing Act of 1954, I suggested that the government, with the co-operation of provincial governments, set up a municipal loans fund so as to make long term loans available for financing important municipal improvements.

The Address-Mr. Bourget
It is well known that many municipalities are delaying many works, even urgent ones, because of lack of required funds, or perhaps also because the interest or the cost of the money is too high. Through that fund, money would be more readily available and it would be possible to make an immediate start on municipal projects which have been neglected up to now.
It is easy to see that such a project would create jobs all over Canada. I know from personal experience that, in the province of Quebec, those urgent projects have been put aside because the necessary funds were lacking, or because the interest rate was too high. Well, with such a plan, jobs would be available all over Canada, unemployment would be greaty relieved, and our municipalities and cities would be supplied with the essential services they lacked up to now.
The purpose and the administration of that fund would be established after consultation with the representatives of the provinces and municipalities. This plan would complete, without ever replacing them, the methods currently in use to finance ordinary municipal projects.
Mr. Speaker, even if this suggestion originates from this side of the house, even if it is part of the program outlined by our leader, I hope the government will not consider this as a good reason to reject it. I am convinced it will contribute a great deal to help Canadians again enjoy the prosperity which was theirs under a Liberal administration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having been a regular reader of the official record of the one and only session of the 23rd parliament-probably in anticipation of what could happen to me and what, in fact, did happen on March 31 last-I know how admirably its Speaker presided over its discussions. This is why I was quite happy when the house showed its confidence and its approval on reappointing him to this post. You will be so kind, Sir, as to express to him my most respectful regards.
I was glad also to see you elected Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees. This is not only because we are old friends but also because I know how remarkably intelligent you are and how you are, by nature, admirably suited to the difficult post you now hold.
I would also like to congratulate the members for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafre-niere) and the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) on the excellent speeches they delivered when moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I also wish to congratulate most cordially the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. O'Hurley)
(Mr. Bourget.]

and for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) on their appointment to the cabinet. They were deserving of the Prime Minister's confidence.
In this house I represent the constituency of Quebec South. This is an entirely urban constituency which includes Champlain ward, the oldest in Quebec, the whole of the old part of the city situated within the walls and including the Citadel, plus that strip bounded on the south by the St. Lawrence river, on the north by St. Jean street and the Ste. Foy road, and extending to the limits of the municipality of Ste. Foy, which takes in the whole of the town of Sillery.
Problems of federal jurisdiction peculiar to this constituency have to do mainly with the improvement of harbour facilities in Quebec city, which are entirely within its limits. This shows how much I rely on the care and sympathy of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees).
I wish again to express here to the people of Quebec South my gratitude for the confidence they have shown me and reiterate my determination to serve them to the best of my ability.
(Text):
In paying a tribute of gratitude to the electors of Quebec South, Mr. Speaker, I wish to mention that 15 per cent of its population is English-speaking. However, the majority of this group understands and speaks French as the majority of the French-speaking group understands and speaks English, which prompted the remark that in my riding we have the best system of simultaneous translation that can be designed. Speaking in English, I wanted it to be known that I am very proud of my one-eighth Irish blood.
You will allow me, Mr. Speaker, to draw the attention of this house to the fact that this summer the city of Quebec will be celebrating its 350th anniversary. I take this occasion to convey to all hon. members and to the population in general an invitation to visit our fair city and take part in the celebration of this important date in our history.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, the founding of Quebec city is really the starting point of the establishment of Canada. Indeed, Quebec city was the first permanent settlement on our territory. And we owe this feat to one of the finest figures in our history, Samuel de Champlain.
It was in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, at the foot of Cap Diamant, close to what is now the rue du Porche, that Champlain built his Habitation. May I quote this well deserved eulogy of the one who was the true founder of our country:

What was most admired in him was his steadfastness in his undertakings, his firmness in the face of the greatest dangers, an indomitable courage in the face of the most unforeseen setbacks, a warmhearted and unselfish devotion to the country, and a great fund of honour and honesty.
The constituency of Quebec South has one of the longest records of historic events and I could not possibly mention all its monuments and all the gallant actions that were accomplished there.
I will say, however, that it is in that constituency, on the Plains of Abraham, which is now a magnificent public park, that on September 13, 1759, a battle was fought between the armies of Wolfe and Montcalm, which was going to change the course of history in this country. As a matter of fact, it is from that time that French-speaking Canadians and English-speaking Canadians began to learn to live side by side, to become later, through confederation, equal partners for the building of the Canadian nation to which each group wanted to bring the wealth of its own culture.
It therefore seems to me that it is appropriate in this year 1958, to pay a special tribute to the city of Quebec and its founder.
Mr. Speaker, it is the first time since 1887 that there is a majority of Conservative members from Quebec in this house. That is the outstanding fact of the election; it means that the province of Quebec wished to join with the rest of the country to give a great Canadian, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), an unprecedented mark of confidence.
To understand the true meaning of the speech from the throne, it is necessary, it seems to me, to study it in the light of the events which happened this last year in this country and in this house.
The speeches delivered by our hon. friends of the official opposition, particularly from our colleagues of Quebec, do not conceal their desire, quite understandable in some ways, to ignore such circumstances. In fact, when they deal with the economic situation, fiscal relations between the central government and the provinces and especially with national unity, no one would suspect that, less than a year ago, they were sitting on the other side of the house.
Yet it is quite true that they were then supporting a government which, through old age and complacency, had become indifferent to the aspirations of the people, which, as was admitted by its leader after its defeat,
The Address-Mr. Flynn was no longer close to the people. That government considered itself infallible and indispensable. Convinced that it had recruited the best minds, it thought that it was impossible for any other party to assume power. It no longer heard anyone, it no longer listened to the provinces, it went its own way.
What have been the consequences of that attitude on the economic situation? For a few years, there had been evident signs of a recession, but because such signs were not accompanied with a drop in the cost of living index, the former government did not see fit to act. By the winter of 1954-55, the number of unemployed had reached serious proportions and during the following winter, the government was warned by some of its advisors that an economic recession was to be expected as a consequence of overproduction in several fields, south of the border, as well as at home. But why worry when events and the electorate had been approving the government for so long, and when luck was on their side?
Such an indifferent attitude is in curious contrast with the horrified concern our hon. friends now display. But most peculiar of all, is that despite the true signs of the slowdown of our economy, the former government showed concern about an increase of the cost of living, and initiated its now famous tight money policy.
Mr. Speaker, as was realized later, this acted as a sedative at a time when a stimulant was required. A remark made at a time by a well known Quebec city industrialist comes to my mind:
This is the first time in the history of the world that a government has willfully started a depression.
To relieve the present unrest, the speech from the throne proposes a series of measures which are going to inject large sums of money into our economy so as to restore its activity. That is why we adopted a measure providing $350 million for housing loans; that is why we are told that a huge amount is to be spent on public works.
But when our friends protest that it is not enough or that it is bad, they forget that, during the single session of the 23rd parliament, other measures were adopted, the benefits of which are now beginning to be felt; they forget that a further sum of $300 million was appropriated for housing loans, that taxes were reduced by $179 million, that old-age pensions, pensions to the blind, to veterans

The Address-Mr. Flynn and their dependents were increased to put considerable money in the hands of the public.
Just as the bad effects of the tight money policy took some time to show, the good effects of all the measures taken by this government to restore economic activity cannot show at once. But already, everything seems to suggest that we can confidently look forward to some improvement soon, thanks to the bold initiatives of the government.
I, for one, prefer to be on the side of optimism, which is an essential factor of prosperity, than on the side of pessimism, which stifles private enterprise.
Now, Mr. Speaker, several of our Liberal colleagues say they are worried about the attitude of the Quebec Conservatives on the question of fiscal relations between the central government and the provinces.
There again, they are forgetting all their past record; they forget-and this is very important-that the problem was created by the former government when, after the war, it refused to give back to the provinces their taxation rights which had been rented from them, while clearly expressing the intention, according to the now famous statement of the former minister of justice, Mr. Garson, to perpetuate the wartime taxation agreements.
Later, our hon. friends had to make some concessions, and the present equalization formula is far from the original agreements, because, when a provincial government makes any direct levy, the taxpayers in such province may deduct from their federal tax a percentage of the provincial charge.
But it is a formula that is not entirely satisfactory. It was forced upon the provinces, the former government having refused to negotiate and stated that the provinces could take it or leave it.
Under such circumstances, and in view of such arrogance, it was normal and natural that anybody believing in fiscal and legislative autonomy for the provinces opposed the previous government, and our friends in the official opposition know but too well that the province of Quebec was not, and is not, the only one to be dissatisfied.
Whatever may be said among the members sitting at the extreme left in this house, the attitude of my party on this matter has always differed from that of the former government. It was never backward in affirming and reaffirming its respect for the constitu-
IMr. Flynn.]

tion. Especially, since coming into office, it has clearly demonstrated that it wishes to negotiate with the provinces as equals so as to arrive with them at a solution of this matter.
Nobody will underestimate the difficulties that lie ahead, because every related problem has to be taken into account.
But it will be admitted that the last people from whom we have to endure compassion or sarcasm are the ones who created and left that problem in the lap of the present government. Those who got us into this mess have no business asking how we will get out of it. In any event we are in a better position than they are to do so.
Besides, federal-provincial relations have considerably improved since June 10, 1957, and the attitude of the present government is most hopeful indeed.
Some of our Liberal colleagues from Quebec have had a great deal to say about national unity. They have claimed that Quebec Conservatives had a philosophy at variance with that of their colleagues in the other provinces.
These remarks are intended to create disunity in our ranks. Such tactics are so obvious that it might be well to say nothing further about them.
However, if certain statements made in this house can be accepted as fair, politics being what they are, others are inexcusable since they are calculated to prejudice national unity for purely electoral purposes.
National unity, or better still understanding and respect between all racial groups, must remain above party politics. It is not the exclusive property of any one of them, no more, incidentally, than patriotism and honesty-including electoral honesty- are the exclusive property of any party. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the great majority of Canadians, be they Conservatives, Liberals or C.C.Fers, sincerely hope for national unity.
No doubt the election of 50 Quebec Con-*servatives this year favours national unity but this does not mean, in my opinion, that our party is the only one to advocate harmony between all Canadians. In anything that may be related to that good understanding, it is imperative that the members of this house weigh their words, here or elsewhere, in order not to stir up motives of division.

I do not contend that all the Conservatives are without fault; their responsibility in this is the same as the responsibility of our friends in the opposition. In any party, there are extremists. But this does not mean that one can unduly stress such statements for merely electoral purposes if, in the end, national unity must suffer from it.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, the Quebec Conservatives are no more different from the Conservatives of other provinces than are Quebec Liberals from their fellow members, and I am convinced that there is unity of thought in our party. The official opposition will come to realize it.
Let not the official opposition worry too much because of the fact that the Conservatives in the province of Quebec have had the support of ministers, members and organizers of the Union Nationale. Let them not worry about that more than about the support they themselves received from the provincial Liberal party.
As for us, the support we received was freely given and freely accepted. We were not dictated any policy nor is there any intention of dictating one to us. We know that ours is a federal mandate, and we are sincerely determined to discharge our responsibilities.
In brief, we are determined to mind our own business, and our Quebec colleagues who like to bring up provincial politics in the house, who have already given a leader to the provincial Liberal party and appear willing to give it another, are certainly not in a position to teach us any lesson in that regard.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne is a substantial one. It deals with the most urgent questions, and that is normal. It does not exhaust the program of the government because it is impossible to implement it all at once.
There is every indication that this session will be a fruitful one. Much will remain to be done. The task taken on by this parliament is a huge one. I am sure that under the enlightened guidance of the Prime Minister, we will manage to give our country a new impetus in the direction of progress, both material and moral, and that is why I am so happy to be here in the house to do my modest share in the achievement of that objective.
The Address-Mr. McWilliam
(Text):

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with others in extending congratulations to the house on the selection of the Speaker as the first commoner of this house and this country. I also wish to extend congratulations to the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. May I also congratulate you, sir, upon your appointment as Deputy Speaker.
The throne speech made mention of many topics that will eventually come before the House of Commons for deliberation. Until that time comes it is not possible to gain any detailed information as to what is actually proposed. One of these subject matters is a proposed bill of rights which is described as a measure to safeguard the rights of all persons in Canada in respect of all subjects within the jurisdiction of parliament. In what form it will be and to what extent this proposed legislation will go are at this time matters of conjecture among most of the members of this chamber and the people of the country. Its extent will be confined to the limits of federal jurisdiction, something which would mean that little if any improvement will be made in what we now enjoy. It is my understanding that the supreme court will be asked to decide what phases come within the legal rights of the federal government.
It takes more than words printed in a legal document to safeguard all the rights and privileges of our citizens. In every case the spirit of the law is more essential than is the letter of the law. When one compares the situation in Canada with that in other free countries, including our great neighbour to the south, it will be found that Canadians have enjoyed rights and privileges to a higher degree even without a bill of rights down through the years. Rights and privileges will prevail only where there is a spirit of fair play, recognition and tolerance, without which a bill of rights would be meaningless.
On the international front the general policy of the present government is the same as that of the former government. It is the fervent hope and desire of all Canadians that Canada's effort toward world peace, in cooperation with other peace-loving nations, will bring the world closer to that desired state.

The Address-Mr. McWilliam
Despite all the moneys made available for housing over the years the Miramichi area of New Brunswick has derived little benefit from government loans owing to the fact that money lending institutions do not look favourably on making investments in that area.
Part of the loans for housing made available by the government should be earmarked for areas like Northumberland county in order to ensure an equitable distribution of public funds for housing. The excuse is offered that municipalities and towns do not do enough promotional work. I feel that is not a very sound attitude. After all towns and municipalities are not in the home construction business. By setting aside a part of the available loans to designated areas, home building to a greater degree would be assured in the less favourable investment areas. Encouragement and assistance should be given those interested who are striving to promote construction of homes in these areas.
It is not my intention to make extended remarks about the unemployment situation and the confusion that arises over figures released by the bureau of statistics and the unemployment insurance commission. However, before I conclude my remarks I will make an appeal to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) to find alternate employment for civilian personnel of Renous naval depot whose services will be terminated on Saturday next. The public across Canada is looking for concrete action from the government for an improvement in the unemployment situation, one that will be beneficial to rural constituencies.
In New Brunswick the wood products industry and the mining industry are at low ebbs. In fact the Heath steel mines in Northumberland-Miramichi and Brunswick Mining and Smelting Company in Gloucester have suspended operations and the machinery is being placed in mothballs. Curtailed pit-wood orders this year and the falling off of the United Kingdom market for long lumber, with future prospects very dim, are matters causing grave concern in the Miramichi and other areas in the maritimes whose economy depends upon the lumber industry.
This situation has an adverse effect on woods work, mining and exploration activities and longshore work with a resultant drop in retail trade. An improvement in woods operation industry is imperative for the future economy of Northumberland-Miramichi.


May I say a few words about the proposed development outlined in the throne speech for Canada's northland and for the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam. These projects will be financed with moneys from the federal treasury. Desirable as it may be to provide these facilities in other parts of the country, the senior members of confederation should receive the same treatment. I imagine the maritime provinces were disappointed that no mention was made in the speech from the throne of the construction of the Chignecto canal or the New Brunswick-Prince Edward Island causeway. These projects are essential to our maritime economy. The Chignecto canal has been promised ever since confederation, before there were any western provinces or northlands under federal jurisdiction. The causeway between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island should be promoted at an accelerated pace and the Chignecto canal project survey should be undertaken now.
The action of the Department of National Defence in connection with the lay-off of civilian employees at the naval ammunition depot at Renous is regrettable. These layoffs become effective May 31 and the action is regrettable because the lay-offs are permanent and there is no hope of other employment in the local labour field.
During the month of March reliable reports indicated that the lay-offs would take place not later than April 30. Protests brought about a deferment but in previous years when this same situation arose and when appeals were made lay-off orders were rescinded on account of the general employment situation. During the election campaign the Conservative candidate and his speakers gave assurance that no lay-offs would take place on April 30 or in the future, and attempts were made to lead those concerned into thinking that the rumour of proposed lay-offs was Liberal propaganda, despite the fact that this serious matter was not raised or discussed by Liberals as a campaign issue.
The reason given for these lay-offs, or 1 should say the permanent doing away with certain positions and work classifications, by the Department of National Defence was that the department must maintain a continuing review of the size of its staff in relation tc work loads. Does this mean that further lay-offs will be made at Renous in the near future? Will lay-offs of civilian personnel be

made at the other two national defence establishments at Chatham and St. Margarets?
The department advised the national defence employees' association of Renous on May 2 that a committee was working on the problem in an attempt to re-locate the employees involved in other suitable employment. What results the committee will bring about remain to be seen. With unemployment at a high peak in this area it is doubtful if these employees will be re-located in employment of any kind. Previous correspondence on the matter from the Minister of National Defence led the Renous federal union executive to believe that alternate employment would be provided before the personnel involved would sever their connections with the ammunition depot. The present unemployment situation and the future prospects in this area are very dim.
Mr. R. J. Martin, the provincial Conservative member for Northumberland, when speaking at a meeting in Chatham on May 12 is reported as follows:
Mr. Martin stated that there should certainly be no lay-offs and that every effort be made by the people concerned to drive home to the federal government the unemployment picture here.
Mr. Martin's remarks on the Renous depot situation were, I would judge, well received by the meeting, but they are hard to reconcile with his provincial government colleagues' statements that unemployment is only a temporary pause, only a seasonal unemployment situation. When Liberals spoke about unemployment both at Fredericton and Ottawa they were accused by the Conservatives of spreading doom and gloom. Do Mr. Martin's colleagues think he is spreading doom and gloom? Do the people of Northumberland-Miramichi think the unemployment situation should be driven home to Premier Flemming and his cabinet, who also have a responsibility in this unemployment situation?
The figures given by an official of the local office of the unemployment insurance commission at this meeting of May 12 were as follows:
Four thousand one hundred and fifty registered as unemployed out of a working force of twelve thousand-approximately 29 per cent of the registered working force unemployed. There are many others unemployed who are not registered.
Is this the situation that condones reductions in personnel by a government department with a promise of alternate employment. The municipal council, the town councils and the boards of trade of Chatham and Newcastle and the Legion branches, all of whom made representations in addition to the general public, feel that the personnel dismissed from the
The Address-Mr. McWilliam Renous ammunition depot-many of them overseas veterans-have been dealt with unfairly. Alternate employment should have been provided before dismissal instead of adding these men to the overflowing ranks of the unemployed. I appeal to the Minister of National Defence to reconsider the department's action and to retain these men on their jobs until they can be placed in some other suitable employment.
I now turn to a matter which is causing much concern to the geological association of Canada. With the closing down of mining and exploration across our country, this is forcing many geologists and mining engineers to seek employment in other fields and there is a grave danger that these specialists, with their wide experience and knowledge, will be lost for all time to the mining industry. As a result, in later years the development of our mineral resources will suffer. It is my understanding that this association will make representations to the government and I appeal for every consideration to be given to finding a solution that will offset a serious loss and a threat to the future development of our mineral resources.
I wish to make a further appeal to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), and I am glad he has just entered the chamber and has taken his seat, in connection with the telephone service-I should say the inadequate service-provided by his department for the people residing between Black River Bridge and Escuminac, on the south shore of Miramichi river and bay. The minister is familiar with the circumstances and I am sure realizes the great handicap here. I trust his department will without further delay provide adequate telephone service for this area and, in fairness, I must say I think the minister has been most co-operative with me in respect to my efforts and representations to him. I trust that with his officials something can be worked out to provide a better service.
The paragraph in the speech from the throne in connection with proposed assistance for small business has created wide interest. The paragraph reads:
In order to assist small business, there will be established a small business section within the administrative machinery of government. The functions of this organization will be to provide liaison between the government and small businesses and to study the problems of small business and to advise on measures necessary to meet them.
As hon. members will see, the paragraph makes it clear that the function of the small business section of government will be to provide liaison between the government and small businesses to study the problems and advise on measures to meet them.

The Address-Mr. Rapp
Most provincial governments have departments of government which carry out this function to varied degrees. In most cases the problems of small businesses can be boiled down to financial problems. The interest costs on capital funds in many cases exceeds the operational profits. What small business needs is a source of credit at interest rates that will enable it to get firmly established within a reasonable time.
Much can be done to assist our economy and encourage small business by providing financial assistance to small businesses at rates which will make it possible for them to survive, operate at a profit and ensure permanent employment. A credit bank for small business providing credit as is now provided for large business concerns through the development bank would serve such a purpose.
There are many other matters in the speech from the throne debate, all of which have been discussed in this debate by speakers of all parties. We look forward to the time when the matters referred to in the speech from the throne are presented here in legislative form so that hon. members may have the opportunity to discuss them in greater detail.
