Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity on my first occasion of rising here in this chamber to congratulate you on your election to your present high office. It gave me a great deal of satisfaction to know that the hon. gentleman to whom I was first introduced upon my arrival in our parliamentary buildings was none other than Your Honour. It gave me a great deal of pleasure and comfort to listen to your very friendly words of encouragement. That, of course, was three weeks ago and today, on the occasion of making my maiden speech, I am in the same shaky position as I was then; I hope your friendly understanding will work the same magic now as it did on that occasion. Before going on to deal with other matters, I should like to associate myself with all those who have congratulated the Deputy Speaker. I should like, further, to extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on their contributions to the debate.
When I arrived here in Ottawa for the first time and walked across from Union station to Parliament Hill I was all eyes, and my heart was filled with emotion when I saw the graceful parliament buildings, the statues and the other historic sights. The first statue that I walked up to was that of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the great French-Canadian statesman, and as I looked up I could almost see


a twinkle in his eyes. I thought I could hear him say these words: "What are you, a little immigrant of just 29 years residence, here in Ottawa for? Didn't I hear you say that all you wanted from life was to come to Canada and make a home for yourself and your family? I thought you were very content when Canada had given you this opportunity and your life's ambition was achieved, but now I see you are here as the new member for Humboldt-Melfort to represent this great constituency in the 24th parliament. As this is the case, go on then, and do the job assigned to you for the glory of Canada and your constituency." These are the words I thought I heard this great statesman say to me, and as I walked slowly away a vision appeared before my eyes depicting the last 29 years spent in this wonderful country of my adoption.
However, I had walked only a few steps before I reached the statue of another great Canadian statesman, Sir John A. Macdonald, the father of confederation, who was so instrumental in uniting two great races and two great cultures into this united Canada of ours. This great statesman's wisdom and foresight made Canada a land which many millions of people outside her borders desired to enter so that they might establish homes for themselves and for their families in a country where there are no racial prejudices and where freedom of speech and freedom of religion are no idle words-in a Canada where you are given the right to work, prosper and shape your own destiny without interference, state control or state supervision. One can only understand and evaluate the meaning of these God-given rights and privileges if one has never had them, or, if at one time or another during one's lifetime, one has been deprived of them. And as I stood before this statue, as a new member of parliament, I made a solemn pledge to safeguard the virtues and to preserve these high principles which are the pillars upon which our democratic system stands, to preserve them, use them and safeguard them until the time arrives to pass them on in all their purity and greatness to those who follow us. This, I felt, was part of my most noble task here in the 24th parliament of Canada, and I know this view will be shared not only by the new members but by all the senior members of this house also.
At this time I should like to associate myself with my fellow members and congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on the overwhelming victory our party achieved under his leadership and on the confidence the people of Canada showed in him on March 31. My heartiest congratulations go

also to the ministers of the cabinet, to members of our party both senior and junior, and to all hon. members of either parties, too, who are here to serve Canada in whatever capacity they may be called upon to do so. We who are conscious of the merits of our democratic system will appreciate very much their constructive contributions so that we can all serve the Canadian people in this parliament to the best of our ability.
I have the honour to represent the constituency of Humboldt-Melfort which is located in the northeastern part of the province of Saskatchewan. It is an agricultural district and predominantly a grain-growing area although livestock raising has increased considerably during the last few years. It is one of the better farming districts in our province. The population of my constituency consists of people of many national and racial extractions such as Anglo-Saxon, French, German, Scandinavian, Russian, Ukrainian and many others. There are no cities within the boundaries of my constituency but there are four larger towns and a number of smaller towns and villages which provide the citizens of the area with all the required services.
We have one agricultural experimental station and through their research and experiments with different grain varieties, grass seeds and livestock breeding they have given the farmers of Humboldt-Melfort many useful and beneficial services of which they have continuously availed themselves. There is a senior citizens' home in Melfort and another will be opened shortly in Tisdale, and there are a number of hospitals some of them very modern in design. We have not very many paved highways but the proposed second trans-Canada highway, if proceeded with, will pass through some sections of the Humboldt-Melfort constituency. The citizens of my riding will appreciate this undertaking very greatly and are looking forward to its inception.
I took notice with a great deal of satisfaction of that part of the speech from the throne where mention was made of amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Although in the past this act gave assistance to many farmers who needed it western agriculturists felt it never went far enough to cover those farmers who had their land under water from the spring run-off or inundated through an abundance of rainfall during the summer. This flooding took on devasting proportions for about four or five years and its effects were ruinous for many farmers. I now wish to bring it to the attention of this house that the proposed amendments to the P.F.A.A. mentioned in the throne speech should contain a definite provision to
The Address-Mr. Rapp cover and classify the flooding of farms, if on a large scale, as a natural hazard and, if larger areas are under water, as disaster areas.
Our agricultural industry in the west is becoming a highly machanized industry and it takes a skilful person to operate some of the implements and machinery on the farm these days. It is difficult to secure skilful farm labourers and there is a reason for this situation. First, the farm labourer is a seasonal worker and in the fall when all the work is finished he must seek employment elsewhere. In years past when winter employment was readily available the changeover was not so complicated and he did not suffer financial loss as a result of this but now in many cases he is left unemployed and still he cannot obtain unemployment benefits or payments because he has not contributed to the unemployment insurance fund. Other seasonal workers such as fishermen are contributing to the unemployment insurance fund and are entitled to unemployment assistance. Why,# then, the discrimination against the seasonal farm labourer? I would like to bring the matter to the attention of the house and suggest that early consideration be given to the plight of the seasonal farm labourer. I noted with pleasure the remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) to the effect that studies and research have been conducted by his department concerning the seasonal farm labourer and how to bring him under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Such a measure would indeed be welcomed.
As I mentioned earlier in my remarks my district is predominantly a grain-growing one and as a grain grower myself I am well aware of their plight and I recognize that the cost-price squeeze for them is growing worse and becoming unbearable. We western grain growers are not a group of people who like to be a burden to our government. We do not like to be subsidized or bonus-supported farmers but we would like to obtain the same protection from the government as other industries in our country are receiving for their products and manufactured goods all of which are protected by tariffs and subsidies. We are supplying our domestic market with high quality bread milled from the best wheat in the world but we must accept the export price that our good customers overseas are establishing for us. In contrast to this, there is not a piece of machinery or any other necessity that we farmers must buy in order to produce our grain that does not come to us with a set manufacturer's price tag on it. Why should there be discrimination against

The Address-Mr. Rapp the wheat-growing industry? This matter too must be given fair and just consideration by all hon. members of the house, whether the solution be a deficiency payment for our grain by taking into consideration the cost of production, or a two-way price system, that is to say one price for the farmer's wheat that is sold in the domestic market and another price for wheat sold in the export market. It, of course, should be left to the discretion of hon. members of this house which of the two is the most workable and just system which could be applied for the solution of this urgent problem which must receive early consideration. The plight of our western farmers must be alleviated. I have in mind in particular the younger farmers and those who were established through the Department of Veterans Affairs under the provisions of the Veterans Land Act. They are the ones who are feeling the brunt of the price squeeze much more than the older established farmer. If for no other reason than this action must be taken and I appeal to the house on their behalf.	[DOT]
I wish now to deal with the subject of education concerning which much has been said both in this house and elsewhere. I do not agree with many who are of the opinion that our educational system is outmoded and greatly inferior to that in the United States, Europe or elsewhere. What is wrong is that many who have the ability and willingness to apply themselves to obtain higher education cannot, owing to the lack of financial means, avail themselves of the opportunity to do so. Although much has been done by our governments in this regard through the means of grants, scholarships, et cetera, much more needs to be done to assist worthy students to further their education. The greatest investment in our future generation is to give them the best education this country can offer.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to express my sincere gratitude to you for the time given me, and to hon. members of this house for their attention and if in future days I am given another opportunity to speak on behalf of my constituents of Humbolt-Mel-fort I will be most appreciative. My constituents have sent me to Ottawa as their representative in this new parliament with many instructions and constructive suggestions. It is my duty to bring these before hon. members of this house and by so doing we then can draft and implement policies that will serve the needs of my constituents and those of the people of Canada. This I will endeavour to do.

Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to say how glad we are that you were returned to the chair of this distinguished house. I have had the honour and the privilege of seeing you exercising your duties in the last parliament and, like all those who were here, I had occasion to appreciate your amazing knowledge of parliamentary procedure and your sense of justice, as well as your impartiality.
In another regard, as a Canadian, you may rightly be given as an example to all those- and they are many-who, in our country, uphold the cause of good and mutual understanding between the various elements which make up our nation. Your behaviour on this point is made all the more eloquent because your statements, or rather your deeds, prove in no uncertain way the sincerity of your words. You and your worthy and charming wife have made several stays in the old capital to take summer courses in the French language at Laval university. Your three children have studied in convents of the province of Quebec. Mrs. Michener even published an essay on the French philosopher Jacques Maritain. You are yourself an officer of the Visites Interprovinciales and one of the founders of the Alliance Canadienne, two groups dedicated to the task of promoting, through more frequent meetings, even more friendly relations between the representatives of the two main racial groups in our country. And, as pointed out to the house recently by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), you have agreed to become a patron of honour of the group devoting itself to the establishment of a bilingual secondary school in Toronto. Your behaviour, Mr. Speaker, is a refreshing contrast, to say the least, to a certain statement which was once heard in this house.
(Text):
I feel I would be remiss in my duty if I did not extend sincere congratulations to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on his outstanding victory last election. From the outset of his political life, notwithstanding certain defeats when running for public office, he has continued to show that tenacity of purpose which has helped to place him in the position of the Prime Minister of Canada.
We must recall that he had an excellent opportunity from the time of his election as leader of his party in December, 1956, until June 10, 1957 to have a full six months to do political campaigning inside and outside of the house. His party did not obtain the complete confidence of the people of Canada

in that election, but notwithstanding that, the resignation of the former prime minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, afforded his party a further period of nine months to mend its political fences. I must say that this period of time is not always presented to a leader of the opposition.
I wish to emphasize to the Prime Minister that he must continue with the tenacity of purpose and exert every effort to do what should be done for the best interest of all Canadians. In particular, the youth of our great nation need an example of leadership and tenacity by the first citizen of our country, and they look for those qualities in the Prime Minister, not as a politician but as a man. I am sure that he will continue to show the qualities which provide a good example to the coming generation. However, I do not wish these sincere words of mine to be misinterpreted by the Prime Minister to mean that he and I will agree on political principals on a common ground. I am as convinced in my political faith in the Liberal party as he is himself in his own party. I intend to reiterate more than once during the course of this session and throughout the lifetime of this parliament how strongly I oppose his political approach in many fields.
(Translation):
While I am still in a congratulatory vein, I wish to express my appreciation to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. members for Quebec-Montmorency and Yukon (Mr. Lafreniere and Mr. Nielsen), who showed themselves worthy of the honour conferred upon them by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in entrusting them with that task. I also congratulate the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) for his appointment as Deputy Speaker of the house, and I wish him every success in the discharge of his high functions. My congratulations also to the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea). And, above all, I wish to mention the two new ministers from Quebec, to whom I want to express my best wishes. During the last election campaign, the Prime Minister had asked us, in Quebec, to send him so many members that he would be embarrassed in choosing among them. Quebec showed great generosity by sending 50 members. Judging from the time the Prime Minister had to take in selecting Quebec representatives for his cabinet, we must conclude that he was indeed embarrassed!
And to close this congratulatory chapter, although I have not been myself sitting very long in this house, I want to wish every success to the new members elected on March 31 last.
The Address-Mr. A. Brassard
Mr. Speaker, on May 1, 1957, I resigned my job in the office of the Minister of Transport to become a candidate at the convention which elected the Liberal candidate for the constituency of Lapointe for the June 10 election. I held that position for about three years, and I wish to tell the house how much I appreciated and admired the ability, the devotion and the sense of duty of all the division supervisors and employees of the department whom I have so often dealt with. May I add that I took great pleasure in my relations with the officers of the many boards, commissions and crown corporations responsible to the Minister of Transport. Finally, 1 wish to express my thanks to the members of the minister's office. Their devotion was always unfailing and their temper was such as to lighten the load on every one of us. I hope that the new minister has not yet managed to spoil this state of affairs.
As for my former employer, the hon. George Marler, I hope I will not be imposing on his modesty when I say that I would like to express publicly my gratitude to him. I experience, in this connection, a little of the filial gratitude the pupil feels towards his master. I can think of no better school to enrol in than that which is provided by close relationship with such a man as he. There is no better way of learning to work steadily and systematically, of learning to devote oneself to the service of one's fellow-citizens, to be at once broadminded and far-sighted, to want to see a job well done, of learning to be a gentleman, in short of learning to be a man in every sense of the word. No one could fail to want to improve and to raise his standards by working side by side with him. All too often unfortunately, the wisdom of the pupil is far removed from that of the master. Being no exception to that rule, I am the first to realize this and to deplore the fact.

I am convinced that all those who know him and who have seen him at work, either in Quebec or in this house, will feel his loss very keenly. This is no reflection on the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Webster) who must not be altogether devoid of merit since he has managed to get elected. Mr. Marler's contribution to the debates of this house would have been far more useful and far more intelligent than that of yours truly, especially in the present position of the Liberal party here. The fates have willed otherwise. This may however make it possible for him as well as for his charming wife to enjoy life for a few years, a very legitimate pleasure which has been largely denied them for almost twenty years.

The Address-Mr. A. Brassard
The constituency of Lapointe, which I have the honour of representing, Mr. Speaker, is a young constituency. It is situated in that part of the province of Quebec called by some the Kingdom of the Saguenay, by others, the Lake St. John area and by others still the Saguenay-Lake St. John region. It includes the cities of Jonquiere, Kenogami, Arvida, as well as several other surrounding municipalities, together with Chute-des-Passes, almost 200 miles from Jonquiere, where in September 1956, construction work was begun on an underground power plant of a one million h.p. capacity. The cost of the project is [DOT]estimated at about 150 million dollars and the Aluminum Company of Canada Ltd is the one undertaking this project which will .surely rank among the marvels of the genius of man. The Price Brothers mills are in Jonquiere and Kenogami, while those of the Aluminum Company of Canada Ltd are in Arvida. The population of the constituency of Lapointe is therefore largely made up of workers, to which must be added a large farm population.
The constituency was represented for the first time, from 1949, by the devoted notary Mr. Jules Gauthier, a Liberal, who a few months before the 1953 elections decided not to run for re-election in order to be able to spend more time in the practice of his profession. Among the main achievements to which !he devoted much of his time, there are the federal buildings in Jonquiere and Arvida. Mr. Gauthier was painfully struck by the recent death of his wife and I wish to repeat to him here how I sympathize with him in his bereavement. From 1953 to 1957, the -constituency of Lapointe was represented by Mr. Fernand Girard, an independent. Mr. Girard was one of those mainly responsible for the coming of the reverend Oblate fathers in Jonquiere where they have opened a classical day college which is a great honour to the community and of which, not only Jonquiere and the constituency, but the whole area is proud.
Mr. Speaker, may I now express my deepest gratitude to the electors of my constituency who saw fit to re-elect me to this house. I was greatly flattered by their decision, especially when I consider I am the only Liberal member of the four constituencies of my area. The results might have been different had more ministers come to my constituency to try and convince the electors to vote against me. This may or


may not be an invitation to do so at the next election! But I am in no way referring to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees).
I must say that my Conservative opponent put up a good fight. I also had the great honour and pleasure of having as my opponent the provincial leader of the Social Democratic party in the federal election. In case my hon. friends to the immediate left of Mr. Speaker do not know about it, the phrase "parti social democrate" is the Quebec version, I was going to say a literary translation, but it is rather almost a literal translation of the phrase "Co-operative Commonwealth Federation". If the universities decide some day to award diplomas for demagogic vocabulary, I am sure that one of the first men to receive one will be the provincial leader of the C.C.F. party in Quebec. I hope however that great care will be taken that such a diploma is not awarded "honoris causa".
I was very much interested in hearing the leader of the C.C.F. party reading in this house, on May 13, part of the second paragraph of the Declaration of Regina of 1933, as recorded on page 44 of the debates official report. This was a confirmation of what I had said during the election campaign.
I feel all the more indebted to our workers who could have allowed themselves to be deceived by the mean exploitation of their misery at a time when unemployment has struck, in my riding, harder than ever before for the past few months. The Arvida factory workers especially, among whom my late father worked for several years, have suffered more than others because, last year, they had to bear, for more than four months, the hardships of a strike which seemed endless. Many workers wondered, and are still wondering, whether the strike could not have been settled in the office of the hon. minister of labour of Quebec, who, for almost five weeks, showed the greatest consideration for the representatives of union as well as for those of the Aluminum Company.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay tribute in this house to these gallant workers of the Aluminum Company who have given to the labouring class of the whole country, in these difficult times for them and their families, the most impressive example of discipline towards their union leaders. It is very seldom that we witness such a frank co-operation and friendly comprehension be-

tween the workers, the tradesmen in general, the owners, the municipal authorities and school boards as well as the professional classes. In a word, everyone joined hands to support those who for four months were without a means of livelihood and I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that we very seldom see such an example of brotherly co-operation among our population.
Today, many problems confront the population of my constituency and of my whole district. I do not hesitate to say the most acute problem, the one which requires an immediate solution, is obviously the problem of unemployment.
I do not claim that the government is entirely responsible for that deplorable situation. It is not by passing the buck that we shall solve the problem. What no one can deny is that in my district, as everywhere else in this country, unemployment has reached alarming proportions; what nobody can deny is that the government has the responsibility of taking steps without further delay. The Canadian National has dismissed a great number of its employees in my area. Some of them had 12, 15 and 17 years of service. These are questions which I propose to deal with in detail on the budget debate in this session, together with the ever growing requests in favour of an increase in family allowances, the implementation of the health insurance plan, the assistance to our municipalities by means of loans as well as the payment of subsidies to our universities.

I regret that the time at my disposal will not permit me to speak at length on the many important subjects of interest to me and my constituents. I must, therefore, limit my remarks to the vital topic of trade and to the so-called trade policy of the government. In order to deal with this matter from the beginning, we should remember that the Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition spoke feelingly of the imbalance of trade between Canada and our neighbour to the south. In the election campaign of 1957 this was a major platform of his party.
Immediately after becoming Prime Minister and on his return from the commonwealth conference he trumpeted to the newspapers of Canada that we would have to divert 15 per cent of our imports from the United States to the United Kingdom. He stated recently outside of the house that the newspapers had misinterpreted the meaning of his statements to the press. This is rather astonishing to me because it seems to be a rare occasion of misinterpretation by the 57071-3-31
The Address-Mr. A. Brassard press when we recall that there were no words of criticism about how well and how often he had been correctly quoted during the last election campaign. In any event, the Prime Minister surely cannot deny in the house that he has stated publicly on numerous occasions that we must reduce our imports from the United States. At no time, however, has he given the slightest inkling of the manner, the method or the products involved whereby this could be accomplished.
I am sure the Prime Minister will agree that this diversion will have serious effects on part of the economy of our country and that it has already had some effect on certain Canadian industries and businesses. By his action with regard to the subject of trade the Prime Minister has not proven himself to be a serious statesman. He should, I submit very humbly, have kept in mind the real need in the western world today to retain our good relations, but it seems that he did not give serious concern to our friendship with the United States before making these statements.
We all agree that the matter of trade is most serious to our country. I believe, however, that the Prime Minister would have been better advised if, rather than making his approach by talking about United States trade and diversion to the United Kingdom, he had given more serious consideration to retaining the trade channels we then enjoyed and at the same time not aiming for trade solely with Britain but seeking new trade outlets which would be advantageous to Canadians.
In order to maintain a favourable balance of trade with all of our customers, as we enjoyed under the previous Liberal government, there is some need for the Prime Minister to take action. But such action should not have been in the hasty manner of the Prime Minister, it should have been taken after serious and careful reflection and consideration, particularly with a view to avoiding the undermining of our good relations with any other country.
In my view, by making these hasty and ambiguous statements for publication our country was left in a position for retaliation by the United States. The Prime Minister did not, and does not even now, give us any firm plan of operation. On the other hand, the United States within a very short time put into effect what we may consider as a retaliatory measure, namely a serious reduction in the import of crude oil. In fact, the reduction took place the day it was announced. This 15 per cent reduction in the amount of our export of crude oil amounts to approximately 72,000 barrels per day. It does have a far greater effect on our population of 17 million persons, than a reduction of 15 per

The Address-Mr. A. Brassard cent would have on the population of about 170 million in the United States.
Let us look at the logic of the Conservative government. In the field of trade and commerce they make unfriendly statements and arouse ill feeling and, on the other hand, in the military field they seem to want to bend over backwards in an effort to co-operate. For example, an American is the commanding officer for the unified defence of Canada, United States and Alaska. It is evident that our continental defence requires the closest co-operation between our two countries. Why, on the other hand, do we salute them by a kiss on the both cheeks and on the other hand give them the boot?
I do not hestitate to say that the Conservative government has not acted in the best interests of Canada in the field of trade. As an example, of what use would it be to purchase more goods in England when they would continue to buy from countries other than ours? The cost of production in England is much lower than ours because, as one example, the wages and the standard of living of our workers are much higher. What will happen if we import from the United Kingdom large quantities of their products? There will be a continuation in a larger form of what has been happening in Canada for the last few months. Our manufacturers will be seriously concerned about the government's continued and future policy on trade, and will have to stockpile because of the lack of sufficient markets in which to sell their goods. We all know that in business a company can continue to thrive only so long as the flow of production is kept going by consistent and steady buying. If this flow is cut off, even to a limited degree, lay-offs of our workers is eventual.
I am not afraid to say that in my view the lack of foresight, the instability and also the lack of a definite trade policy by the present government did not in any way give assurance to our people for a continued expansion of trade or full employment. The Canadian people, by their vote in the recent general election, have indicated that we should now have more stability in government. However, if the government persists in following the obstinate, vague policy of trade as has been expressed, I am much afraid that our figures of the number of unemployed in this country will continue to astonish us.
I wish now to deal briefly with the subject of trade relating to the United Kingdom. Over the years Canada, under previous administrations, has encouraged trade with the United Kingdom but we must take into account the complexities involved. As I understand it, the basic principle of trade is that individuals, groups or countries exchange goods and services that each one needs for his 
own good living and betterment. We have, as I have said, had exchange of goods with the United Kingdom to the point that has been of mutual advantage to both countries. Can the government let us know how and in what way we can increase the number of products that we can supply when the United Kingdom can purchase these items at a more favourable price from European countries. In line with the same thought, the United Kingdom has been faced with similar problems in this connection because the right hon. prime minister of the United Kingdom, when speaking of trade last fall, said: "We have no friends, we have interests".
I do not want to be misunderstood about my feelings in this regard. My reaction is not an ethnic one. It is simply a matter of sound economics and good business. In this connection, I should like to mention that if the former prime minister, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, had advocated a policy of trade with France similar to the one proposed by the present government with the United Kingdom I would have objected as strongly as I do now. Every one knows that the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent had so deeply in his heart the welfare of Canadians that he would not espouse an approach of this type.
I think it would be of interest to look at a few matters having a direct bearing on this relationship. For example, the present government had a block of advertising posters about Canadian bonds printed in the United Kingdom. In answer to a query in this house, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said that the number printed was negligible. If this was the case, of what particular advantage was this order to the British people? I would think that the cost of shipping from England to Canada alone would be high in comparison to that of shipment from Montreal or Toronto to Ottawa. Was consideration given at the time to giving the entire order for those posters to our own competent Canadian printers?
A trade mission appointed by this government was sent to indicate to the United Kingdom producers that we wished to buy additional products from them. It was of interest to read in the press that during a visit of the mission to a shipyard the members were informed that the yard had a five-year backlog of business. Is it not surprising that we should show a desire to purchase under these conditions when some of our shipyards are barely existing? Is it any wonder then that there seems to be a feeling on both sides of the ocean that this mission was in fact a present to the people of the United Kingdom.
I look at this problem of trade with the feelings, as I understand them, of a Cana-

dian. Our fellow countrymen expected that the government in this great country of ours would develop a continued policy in trade and in all other international matters that would reflect wholeheartedly the views and opinions of the majority of Canadians. In this whole question of trade this government has ignored the interests of the Canadian people. Under no circumstances should we try to trade with any country on a sentimental basis. It is an old adage that there is no room for sentiment in business. Those people who have had more centuries of experience in this field and from the experience have the most logic, namely the British people themselves, give us the most eloquent lesson from which we should learn.

Like many other hon. members I would have been most interested in finding out if this assistance was received with as much thankfulness as was the withdrawal of the two original Conservative candidates in Quebec East and Quebec West.

speechtext:
My first words to you, Mr. Speaker, are of congratulation upon your re-election to the high office which you hold. Your impartiality, wisdom and humour during the 23rd parliament very clearly indicated that the rights and privileges of all hon. members would be jealously guarded.
I also wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the chairman (Mr. Sevigny) and the deputy chairman (Mr. Rea) of the committees of the whole house and congratulations are also in order for the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is indeed an inspiration to hear men of the same age as myself rise and acquit themselves in such an outstanding manner.
57071-3-314
The Address-Mr. Coates
The constituents of Cumberland, whom I have the honour to represent, discovered before confederation that the party of progress and imagination was the Conservative party and have seldom changed their minds since 1867. Indeed, in 18 of the 24 parliaments we have seen since that year Cumberland has been represented by Conservative members. Of the 33 fathers of confederation, four came from Cumberland. Probably no other constituency in Canada can boast of a similar contribution. All of these men went on to make further outstanding contributions to the political life of this young nation, and Sir Charles Tupper-known in his day as the warhorse of Cumberland- served this country as prime minister in 1896. Cumberland continued to contribute outstanding members; the Hon. A. R. Dickie, the Hon. E. N. Rhodes, R. K. Smith and Percy C. Black. Many hon. members of this house are well aware of the abilities of the last mentioned member and his friends here will be pleased to know he is enjoying good health and still takes a keen and active interest in the affairs of the citizens of Cumberland.
Cumberland also contributed two outstanding gentlemen to the Liberal party in the Hon. J. Layton Ralston and the Hon. Norman McLeod Rogers. Their contributions to the Liberal party and to Canada will not be forgotten.
Cumberland county is the first county in Nova Scotia as one enters from New Brunswick, and those who have travelled to Nova Scotia by car will bear me out when I say it has the most impressive entrance of any county in Canada. It is here that the Nova Scotia government has its beautiful information bureau. The Cumberland beauty only begins at the border and the scenic grandeur throughout the county is almost overpowering. The beaches between Amherst and Pugwash along the Northumberland strait, with water as warm as can be found anywhere on the east coast, the drive along the Parrsboro shore, the ruggedness of the Wentworth valley and the friendliness of the people have for many years made it a tourist playground.
Cumberland county is surrounded by the Tantramar marshes, which have for centuries been worked by the settlers of Cumberland and Westmorland. The potential of these marshlands has never been truly tapped. Before the day of the automobile they were valuable hay-producing lands but since that time have to a large extent been allowed to deteriorate. With the establishment of the M.M.R.A. many of these lands have been redyked and thereby saved from the sea. In the very near future work will start on the
484	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Coates Tantramar dam. This will have the doublebarrelled effect of providing needed employment and still further protection from the sea for the marshlands. I hope to see in the not too distant future thousands of head of cattle roaming on these marshes, for it has been proved beyond doubt that they have tremendous potential for this line of agriculture.
Agriculture is a very important industry to Cumberland and a large proportion of the population look to it for their livelihood. In my travels throughout my constituency I have seen many abandoned farms or farms worked by part-time farmers. It is my belief that most of these part-time farmers wish to work their lands but have found this to be an impossibility as a full-time proposition. Credit restrictions have been so tight that they were unable to enlarge their units and to stock them properly. I feel the prosperity of the east depends largely on the prosperity of our farming industry and I know that if credit restrictions were such as to allow them to obtain economical units, properly stocked, long strides would have been taken in the right direction.
The coal mining industry has always played an important road in the economy of Cumberland. May I take this opportunity to thank this government for its prompt action to ensure the continued operation of No. 2 colliery at Springhill. Today Springhill is, however, faced with a situation over which governments have no control. In the past two months four bumps have occurred in this mine. For those who are unfamiliar with this term, a bump is the meeting of the roof and the floor of a mine as a result of pressure. This mine's continued operation is necessary to this disaster ridden town of 7,500 people and it is the prayer of everyone that nature will correct the situation.
When one speaks of coal in Cumberland, Springhill comes immediately to mind, but there are two other important coal producing areas-River Hebert and Joggins. They as well as Cumberland have been more than gratified by the action of this government in respect of the coal industry.
Although the present marketing problems in Springhill have been solved, those of the Nova Scotian coal industry are very real. Indeed, during the past winter we have seen stockpiles of coal built up estimated to be in the vicinity of one million tons. It would appear with the continued mechanization of these mines and as the result of increased output per man a new look must be taken at the present subvention and subsidy policy. It is my humble opinion that these problems can best be solved by the establishment of a

federal coal marketing board which would take, not a year by year look at markets as under the present arrangements but the long-range view needed to provide a solution to the problem.
The change in ownership of our major coal mines was watched with deep concern by the people of Nova Scotia. There was, indeed, the feeling that parts of this huge empire might be transferred to the central Canadian firms which this company also owns. Today this concern has disappeared. We know that as a result of the forward looking policies of this company-one of which was the aforementioned stockpiling of coal-a great deal of hardship in our coal mining areas has been prevented and the coal industry has received a much needed shot in the arm.
When one speaks of concern being shown with respect to the closing of industries it might seem strange to some hon. members, but I can assure them that there is some foundation for such fears. My home town of Amherst was once known as "busy Amherst", a thriving community owing its prosperity to a large number of small industries. Our people watched as large concerns from central Canada came in, purchased and shut down these industries. As a result, there were hardships and unemployment. Amherst came back during world war II when a large aircraft plant was established there, employing 2,000 or more people, but before 1945 this was closed and once again the people braced themselves and for a time after the war it looked as though we would suffer as we had in prewar days. Through the efforts of prominent citizens in the area this firm was re-established and, coupled with the continued operation of a firm which has been part of Amherst for close to 100 years, this has helped to maintain the employment level.
We find in Canada today that a large portion of our major industry is located in Ontario and Quebec. This is necessary to a certain extent, for in these areas are located the larger concentrations of our population. However, defence industries located in these two provinces could just as conveniently be established in the east; in fact, from the defence point of view, this would appear to be a logical move. To keep all our eggs in one or two baskets means that one or two hydrogen bombs could cripple our defences completely. Problems would be presented if such a policy were adopted as the giant companies undertaking this work are also located in these areas I have mentioned, but I do not feel the problems are unsurmountable and, once tackled, I believe we would see

the economy of the east rising and our defences would be more secure.
The industry mentioned earlier attributes its existence to defence work and has the facilities and technical help necessary for further expansion. Might I say also that it would be difficult to find an area in Canada that has a better employee-management relationship, or a finer and more dedicated type of citizen.
Both the fishing and lumber industries are watching the progress of this government's foreign trade policies. At one time both these industries enjoyed considerable export trade with the United Kingdom, and have through the years watched it disappear. Indeed, I was told by the biggest lobster packer in my constituency, when it was suggested that this government's trade policies threatened his industry, that at one time he shipped 90 per cent of his vacuum packed lobster to England, and that with a Liberal government in power he had watched this market disappear completely.
We see a new industry looming larger and larger on the horizon in Cumberland. We have had a salt mine at Malagash for many years. In recent years a salt plant was established at Nappan and has remained at full production since its establishment. We now have another company drilling for salt at Pugwash, of Cyrus Eaton fame, where the reserves are estimated in the billions of tons.
It is the expectation of the citizens of Cumberland that with cheaper power resulting from the thermal power program we will see new industries established there. We have seen more than our share of industries being brought out by Upper Canadian firms and closed down, and we now look with optimism to this power program as a means of establishing industry with the knowledge that our children may remain with us and have opportunities for a future the equal of those in other parts of this great country of ours, something impossible to imagine during the 22 years of Liberal reign in Canada. It is amazing to see the change in attitude of the people of the east. I remember very clearly their remarks after the increase in freight rates was disallowed by this government. They add up to the fact they have again been discovered, that this government realizes there is an Atlantic area, and plans to see equality of opportunity from coast to coast.
We in Cumberland are keenly interested in the results of the survey initiated by this government for the construction of a causeway from New Brunswick to Prince Edward Island. There is hardly a maritimer who at some time in his life has not been delayed at either Cape Tormentine or Borden, and
The Address-Mr. Ratelle it is no exaggeration to say that during summer months a half day's delay can be anticipated. It would be difficult to estimate the number of tourists visiting the Atlantic area who refrain from visiting Prince Edward Island because of this anticipated waiting period. This is not a criticism of the present facilities, for we are all aware that from a business standpoint they are the best that can be expected; a causeway is the only answer.
One of the prime reasons for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick confederating with Ontario and Quebec in 1867, was the hope that one of the immediate projects resulting would be the Chignecto canal. We have discussed the building of the canal almost continually since that date, but it never seems to get beyond the discussion stage. Surveys have been carried out in the past. Today, however, we do not possess up to date information on this matter. I feel information on this canal should be brought up to date, and a survey carried out to determine its feasibility from an engineering and economic standpoint. Only then can we truly pass judgment on the merits of this project.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to congratulate you on your election to the speakership, a post which you have occupied with dignity and impartiality.
I also congratulate the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) on his appointment to the deputy speakership.
I also would like to congratulate the hon. members for Lotbiniere (Mr. O'Hurley) and Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) on their appointment to the portfolios of defence production and Secretary of State respectively.
Finally, I congratulate the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere) and the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen),, who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have worthily acquitted themselves of the task which the Prime Minister had entrusted to them. I am sure that the electors of their respective constituencies will be proud of them.
I feel it my duty, and not the least, to thank in this house the electors of the fine constituency of Lafontaine for showing me the same confidence they have given me ever since I have had the honour of representing them, that is for almost 20 years.
I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, that it is not through the help of the Union Nationale that I am here today.
486	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Ratelle
I listened to the speech of His Excellency the Governor General, and read it afterwards, but I found with regret that there was no mention of more favourable labour legislation.
It is true that an eight week extension of unemployment insurance benefits has been granted to seasonal workers in order to help those who have not yet gone back to work. This assistance represents little improvement in their situation. I will give more details on this question later.
It is the same thing with the funds to be voted for public works. Of course, this will be a benefit to some groups of the working people. However, we should not forget that such works perhaps will not be started soon.
I will now try to explain the reasons for those hardships suffered by the Canadian people.
In 1957, those of our friends opposite who were sitting on this side repeatedly said that we were rich, that we had surpluses but none of them could speak of unemployment because there was no unemployment. There was prosperity everywhere; people were happy and it was good to live in Canada. Elections have been held. The Prime Minister and his lieutenants, when they came in the province of Quebec, just as they did in the other provinces, stated repeatedly that Canada was prosperous, that we had a reserve of 250 million dollars and that we should now return that money to the people because we had collected too much in taxes in comparison with their income.
On June 10 last, our friends got more of their candidates elected than we did. That was the will of the Canadian people. What I can't understand, however, is that hardly three months had passed after they came to power, when uneasiness began to be felt. Trade was no longer reaching the same level, industries were laying off people. Very few of the hon. members who were then sitting in this house and have been re-elected have not been asked by their constituents for help in finding a job.
You will admit, Mr. Speaker, that there is something unusual in that, in so short a space and rich as we were, we should have become so poor.
I would be very much obliged if the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) or the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) could explain to the house how it is that our industries and our trade, which were so prosperous, have seen their prosperity vanish so soon.
Before 1896, the population of Canada was rather poor. In that year, the right hon. Sir

Wilfrid Laurier became prime minister of this country and within two short years he not only threw wide open the doors of Canada but succeeded in expanding our trade, so much so that, in 1898, as statistics prove, our country was prosperous, Canadians were staying here instead of going to the United States and many of those who had left the country even came back.
That prosperity continued until 1911 when the Conservatives, under the leadership of the right hon. Sir Robert Borden, came to power. In 1913, two years later, the prosperity we had known had completely disappeared and we were back to the state of economic despondency experienced prior to 1896.
In 1921 the right hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King came to power. Needless to say the Canadians of that time had not known prosperity before the arrival of the Liberals. But could the country have been more prosperous than between 1921 and 1930? Everybody was happy, trade, industry, house building and the building trade generally had once again undergone considerable development.
Subsequently those who lived under the administration of the Hon. R. B. Bennett in 1930 lived through the worst times of their lives, the like of which I hope we shall never see again.
In 1935, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King again became prime minister of Canada and was succeeded a few years later by the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. The prosperity which the Right Hon. Mr. King had brought back to the country continued under the administration of the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, without interruption until 1957.
One is forced to the conclusion that, if there is no malice on the side of the Conservatives, they have had really hard luck. You will admit, Mr. Speaker, that every time the Conservatives have come to power, prosperity has disappeared within a few months and there has been uneasiness among the workers.
I would suggest to the present administration that if it wishes to have prosperity, it must carry out the Liberal program by fostering trade which is the very basis of progress in any field connected with the welfare of the population.
Secondly, until trade has been restored once again, do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that instead of providing for eight additional weeks of unemployment insurance benefits for certain classes of workers, it would have been better to extend those benefits to all the unemployed who are not entitled to unemployment benefits, so that they might support their family until they find some work

to do? There is no reason for leaving our workers without money, especially after they have enjoyed some prosperity, and for not helping them so that they may live and provide for their family.
We have accumulated large sums of money; we cannot keep that money while people are suffering. Since we were wealthy last year, we must have the means to help the unemployed.
My colleague the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Meunier) has urged the government to do the impossible to come to an understanding with the premier of the province of Quebec about the construction of the Trans-Canada highway. I agree with him and I wholeheartedly support his request. This would give a job, of course, to those who work on the highway, as well as to those who will carry the materials required, and even to the city workers, because staff will be needed to prepare and distribute stone, cement, etc. This would be a great help to the unemployed, and to that end it is essential that the premier of the province of Quebec agree to come to terms.
It should certainly be easier for the present Prime Minister to have his views accepted by the premier of the province of Quebec than it used to be for the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. We now have two Conservative governments; one of them is named Union Nationale, but it is only, as everyone knows, a mask to hide its real identity, but not, of course, to the Conservative members who have been elected on March 31 last, in the province of Quebec.
The speech from the throne refers to an increase of several million dollars which will be made to the National Housing Act fund. I find that amount quite normal, and it is certainly going to help people who want to become homeowners. However, I feel that a 6 per cent interest rate is too high and that it should be reduced to 5 per cent. The government would lose nothing since it borrows at 2i per cent, 3J per cent, and 3J per cent. There is therefore no reason why the government should make a profit on the loans granted to workers. To that reduction of one per cent, which I feel is justified, could be added an insurance which would cover the payments the borrower has to make each month, when he would be unemployed. This would make things easier to more people who would not have to fear the loss of their savings when they want to borrow money under the terms of the National Housing Act.
The Address-Mr. Pascoe
There is nothing new to such measures. They were enacted by the Liberal government several years ago. It is only a matter of extending the provisions of the act in order to ensure greater security to our workers and allow a greater number of persons to own their own house.
I should like to add a word on personal income tax. I would ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), when preparing his budget speech, kindly to examine the possibility of raising the basic exemption to $1500 for single persons and to $3000 for married people. This would allow all Canadians to enjoy the same exemption as was granted by the government of the province of Quebec when it imposed the personal income tax.
I would also ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), in the course of this session, to define the word "obscene" so as to be able to prevent unwholesome literature and indecent shows from spreading in the future.
In conclusion, I wish to say that I am relying on the good intentions of the government. I hope it will be able to help workers out of their present difficulties and towards better things.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is my first opportunity to add my congratulations to those already extended to you, to the Deputy Speaker and to the deputy chairman of the committees of the whole house and to the mover (Mr. Lafren-iere) and to the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The two weeks we have been here have shown very clearly, Mr. Speaker, the reasons why you have been chosen for the high office of first commoner.
I welcome this opportunity to speak after the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) invited us to express our views as new members. Also, I want to make it very clear that we in this section of the house, the biggest proportion of the members sitting to your left, Mr. Speaker-and if I may say so, the most enlightened; politically at least-are very strong supporters of the government. We may be separated by the seating arrangements, but we are united with those on your right, sir, in the conviction of what we have been called on to do for national development and for a greater Canada. It may be, too, that we have been chosen to sit on this side of the house because our political faith and our confidence in our national destiny are so strong that we
488	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Pascoe cannot possibly be influenced by proximity to other lines of thought. We may even be over here as missionaries seeking converts.
I am proud to speak as the representative for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. I want to thank the wonderful people of that constituency for the confidence they have shown in me. I will do all in my power to justify that confidence.
The name "Lake Centre" was made a byword in this house by a previous and an illustrious representative, none other than the Prime Minister. The Moose Jaw portion is well known, not because of former representatives, but because of the name "Moose Jaw, the friendly city", and because of the reputation of the Moose Jaw farming district, one of the best in the west. Moose Jaw-Lake Centre can be described as a farm and city constituency. It includes the city of Moose Jaw, a large and growing part of the city of Regina and more than a dozen very important towns and, as I indicated before, some of the finest farming communities in the west. Few other ridings combine farmers, labour groups, business and professional men in such nearly equal proportions.
Other speakers have boasted of the recreation spots and tourist attractions in their ridings. In my constituency we, too, can boast of the summer pleasures along the beaches and on the waters of Last Mountain lake and Buffalo Pound lake. Even the names of these lakes are an invitation to those seeking new places to visit.
The speech from the throne is of great interest to those farmer, labour and business groups I mentioned earlier, not only because it forecasts a great development program for all Canada but also because of the promise of government action on particular problems.
I am one of 47 members, who have been sent here from the three prairie provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba to support the government, 47 members elected out of a possible 48, and even the 48th had a close race, although he may want to argue that point. I suggest that these 47 members can speak for the prairies and express the general views of that section of Canada better than any other group in this house. We are not here from the prairies as a pressure group; we are here to work in the best national interests but we shall be expected, I am sure, to speak out for our own constituencies and for our own particular part of Canada whenever there is need to consider local or sectional problems.
My remarks perhaps should deal directly with the amendment to the speech from the throne; but I suggest, sir, that the speech itself contains all the essentials necessary for


Canadian development and, therefore, no amendment such as the one before us needs to be considered.
The speech from the throne emphasizes what has always characterized our party, namely practical policies for present needs, coupled with a great and abiding faith in the future of Canada. The speech does not deal with generalities; it concerns itself with those things which we believe are necessary for the good of the people of Canada now and in the years to come. The future of Canada can be seen in the program set out by the government in that speech.
The speech pledges the government, "to make unremitting efforts in the peaceful solution of international problems". The hopes and the prayers of all groups will be with our leaders in this endeavour.
The speech pledges the government, "to major concerted efforts to encourage the expansion of trade." In this connection the commonwealth trade and economic conference in Montreal in September will be watched with great interest and with a great deal of expectation and hope. Export trade is essential for prosperity in that section of Canada I help to represent. The government can find no stronger supporters than those on the prairies for its commonwealth trade policies.
The speech promised an extension to June 28 of the benefits of unemployment insurance. This was not merely a promise; it was a pledge for quick action on a pressing problem. This pledge has been fulfilled. Already the measure granting this extension of benefits has been passed and has received royal assent. The opposition members spoke in criticism of the measure, spoke at great length, but they all voted for it. The quick fulfilment of this government's pledge will be well received in my constituency and in others. It was an emergency measure to help those temporarily without jobs.
Further amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act are indicated in the speech. There will be opportunity for us then to inquire into the possibility of unemployment insurance for hired farm labour. This question is of interest to many in my constituency, to both farm owners and to hired workers. Members from rural ridings will be pressing this matter further later in the session.
The speech from the throne promised a vigorous program of home building. Here again we have had quick action. In the first week of this new parliament the government put through a measure adding an additional $350 million to the public funds available for house builders under the National

Housing Act. This extra help for those who desire to own their own homes will be well received in my constituency, especially in the new development areas of Moose Jaw and in that growing portion of Regina that is in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. I hope that help for house building will be made available in greater degree for those living in smaller towns and villages.
The speech promises "a small business section within the administrative machinery of government" to assist small businesses. We have many of these small businesses in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. They play a big part in the life of the community. Owners of some of these small businesses came to me during the election campaign and indicated great interest in this government proposal. In the short time since the speech was made public I have had requests for more information and many expressions of approval of such a plan.
References in the speech to "national development on our frontier of the north" fire the imagination with the possibilities of this northern expansion. The whole government program of Canadian development has a special interest and offers great possibilities for our young people, hundreds of whom we have seen passing through the galleries of this house in the last two weeks. It is gratifying and reassuring to see these young people becoming familiar with the processes of government and showing such interest in public affairs. Everything we do here in this house will have some bearing on their future.
In this connection, I would like to congratulate the 190 Rotary clubs on their participation in the "adventure in citizenship" for high school students from all across Canada.
From my own constituency the Rotary clubs of Moose Jaw and Watrous sent worthy representatives with whom I had the pleasure of sharing an evening banquet program. We hear much these days about juvenile difficulties. I am sure that those hon. members who have had the privilege as I had of sitting with and talking to the young people in the Rotary groups will agree that the average young man and young woman of today also have a vision of the great future of Canada and realize the part he or she will be called upon to play to make that future a reality.
The speech from the throne contains references of special interest to western farmers. As a farmer myself and as a member who received a large farmer vote on March 31, I can say that there is intense interest on the prairies in the government's agricultural program. The speech from the throne indicates 57071-3-32
The Address-Mr. Pascoe that it is "the desire of parliament that agriculture should be assisted to realize fair returns for its labour and investment." That is the policy we advocated in our election campaign. That is the policy which western voters, not only farmers but all groups, supported. It is the policy which, as I said, brought about the election of 47 prairie representatives out of 48 as government supporters.
The prairies are necessary in Canada's business and industrial life. One need only look at the big map in the railway committee room to see the great area of the three prairie provinces and to realize their importance in the whole Canadian economy. Everyone in the house should take a long and careful look at that map to see just where Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba fit into the national picture.
Putting more purchasing power in the hands of western farmers is in the national interest, in the interest of all sections of Canada. The Agricultural Stabilization Act was made a main election issue on the prairies by the opposing parties who probably now wish they had never opposed it. The vote results show that the act was endorsed overwhelmingly. It offers great hope for the future of agriculture.
But we all know that no single piece of legislation can provide the complete answer to prairie farm problems. There is need, among other things, for a more extensive farm credit program. We will have an opportunity later, I trust, to offer our views on possible changes in the operations of the Canadian farm loan board for the benefit of small farmers and young people who want to start farming.
There is hope on the prairies that some effective form of crop insurance can be worked out between the federal and provincial governments, perhaps through an extension of the protection now offered by the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. There is reference in the speech from the throne to possible changes in that legislation. We western members will have opinions to offer in this regard, particularly with respect to expansion into a crop insurance plan in which the provincial governments will play a large part.
Another big hope lies in the improving record of the government with respect to increased wheat sales. Because western wheat farmers are in competition with subsidized farmers in other lands, extension of our wheat markets is not easy. While new markets are being found and while present markets are expanded emphasis will be placed on the great value of the government's policy of cash advances on farm-stored grain. In the past

The Address-Mr. Pascoe year over 50,000 farmers availed themselves of these advances, advances of what actually is the farmer's own money against later sales of his own wheat. As soon as harvesting starts this fall these advances will be available for the threshed grain while the farmer waits for delivery quotas. At that time the great benefit of these cash advances will become more apparent.
While I am on the subject of added revenue for the farmers, may I say that I welcome the statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) that he will soon announce the final payment on the 1956-57 wheat sales. The wheat board cut-off date for these sales was May 9. A final wheat board payment at this time would help the western farmers meet the cost of their seeding operations.
We in Saskatchewan are gratified with the progress the government has made in trying to reach final agreement on the South Saskatchewan dam. The benefits from that project will extend beyond the province and will be felt in the national economy. This is another election promise that is being kept as fast as the Saskatchewan government will assume its full responsibilities for its share of the project.
This brief reference to items in the speech from the throne gives some indication of the government's farm program. I was greatly surprised to read a newspaper interview with the Saskatchewan minister of agriculture in which he is quoted as saying that he was most disappointed to learn that nothing will be done for our farm people at this session of parliament with the possible exception of minor amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. It would be more helpful to Saskatchewan farmers if the Saskatchewan minister of agriculture stopped taking this negative attitude and took some positive action on provincial farm policies that might receive federal support.
For instance, he might help to work out some form of provincial-dominion crop insurance with the province taking the lead. As a farmer myself I think we should have a crop insurance plan and I think that the Saskatchewan government should work out the details of the plan and pay at least part of the cost. The Saskatchewan government through the Saskatchewan minister of agriculture should assume its full responsibilities towards the farmers and not attempt to put the whole burden on the federal government. The speech from the throne has emphasized that the federal government is ready to meet its agricultural pledges. The Saskatchewan


minister of agriculture should indicate the willingness of the provincial government to do its part.

Mr. Speaker, before we conclude the debate on the address in reply, I would like to bring to the attention of the house a very important matter. No reference was made in the speech from the throne, as far as I could see, of any intention on the part of the government to introduce legislation intended to provide every citizen of this country with a compulsory identity card. Nevertheless there are a number of important reasons why such legislation should be introduced.
It is a well known and incontrovertible fact that, at this time, Canadian citizens are unable to produce an efficient means of identification. Yet everybody knows that the introduction of legislation designed to remedy this situation would be highly advantageous.
Several countries of the world adopted such a provision many years ago. They are constantly reminded of its benefits in all the various aspects of modern social life.
We should make it compulsory for every citizen aged sixteen and over to carry an identity card. This is an urgent need in a country such as ours, especially in times such as these.
What are the advantages of legislation such as this? A national identity card would protect the banker against the counterfeiter, the hotel keeper against the undesirable individual who attempts to register under a false name. It would make police investigations easier. It would make it impossible to use a credit card lost by a citizen. It would allow owners of night clubs, hotels and places of entertainment to detect young people who have not yet reached the legal age of admission to such establishments.
57071-3-32J
The Address-Mr. Dupuis
From the government's point of view, a national identity card would make census taking and preparation of statistics easier, besides making it easier to apprehend people who have entered this country illegally. Finally it would protect the voter's right by making it impossible to impersonate an elector on voting day.
Mr. Speaker, there is social uneasiness today, not only in the province of Quebec, but in all parts of the country. In my opinion, too often do we see young people 13, 14, 15 or 16 years old going into night clubs, taverns, licensed establishments of all kinds, to see shows which are not good for young people. And there is no way of checking the age of these people. When asked what their age is, they answer that they are 18 years old and there is no way for the owner of a night club or other establishment of this kind to check upon their age. Young boys or girls of 13 or 14 years of age often have the appearance of 18-year olds though their mental development is that of a young child for whom it is bad and dangerous to see shows of poor quality, to find themselves in night clubs among older people.
Mr. Speaker, there is also civic uneasiness, which could be eliminated with the national identity card. It is an uneasiness observed after each municipal, provincial or federal election. In every election, specially for the past two years, we have noticed that, for the three levels of government, there are people who specialize in passing what is called, at least in our province, "telegraphs". Well, Mr. Speaker, such dishonest tactics to win elections must absolutely be prevented and, if citizens are required to carry an identity card, we will manage to cure this uneasiness which allows some members to win elections fraudulently, not only here in the federal parliament but also in provincial or municipal parliaments.
What does the Canadian citizen have today by way of identification? We have nothing but secondary documents: a driver's licence, a pass, a credit card, all of which can be stolen by someone else and used fraudulently. In my opinion, it is absolutely necessary that people have a real identity card, so made that it could not be imitated. It would be an authentic document which, besides showing a photograph of the bearer, would include all useful information for a complete identification, such as name, address, place of birth, date of birth, racial origin, religion, marital status, occupation, signature of the bearer, and so on.

The Address-Mr. McLennan
I respectfully submit that this should be entrusted to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and I am sure all Canadians would be glad to carry a proof of their identity.
Who would feel wronged by such a government measure? The crooks, forgers, swindlers, racketeers, juvenile delinquents, smugglers, murderers, stool pigeons of the underworld and, finally, election tricksters.
On the other hand who would stand to gain by it? Every honest citizen, without exception, every Canadian who is proud of his nationality, and of our democratic institutions, all the various organizations in this country, official institutions, banking houses, social, commercial or cultural organizations of all kinds.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that there is no mention made of this important matter in the speech from the throne. That is why I made so bold as to rise this evening and why I intend, in the near future, to enter a motion on the order paper in this regard.
