Mr. Speaker, may I extend to you my heartiest congratulations upon your election to your high office, and also for the high regard and esteem in which you are held by all hon. members of this house. I would also like to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne and for the wonderful job done by these two young men. I would also like to extend my congratulations to the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Sevigny) and to the Deputy Chairman (Mr. Rea).
It is my honour to be the first Progressive Conservative elected from New Westminster riding for 32 years. New Westminster is the largest riding west of Ontario with a population of some 120,000 people; it covers the western portion of the lower mainland of British Columbia and is, I think, one of the most diversified ridings in Canada. At this time I would like to pay tribute to the candidates who opposed me on March 31. The Liberal, C.C.F., Social Credit and L.P.P. candidates were all real gentlemen. Never in any riding in Canada was there a cleaner campaign.
With all due respect to the hon. member from our capital city, the hon. member for


Victoria (Mr. McPhillips) I would like to say that I represent the first capital of British Columbia, Fort Langley, and I extend a very hearty welcome to all hon. members to visit that historical fort, which is now being rebuilt, when they next visit British Columbia. I also represent the second capital of British Columbia, affectionately known as the royal city and the home of the famous salmon bellies, and the Adanac lacrosse teams-the thriving city of New Westminster. I also represent the fertile municipalities of Langley, Surrey and the Delta, as well as those two fine young cities born within the last year or two, White Rock and Langley City.
There have been many postmortems held on the results of the last election but one thing is certain

the Canadian people knew they could trust the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his government and, above all, they wanted a strong government with a united Canada policy.
I congratulate the government on the additional money being made available under the National Housing Act, and I am sure this step will be received with great satisfaction by people in all parts of the country, especially the people of British Columbia.
I would suggest to the government that they might go further and make available to fast developing municipalities low cost loans for essential services such as sewers, water lines, hospitals and schools. This would I am sui'e it would not cost the government create a great deal more employment and a nickel.
We are all very happy with the extension to the benefit period provided under the Unemployment Insurance Act. This, at best, is only a stop-gap to alleviate hardship until industry and the development program of our government provide employment for our fellow Canadians. I am sure we all hope that our industrial and labour leaders will refrain from demands which will raise prices, the cost of living and the cost of production.
I would urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), in conjunction with the provincial government of British Columbia, to have a survey made of the drainage, erosion and soil conservation difficulties of the fertile Fraser valley. I do hope some consideration will be given to this matter during the session and also to the plight of some of our senior citizens. I have in mind those unable to work and living on a very small income apart from their present $55 old age pension. Even a small increase if necessary under the means test would help them to keep body and soul together.

I would like also to say a word in regard to the position of our veterans, especially those of the first world war. I believe the means test should be abolished in respect to those who have drawn pensions for more than five years. Such a step would give them new hope and they would feel they still had something to contribute to this nation and that they were still honoured citizens in the country for which they had sacrificed so much.
I thank the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) for having authorized a survey of the lower Fraser river and the port of New Westminster. This harbour is potentially one of the greatest fresh water ports in the world and with the right planning and under good management this port could become the Liverpool of the west coast. True, it would cost money to put it into good condition and keep it open. This is the case with all river ports, but the revenue it would produce and the employment it would create would be of great benefit to Canada and especially to the coastal area of British Columbia.
The feed grain situation is a problem of great concern to the farmers of my province. They are a unique group; they do not look for additional subsidies, but they do want a fair chance to compete as businessmen. They cannot understand why they should have to pay three times the price for feed grain paid by their counterparts in the state of Washington and in their sister province of Alberta. They feel that if this is a free country they should be able to buy for their own use in competition with farmers in other provinces.
I would add my support to the hon. members who have spoken in favour of assistance to and support for the soft fruit growers of British Columbia. The strawberry acreage of the Fraser valley has dropped from 3,500 acres in 1948 to 1,500 acres in 1957. I know the product of this area is much superior in quality but it does not come on to the market for two to three weeks after the products of Washington and Oregon. A few thousand tons dumped on the local market means nothing to the producers south of the line, but it depresses the local market to a point where the local growers barely get their cost of production.
We have hundreds of commercial fishermen who have fished for generation after generation in the Fraser river between the Pattullo and the Mission railway bridge. Some two years ago this section of the river was closed to commercial fishing and this has uprooted many families and caused hardship to many others.
I would like now to pay a tribute to a fine group of men and women who seldom get
The Address-Mr. Fisher credit for the services they render to this country. I refer to the members of the press. I congratulate them on their fairness during the last campaign and upon the exceptionally fine job they did on election night.
British Columbia is a province which depends very heavily on exports. Over 50 per cent of her citizens are dependent, directly or indirectly, on the forestry industry. It is indeed encouraging that this government has arranged a commonwealth conference to be held this September, and I urge the government to do everything within its power to build up our trade with all countries, United Kingdom in particular so that British Columbia may develop markets for our forestry, fisheries and fruit products.
This parliament faces a great task and a still greater responsibility. I think it is the wish and the desire of every hon. member of this house that the youth of today, the leaders of tomorrow, should say when this 24th parliament is over that it was one of the best Canada ever had. We are a great, fertile and wealthy nation. We have the greatest leadership we have had in this country for 50 years. If we work in co-operation, jf we believe in Canada, if we believe in ourselves and our fellow Canadians, we cannot fail.

Mr. Speaker, may I add a small drop to the full measure of congratulation you have already received? I trust that some day it will be possible for hon. members to know that you will continue in the chair both until their old age and your old age. I should also like to mention what a pleasure it was to see the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea) appointed deputy chairman of committees. We all remember his forthright decision last year in committee on the question of the excise tax reduction, and that commended his impartiality to us.
To my mind, however, there is no question that the gentleman who merits a real extravagance of congratulation is the man who set up the speech from the throne. He, of course, is the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker). The first job of a political leader is to get power. An able politician, journalist, and Conservative member of the British parliament has written: "If you would go into parliament, you must be a little vulgar and more than a little vain. You cannot do this unless you like being noticed and standing on platforms and people cheering you. Vulgarity and vanity are not serious vices, but they are vices, and if you would be a politician, it is important to make sure that you have them."

The Address-Mr. Fisher
As Macdonald's great biographer has said of him: "Every device, every ruse, every conceivable subtlety was instantly at his command."
Such observations are generally applicable without any niggling or nasty intent to the Prime Minister. I think any connoisseur of North American politics knows that a successful leader needs toughness, ruthlessness, deception, a sense of timing and a tight grasp on his party. It is not a game for patsies or sweet sayers, although a bit of sugar helps. I would not want to stop at this point, having presented a rather lurid caricature without commenting on the political revolution-and it is a political revolution-that the Prime Minister has carried out. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) has commented on it as a feat of superman, "a triumph of the cult of personality". In the wasteland of our shattered hopes we all need to assess the victory, to examine our defeat. It is a most significant one. To my mind it is analogous to, though a sharper expression than, the political revolution in the name of the Republican party carried out by Dwight D. Eisenhower in the United States. A quiet but fundamental change in communication, in the whole concept of political presentation, has taken place. The Prime Minister and/or his immediate advisors organized this. In essence, it is the simplification of symbols. The common denominator of the public mind is made available more easily today because of television and the concentration of the press on personality and simple statement.
Northern and northwestern Ontario was a redoubt, a Berchtesgarten, if you like, that resisted the Diefenbaker tide. This is a superficial assessment. The Prime Minister polled very well in northern Ontario, in each constituency from 2,000 to 5,000 votes more than one might have expected in ordinary circumstances. Any member of parliament in the area who denies the power of the Prime Minister's campaign is afraid to face the facts.
Why is there still a redoubt? Perhaps the strongest factor was the vigour of both Liberal and C.C.F. candidates in the region, perhaps a general weakness of Conservative candidates in finding the coat tails, and, certainly, a blase reaction towards the main Diefenbaker symbol, a vision of northern development. That is something which is not particularly new in northern or northwestern Ontario. I may comment in passing that one of the planks in that particular platform, the undertaking to build a railway from Churchill to Moose Factory is almost an insult to the common sense of the people in that area and, I think, to the common sense of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton). I suppose I should paraphrase


the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and say it would be a railroad from wigwam to wigwam. Certainly it would be a railroad that went nowhere, and if this government is considering putting railroads into the north it might remember that we have quite a large number of low-grade iron ore deposits which are closer to the centre of things than a railroad from Churchill to Moose Factory would be.
And now to return again to the details of the election campaign. Willy-nilly, we have to live and work with the new means in political presentation. If there is to be a cult of personality, we must make it a cult of personalities. If there is to be a simplification of symbols, we must do our simplifying too. A major factor in any campaign in the future from a constituency point of view is a large campaign treasury. Our party has long advocated a ceiling on election expenses. If this cannot be attained, we must go out to see our war chests are as able to present the modern political message.
The Progressive Conservative party has an exceptional leader. His party is not the Conservative party as we have known or thought it was. It is more progressive, more socialistic than conservative. The inherent compulsion of its leader to act, to be at the centre of the stage, means that it may continue to be progressive and not to swing right, as parties traditionally do on attaining power. North American politics create paradoxes within any parties successful on a national scale. The regional and occupational conflicts of interest prevail within the one framework

Bay street and Portage avenue together, though restive; the balanced-budgeters and the deficit budgeters; the free trade farmers and the high tariff industrial workers. In the speeches so far in this dull debate the- Conservative backbenchers have shown no common indication of what we call conservatism. Within 18 months to two years we may have a rump within the ranks of the majority; perhaps one dissident against the progressivism of the leader; the other dissident over regional disabilities and inattention. We will welcome both. It may be fascinating to watch the way in which the leader handles them.
Much of our interest in this parliament will centre on heirs-apparent. A long reign may legitimize and then destroy some aspirants. The outcome is more than casually important for the Liberals and ourselves. It is tough being left of left when the extreme left is impossible.
Members of parliament and their duties are roughly to be classified into four fields with, of course, a certain amount of overlapping. First, there are the personal

problems of his constituents that relate to the federal government; secondly, the presentation of constituency and regional needs to the government and in parliament; thirdly, matters of national significance that he should understand; and, fourthly, the duty to outline and to follow party policies and ideas.
There is little difference, I think, in any of the responsibilities which lie on ministers, as opposed to backbenchers, with regard to looking after the first section, whether the member belongs to the government side or to the opposition. Those of us who do reach parliament seem to be fairly able to assess constituency needs.
I think I can do no better than to repeat what I said last year to the effect that the average member of parliament unfortunately is often uninformed, misinformed or uninterested. Naturally each one of us cannot hope to cover all topics. There is the prospect, and postulated action as the Prime Minister has indicated several times, that this parliament's plethora of government members could lead to a lax or stultified parliament. Reform within parliament rests on more than respect or a return to respect of parliamentary rights.
The suggestion that committees shall have much more work is worth close attention but I raise this question: Is our reference, our informational service for parliament, as distinct from the services available to ministers, adequate to serve a new conception of duties for committees and members of parliament? Are our secretarial and office facilities adequate? There is, of course, the fact that those qualities which lead to our election by the voter are not necessarily the qualities that make us informed active members within the House of Commons framework. We can improve ourselves and we all seek in our own way to do so.
I would propose a number of drastic changes in the services of the House of Commons. The raison d'etre stems from my experience as a librarian and the contact I have had with the academic community. I propose a rota of House of Commons research fellowships awarded on a merit basis to graduate students and professional-rank people in the fields of economics, statistics, political science, sociology, labour relations, history and bibliography. To dovetail this with work of hon. members I propose a coordinated reference centre with a small permanent staff associated with the library of parliament and the national library. The fellowship holders would work for two years, with some time allowance for their own work but their main purpose would be to be research talent for members of parliament, available to hon. members on the
The Address-Mr. Fisher latter's presentation of a subject field related to political matters within the scope of the House of Commons. Such fellowships would stimulate and increase the political knowledge of our best talent in the social sciences. It would improve the calibre of our members, deepen their knowledge of national problems and give some compensation for the disadvantages they are under in an informational way compared with their counterparts in the United States congress.
In passing, a reference to the problem of leadership in the library of parliament is in order. Three years ago a debate on the library of parliament in this house showed some attitudes, notably on the part of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), which were very discouraging to the library profession in Canada. The Canadian library association argues that the head of this pivotal library should be a trained librarian skilled in all phases of that social science. The association cares not if he or she be French or English. They want the best trained librarian available for that post. The present honoured incumbent of the post is on the eve of retirement. Let us hope the government will reconsider the stand taken by the former government and follow the arguments presented three years ago by the lady member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken).
In this session the secretarial and office arrangement so far as our party is concerned are fair. Might one suggest in view of the relative responsibilities of those in the other house and members of parliament that there will always be a sense of indignation at members of parliament sharing rooms and sharing secretaries while the hon. gentlemen from the other place operate in their present spatial surroundings and secretarial glory.
We were all pleased to note in the speech from the throne reference to the forthcoming visit to Canada of President Eisenhower. On May 16, 1958, the senate foreign relations committee of the United States had the American ambassador to Canada before it as a witness. At that hearing we learned that Senator Morse of Oregon possessed a confidential letter from the Prime Minister of Canada to his ambassador in Washington. The letter did not go with the accompanying aide-memoire to the state department and therefore the responsibility for its reaching foreign hands lies within the Canadian service. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) is satisfied that Canadian embassy officials are not responsible for the leak. Are we to assume that ghostly gremlins are spiriting letters away from the Canadian embassy in Washington? Obviously someone had the

The Address-Mr. Fisher time to creep in and make a phototatic copy of this letter or remove it entirely and surely someone in the service of the Canadian embassy must be responsible if it has fallen into other hands.
I wish to put on record a portion of the transcript of the proceedings before the United States senate foreign relations committee during which the following exchange between Senator Fullbright and Ambassador Merchant occurred:
Senator Fullbright:	The Canadian government
has strongly argued that under the terms of the tax treaty its tax ruling should be recognized. The United States tax court also held our own tax court held unanimously that for the United States to impose taxes in this case was a violation of the treaty with Canada. Is that not so?
Ambassador Merchant: That is my understanding.
Senator Fullbright: Why did you issue a formal statement at Ottawa (April 9) claiming that a favourable judgment for the United States treasury department would not affect the treaty? You did make such a statement, did you not?
Ambassador Merchant: Yes we did, senator.
Senator Fullbright: Why did you do it?
Ambassador Merchant: My understanding, senator, is that the appeal relates to the determination of the facts surrounding the case. That when judicial determination has been made on the facts, that then the question of the applicability of the treaty arises. This is a very complicated case and I am not a lawyer, sir.
Senator Fullbright: But you did make such a statement?
Ambassador Merchant: Yes.
Senator Fullbright: Who asked you to make that statement?
Ambassador Merchant: We felt in the embassy, sir, that a statement clarifying the position would be helpful. There has been a considerable amount of publicity in the Canadian press on this.
Senator Fullbright: The Canadian press has been very exercised about it, hasn't it?
Ambassador Merchant: Yes.
Senator Fullbright: Who instructed you to make that statement?
Ambassador Merchant: It was our own suggestion from the embassy, sir.
Senator Fullbright: I know, you were the ambassador. Who instructed you, who in our government in Washington instructed you to make that statement?
Ambassador Merchant: The idea was mine, sir. I requested authority to do it.
Senator Fullbright: You apparently knew very little about it. At least you seemed to in the beginning. Why did you do that?
Ambassador Merchant: There had been a considerable amount, sir, of we felt in the embassy-
Senator Fullbright: You said that. Who instructed you? Did our treasury ever discuss with you?
Ambassador Merchant: I was never instructed to do that sir. I was authorized to do it. It was my recommendation.
Senator Fullbright: Who authorized you?
Ambassador Merchant: I am authorized by the state department, sir.
Senator Fullbright: Do we have a representative of the treasury in Canada in connection with your embassy?
Ambassador Merchant: Yes sir.
Senator Fullbright: You never discussed this with him?
Ambassador Merchant: I discussed this with him, but I was not instructed.

Senator Fullbright: Did he suggest that you do this?
Ambassador Merchant: No sir.
Senator Fullbright: It originated with you?
Ambassador Merchant: Yes, sir.
Senator Fullbright: Although you had no background in this matter and you are not a lawyer, as you say?
Ambassador Merchant: That is right.
The point I wanted to make with this quotation is not that United States senators seem to attack civil servants with a considerable amount of relish-and perhaps we cannot have that kind of attack with that degree of relish in our situation because of ministerial responsibility-but it is that the statement issued on April 9 came after the state department was in receipt of a message from the Canadian government. As indicated in the house the other day by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith), this message said in effect that the Canadian government would have to reconsider the whole tax treaty if the decision went in favour of the United States tax authorities and yet after this letter was sent by the Secretary of State for External Affairs the United States ambassador in Canada issued the statement that that interpretation was completely wrong. The effect of Ambassador Merchant's statement of April 9 was simply that the Canadian government did not have to worry. I would suggest that this case is a typical example of the kind of misunderstanding and the kind of sloppy work concerning which something might be done when the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Canada get together this summer as indicated in the throne speech.
Returning to the transcript of the proceedings before the United States senate foreign relations committee, the following exchange took place:
Senator Fullbright: It strikes me as the kind of thing that does not really affect the major interests of this country. I am very sympathetic with people who have industries that are being injured by foreign competition wherever they are. I have tried to be a liberal in trade policies, but there are real substantial interests involved in that. But here is an instance, it seems to me, of going out of our way to irritate the Canadians in an inexcusable way. I think it is very suspicious that this matter was let lie. No one ever thought of bringing it until ten years after it took place. This exemption was given in Canada in order to increase, accelerate the production of war materials, and then years after this case is brought and our tax court unanimously held for the Canadians and still we pursue it. I must say I do not see any justification for this kind of action on our part.

At least we in this corner agree with Senator Fullbright.
I want to touch on another question that involves United States relations with Canada, and that is the great lakes pilots' dispute, the dispute between the so-called shipping federation of Canada and the great lakes pilots' association. Here is another case, a little bit in reverse, where we are going to find the United States congress protecting Canadian pilots. There is at present, waiting to be approved in Washington, a law that would require any British or foreign ships on the great lakes to carry a pilot who is certified by the United States coastguard or by the Canadian Department of Transport officials. What is the Canadian government doing in this particular case? It appears as though we are taking the usual stand. We are waiting for the United States to take the initiative and then they may solve some of the difficulties, for example, that are involved in this dispute. It seems almost incredible that deepsea ships, once they pass Kingston, do not require pilots. There is no pilotage district laid on that requires them to use pilots on the lakes, despite the very valuable canals and other shipping facilities that the Canadian and the United States public have provided. This rather shocking condition is something for which the Department of Transport must accept some responsibility.
The key to this dispute seems to lie in the fact that British and foreign shipowners have organized a shipping federation, called the shipping federation of Canada, and its obvious purpose seems to be to establish some sort of relation with pilots that does not involve a union organization. The effect of the ships sailing without pilots can be gained from this excerpt from the Hamilton Spectator of Friday last:
An 18-foot steel beam was torn from the bottom of the Burlington bascule bridge by a British freighter passing through the canal last night.
Bridge officials said the beam was left dangling in the path of small craft under the bridge.
Damage will not interfere with the operation of the bridge and passage of large ships.
Officials said a strong northwest wind forced the ocean-going freighter Manchester Pioneer to the side of the canal, the ship's stern dragging along the wall.
I will skip a bit. It goes on:
Seven years ago the northern bridge section was knocked into the canal by a loaded sandboat. The
The Address-Mr. Fisher huge crash that sent 400 tons of wood and steel into the canal gave Hamilton one of its worst traffic problems.
This ship, the Manchester Pioneer, was one of those vessels that was sailing without a Canadian pilot. Hamilton harbour is very difficult and dangerous to get into and out of and the master of the ship had an accident. In this particular instance it was not a serious one; but what would have happened had it been serious and the ship had sunk in that particular place? I think hon. members can realize the howls that would have gone up if this foreign ship-a British ship in this case; I call it a foreign ship, not a Canadian one-had sunk while without a Canadian pilot.
Since March 31 the shipping federation of Canada has attempted to carry out a completely new policy for sailing on the great lakes with no pilot except between Port Weller, which is the entrance to the Welland canal, and Sarnia at the north end of the St. Clair river. The purpose of this seems to be, as I said before, to break this organization of the great lakes pilots' association. In order to explain the remarkable and drastic departure that this is from the previous practice I think it is worth noting that up until this time all foreign ships always took on a pilot in the great lakes in any of their travels. Canadian and United States ships operating within the great lakes-St. Lawrence system, of course, have masters and other officers on their ships who must meet the Canadian standards and they know the lakes very well. Now we have foreign ships-and the number of bottoms is increasing very much each year -this year taking the stand that they do not need pilots. You can have German, Norwegian and Dutch skippers, with very little knowledge of sailing on the great lakes, without anyone in the pilothouse who is able to handle radio communications in the English language. The problem is further aggravated by the fact that on the lakes there are a number of whistles and other types of signals that are completely different from the kind of signals on the ocean-shipping routes.
We have no doubt at all that more and more ships will be coming into the lakes this year and next year, and unless we are saved by the United States law we could have a continuation of this situation where foreign ships are dragging around our lakes, through our valuable installations, without having any Canadian on board.
I think one point worth noting is that both the lake shippers' association, which is an American association representing the employers or the shipping interests on the great lakes, and the dominion marine association
498	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fisher are both against the shipping federation in this particular matter. The dominion marine association has tried to arbitrate or get the parties to the dispute together, and they are certainly very much against this practice for the same reasons, of course, that the great lakes pilots' association are against the practice, namely that of having foreign ships in our waterways without pilots who are familiar with the waters.
One of the other factors involved is that on Canadian and United States ships, as a consequence of regulations issuing under the Canada Shipping Act, Canadian and United States sailors have to be very thoroughly screened for security reasons, finger-printed, their past investigated and all the rest of it. Here we have foreign ships without any contact at all, really, with such regulations, without a Canadian on board to watch them in their various moves, and they are allowed to get away with it by the Department of Transport. An indication of what the United States thinks about the situation is that they will not allow foreign ships to use their Sault locks. Foreign ships going up into lake Superior have to use the Canadian locks. Anyone who is familiar at all with the locks realizes that in almost every lake of the great lakes, but especially in lake Erie, lake Huron and lake Superior, there are a number of very dangerous passages and we have dangerous weather. We have fog conditions that can come up at any time and create difficulties for very experienced mariners, and ocean mariners are not familiar with these conditions to the extent that our pilots are. That leaves the whole situation wide open.
One of the points that makes the United States law, when it comes into effect, effective in Canada is that any ship plying the great lakes has to cross the international boundary line quite a number of times. That point should be mentioned in order to emphasize that we may be saved in this particular instance by the United States law.
But in seems to me that the Department of Transport could have anticipated this whole situation by stepping in and creating pilotage districts between Port Weller and Sarnia or between Sarnia, Detroit, Windsor and Fort William or Sault Ste. Marie. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) has the authority to create pilotage districts at any time, to lay on pilots for a particular area and even to set fees, but so for no action has been taken. The Department of Transport has pilotage areas up to Quebec city, from Quebec city to Montreal and from Montreal to Kingston but beyond that foreign ships are on their own.
When the shipping federation of Canada first refused to negotiate with the great


lakes pilots association in this particular case they came out with the statement that they had created a pilotage district from Port Weller to Sarnia, that is, they had set it up on their own. I understand that the deputy minister of transport sent a letter to the shipping federation of Canada telling them that only the Minister of Transport had the authority to set up such a pilotage district, but so far there has been no indication that the minister is going to act in that regard.
Furthermore, not enough pressure has been put on the shipping federation of Canada to bring them into conciliation talks. So far they have refused all offers extended through the Minister of Transport to get together with the great lakes pilots association. It seems to me that this is particularly a case where we could ask the government to take a forthright stand, show a bit of Canadianism and keep our pilots working on our inland waterways.
I should like to make a brief reference to another phase of anti-Americanism that is very rampant in the particular part of the country from which I come. It has to do with the trans-Canada pipe line and the construction work that is going on on the five spreads administered by the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. I think it is worth while to hand out bouquets now and then even to those opposed to myself, and I should like to compliment the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) for his efforts to see that the men who are working on the pipe line are bona fide Canadians and also for his efforts to try to keep as many Canadians ready and trained for the job as possible.
There are many difficulties in the way. There is a great deal of misunderstanding but at present I would say there is nothing more unpopular between Port Arthur and Kapuskasing than these people whom we call "You-alls". These "You-alls" come from Texas, Arkansas, Kentucky and places like that. They call themselves "pipeliners." They are experts in doing their job and unfortunately in Canada at the present time we do not seem to have enough people who are capable of doing the more complex jobs, certainly not welding. We have very few back hole operators or cradle operators or anything like that.
I should like to suggest to the minister that under schedule M, which gives him the power to institute training in conjunction with the provincial authorities, a really serious effort be made this fall and winter to train operating engineers and various other kinds of pipeline workers so that in the future we will not have this running feud that is

going to go on all summer between native Canadians and the "You-alls" from the southern states.
It is most welcome to hear that the government is going to introduce something in the way of support for university education. It certainly has not been spelled out yet. Welcome as that will be, may I suggest that the other problem of retraining within the ranks of the unemployed is at this particular stage really of critical importance. I feel that one reason unemployment was not as great an issue as many people hoped it would be in the last election was that the majority of the people who are unemployed are those who are stuck, shall we say, with a low level of education. You can be fairly sure that almost 70 per cent of them have a grade eight education or less. In no mood of snobbery I should like to suggest that these people tend to be inarticulate but the fact that they are inarticulate should not be used to deny their great need for further education, especially of a technical kind, at the adult level. If we are saddled with seasonal unemployment we not only want to have campaigns to "do it now" but campaigns to train these people.
Along with the government's program to do something for the university people I suggest the government should take action with regard to something that is much more extensive and serious and retrain the unemployed or give some of them the first training they have ever had. In the main these people would appreciate it very much because with unemployment they recognize not only their personal need but the general need for more training.
I should like to comment on one issue that came up in the campaign. It was mentioned by the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) and has to do with pulpwood and support prices for pulpwood. The provincial legislature of Ontario has passed an amendment to an act extending the farm marketing facilities to pulpwood but I have checked and I gather that it is not planned to make it effective in northwestern Ontario. We know that the combines investigation people have brought out a report charging a number of pulp and paper companies with a combine and suggesting that they have set prices to the pulpwood farmer of Quebec and deliberately kept them low.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) has a problem. If he does decide to bring pulpwood under the agricultural support legislation he has the problem of determining whether it will be done on a regional or national basis, and obviously because of the nature of the market we in northwestern
The Address-Mr. Fisher Ontario think it has to be done on a regional basis. The difficulty with setting pulpwood prices on a national basis lies in the fact that the pulpwood farmers of Quebec have been receiving such outrageously low prices for so long that any price set by taking their figures would put the Ontario pulpwood farmer in a very bad position.
There is another factor in this regard on which I think action by the minister might be worth while from the point of view of enhancing or maybe salvaging the reputation of some of the pulp and paper companies in our part of the country. Three of the pulp and paper companies in our area are included in the general charge made by the combines investigation branch and I think those companies would be encouraged if the minister would step in and set a floor price for pulpwood because it would certainly get them off the hook with respect to any possible inference that they were guilty or would be guilty of setting a price that was unfair to the pulpwood farmer.
I should like to say a few words about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which seems to be all alone in a hostile world at the present time. One of the central issues has to do with what will happen if big city television service is provided by private stations, something about which some members of the government are so vociferous in their demand. At the present time the C.B.C.'s production facilities are partly supported by advertising and if the corporation is forced into a situation where the advertisers are going to turn over their programs to the private stations in order to get the big city audiences what is the C.B.C. going to have left with which to provide service in the hinterland where we are still clamouring for television? We still have not got it in many places and we know we are not going to get it from private television station operators. That is just realism on their part, not a refusal to give service.
As the house has been told, there is a tremendous demand for television service in the bush country all across Canada. We are not going to get it from private operators. The C.B.C. is going to have to provide it and the people are anxious that the C.B.C. should do so. People in many parts of the country are demanding that it be provided because their taxes help to support the C.B.C. If the C.B.C. is taken apart under any new legislation and not left with the money and power to provide this service, then a situation will be created that will cause a great deal of dissatisfaction. Much as we appreciate the fact that the C.B.C. is not popular in certain areas, we would suggest that the government

The Address-Mr. Martel be cautious in its approach here and follow generally the outline of the Fowler commission report on broadcasting.
In closing I should just like to refer to the fact that the leader of this party in the last house and in many other houses has gone, as well as the deputy leader, and to say that those of us who are left here will aim, although we shall most certainly fall short, for the same standard of parliamentary conduct as those gentlemen managed to show during their many years in this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be words of thanks to the electors of the constituency of Chapleau for the confidence they have placed in me. I want to assure them of my full co-operation, which in any case will apply to the whole valiant population of my constituency to whom I have promised, in the last election campaign, my complete devotion. I will do my best to represent them well.
I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to offer you, on behalf of my electors and fellow citizens of Chapleau, and on my own behalf, my congratulations on your re-election to the post you so brilliantly occupy.
I also take this opportunity to congratulate the Deputy Speaker of this house and chairman of committees of the whole, the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny). I know that this honour is in recognition of his personal merits, but is also evidence of the right hon. Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker) consideration for the new Quebec members.
I also take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea) on his election to the post of vice-chairman of the committees of the whole house.
I want, moreover, to associate with previous speakers in tendering very special congratulations to the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, to whom was bestowed an honour which reflects on all young representatives in this house, and on all young people in this country who have taken an entirely new interest in public affairs during the recent years, and more particularly during the last federal election.
At the same time, I want to tender my warmest congratulations and respects to the new ministers in the cabinet, i.e., the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fair-clough), the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche).

The appointment of two new Quebec ministers is a clear demonstration of the ground gained by the Conservative party in that province since last year and the attention given to the fine people of Quebec by the Prime Minister of Canada and his government.
I have a special reason to be drawn to the two new Quebec ministers since both of them, along with the member for St. Hyaeinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), came to Amos last January to preside over the convention where I was chosen candidate. To do so they had to travel several hundred miles through a snowstorm and return to Ottawa during the night to take up their duties on the following morning. I am convinced that they will long remember this flying trip and that even if they had to leave as soon as the convention was over, they will have fond recollections of their visit to the constituency of Chapleau and of the well known hospitality of the people I have the honour to represent in this house.
I also thank the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) who was kind enough to come and officially open my election campaign last winter.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne gives an excellent general picture of the program which the new government intends to put into effect in the coming months so as to give Canadians all the attention they have a right to expect from their leaders and holds out prospects of a brilliant future for our great and beautiful country. The strong measures already taken by the Conservative government at the last session bode well for the future and are a guarantee that the projects announced by the new government will serve the whole of the Canadian people in years to come, and at the same time be of substantial assistance in the present period of stabilization.
I have noticed in the speech from the throne that very special attention is being paid to the progress of science for peaceful purposes. I am all in favour of this policy-Of what use would all our weapons be-and in many cases they are already obsolescent- if our Canadian fellow citizens were not making every effort to promote higher learning, or if, one day, they were to lose even the will to defend themselves? We should neglect nothing to improve the lot of humanity as a whole and to apply scientific progress to peaceful purposes. The Conservative government, as recently as last year, first by way of more generous social security legislation

for Canadians and then by way of increased gifts of wheat and other commodities to underdeveloped nations has demonstrated its concern in this regard.
As for other social security benefits put forward by the government, such as family allowances, I wish to go on record as agreeing with the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Belzile) who last week asked that these be increased in proportion to the higher cost of living.
The speech from the throne also mentions the improvement in the economic situation. I should like to draw to your attention the fact that trade should be encouraged, not only with commonwealth countries but also with all countries in the world, to the extent where it would not jeopardize the best interests and the security of Canada.
With regard to public works, I must of course begin by thanking the government for projects already carried out. I take advantage of this opportunity to thank the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) for the works that have already been carried out in my constituency and I would like to ask him to take under serious consideration requests for public works that will be made to him by various localities of my constituency which covers a vast territory.
Efficient steps will have to be taken to guarantee the very survival of one of the main industries of my constituency, the common metals mines, which would incidentally be of assistance to the whole Canadian economy.
As was suggested in this house, a one year additional tax exemption for any new mine would perhaps be a good solution but, in my humble opinion, the speech from the throne proposes a much more lasting solution which would promote the prosperity of our mining industry.
In fact, the house will be asked to approve a research program on the use and processing of our natural resources in Canada.
In my riding, Mr. Speaker, at lake Mat-tagami, a large commercial deposit of zinc, copper, silver and gold has been located recently. It will be necessary before long to build a new railway branch line running from the new Beattyville-Chibougamau line which started operating last year, and which would extend, I hope as far as James bay, still within the limits of the constituency of Chapleau. Mineral deposits already explored in this area
The Address-Mr. Martel seem to indicate that the lake Mattagami discovery will rank with that of Pine Point in the Northwest Territory where the present government proposes-and with good reason -to construct a railway line.
A project such as this, in the north of my constituency, would lay open to the sense of initiative and enterprise not only of the people of the Chapleau riding, but also of all Canadians, a vast and rich territory, most of which is thickly wooded. Canada's future lies northward, and opportunities await the young and venturesome who will go out and settle there.
As far as unemployment insurance is concerned, the speech from the throne proposes a few amendments to the act. We have already enacted several measures to improve the situation; however, a more urgent need would be to open employment and unemployment insurance offices in my constituency, where there are no such offices. Requests to that effect have already been submitted to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). The steps already taken by this parliament and those that will be introduced by the Conservative government, in order to improve the Unemployment Insurance Act, will be heartily welcomed in my constituency. In fact, they are absolutely essential, in view of the character of the valiant working population there who, more often than not, can only get seasonal jobs, or else have to travel very long distances, or to go outside the limits of the constituency, to find work. At present, there is neither employment nor unemployment office in Chapleau. Yet it has been repeatedly requested from the former Liberal government, but the matter has always been shelved, and that is perhaps why our people often have to seek jobs far afield, whereas if there were an employment office on the spot, our workers could always hope to find jobs closer to home. I think the situation deserves special consideration, and in view of the government's intention to improve the act, I hope that the requests repeatedly made by the people of my riding will be heard at last.
The speech from the throne also announces an important small homes loan program. I want again to thank the government for all it has done so far and to ask that particular attention be given to the manner in which small individual loans are processed by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in

The Address-Mr. Martel the more remote districts, far from the large centres, where requirements should really be less strict.
We want to favour the development of the northern areas. Therefore we must think of the families who are already living there, and want to find accommodation, or of the young people who want to settle in that part of the country and of families who are going north with the future of their children in mind.
The pioneers of our area have put up with great hardship to establish themselves in a new district. Even today they are still doing so in several parishes of the constituency of Chapleau.
There was another matter in the throne speech which attracted my notice. That was the policy with regard to the construction of new airports and the opening of new airways across Canada. There is absolute need of an airport in my constituency and I am sure that the Minister of Transport, having had the opportunity of visiting my constituency upon the opening of the Chibougamau railway, will give this matter particular attention. On this occasion he had to land at the single airport we have, even if it had not yet been licensed by the Department of Transport. He realized that we greatly needed one for the development of the north.
As far as the regulating of television and radio broadcasting in Canada, the speech from the throne indicates that improvements will be made to the relevant statute. On this point, I believe this government would be well advised to pay particular attention to remote areas such as my constituency where people are scattered over a large territory. Those Canadians often feel very far away from their fellow citizens. More powerful radio stations, low frequency relay transmitters, or satellite television stations would often take them out of their isolation at little cost.
I also hope that the amendments to be made to the Canadian Broadcasting Act will provide for ridding the national networks of some so-called neutral commentators or those commentators whose tendencies, if not communist, are at least questionable.
I have also taken note with satisfaction of the amendments which the government proposes to bring to the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Besides the many products already covered by that legislation which will be of great benefit to the farmers of the constituency of Chapleau, I understand that a minimum price will be set for pulpwood. This is very important for a large part of


my riding. I hope therefore that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) will require his departmental experts to take into account the report on commercial restrictive practices -under the Combines Investigation Act-in connection with the purchase of pulpwood in certain areas of eastern Canada, a report was submitted on March 31, 1958, by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and filed with the Clerk of the house on Wednesday May 14 last. In view of certain restrictive and I daresay at times illegal practices on the part of some of the companies buying pulpwood not only in my area but also in the whole province and eastern Canada, I believe that in the setting of a base price or a support price for pulpwood, account must be taken of the information contained in the report from the Minister of Justice. In all fairness, I must add that buyers of wood or lumber companies are not all involved in this investigation and that some of them, in fact, were paying reasonable prices, if not each year, at least some years. It is to be noted also that price fixing on pulpwood occurred during a Liberal administration.
However, in the field of agriculture, which is of particular interest to the residents of jny constituency, the majority of whom derive their living from that industry, and in view of the huge agricultural possibilities north of Chapleau, and even in the parishes already in existence, I should like to direct once again a request to the Minister of Agriculture. Our district, and the whole northeastern Quebec area for that matter, has a great need for an experimental farm, since at present, our farmers have to travel over 300 miles in some cases to obtain information or services from an experimental farm located in northern Ontario. Not that the employees of that particular farm are inefficient or unwilling to co-operate with our farmers, but the fact remains that our farmers find the present service definitely inadequate.
It was also proposed in the speech from the throne that amendments be made to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. Well, here again, I earnestly trust that special account will be taken of the requests made by farmers of remote areas, and that the relevant rules shall be improved or relaxed, so that the farmers of the northern areas, from whom income guarantees are often asked as if their farms were located near large cities like Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto, may obtain those loans with less difficulty. Our farmers are an honest and hard-working group. They have often proved it in the past, more

particularly in the province of Quebec, where the government of the Hon. Mr. Duplessis put his trust in them as soon as he came into power in 1936. I am therefore confident that our government will trust them still further and continue to introduce legislation to help them. As a matter of fact, I am sure that such action will in the long run benefit the whole Canadian people.
I also read in the speech from the throne that the government intends to establish within the administrative machinery of the government a small business section. This legislation would be of great help to secondary industries located away from the larger centres in remote towns or villages. There again, Mr. Speaker, I am very confident that the new government will see to it that our industry is decentralized, particularly our war industries, which action has been entirely neglected by the former centralizing governments who preceded the Conservatives at the helm for the past years. This will, I am sure, promote the future development of our wealthy land, while making our country less vulnerable in the event of war.
I fully approve the government's decision to consider amendments to the Citizenship and Immigration Act. As to the Indian Act, I shall merely say that it contains some unfair provisions with regard to this group of people. The northern part of my constituency has a number of Indian residents. In spite of the somewhat tardy efforts of the former Liberal government, amendments brought to the act do not seem to have filled the present needs of the Indians who are, in fact, the original inhabitants of this country. I am sure that the new government will set this matter right, not only in the constituency of Chapleau but everywhere in Canada where there are Indians. As a matter of fact the Conservative government has already indicated its good intention in this regard by appointing an Indian to the Senate. This is the first time this has happened in the history of this country.
With regard to amending and extending the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, I might say that this is a matter of particular interest to northwestern Quebec and to several other mining areas in Canada. For my part, I am sincerely convinced that this question must be solved once and for all. I therefore suggest that the official price of gold be doubled and raised to $70 an ounce, whatever our neighbours to the south may think of it. In the long run, this measure will be necessary not only in Canada but also in the United States where the value of the dollar is deteriorating more rapidly than in Canada. An official increase in the price of gold
The Address-Mr. Martel in Canada would undoubtedly stimulate the development of northern Canada and bring about an unprecedented rush to the north. We would thus give practical form to the future development of Canada and make sure of the expansion of the rich areas of the north for several generations to come. If we do so as early as possible, we will prevent an economic depression which, under the present system, will follow sooner or later. The more we delay, the less effect will such a measure have.
There are no gold mines yet in production in the constituency of Chapleau. However, whenever the price of gold is raised, several prospective mines will be opened, and the same will happen in many areas of Canada, which will help the Canadian economy. Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote a paragraph from the mining paper called Northern Miner, which has long been in favour of an official raising in the price of gold.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, I should like the Canadian government to do all in its power to increase the official price of gold to $70 an ounce. This will help the development of the north country more than anything else. In 1933, the official price of gold was increased from $20 to $35 an ounce, and this action was taken only in the light of the 1929 prices. The price has been fixed at $35 ever since. I should like to mention in this connection an editorial in the Northern Miner, a prominent mining newspaper which had this to say about the question:
The big monetary change of the past 20 years has been a growing reliance on American paper of various kinds. When, in the days of the old gold standard, a country got into financial straits it could not dare to lose its gold reserves and fought to maintain them. It put a ban on imports of goods, worked at low wages and long hours to build up exports in order to restore the gold position. Nowadays a country in difficulties simply borrows from the fund or elsewhere, and the borrowings are in the form of U.S. dollars, like the recent ones of Britain and France. Such a state of affairs has weakened the foreign case for an increase in the international price of gold. If you don't play along with the American ideas on gold you don't get a loan.
In the past these monopolies in paper money have ended disastrously. I believe we should put ourselves on record as advocating an increase to $70 an ounce in the price of gold right now if we want to prevent a repetition of the 1929 depression.

My first words will be of congratulation to Mr. Speaker upon his reappointment to the high office he now holds. The unanimous approval with which his appointment was received by all members of the house speaks eloquently of the high qualities which he brings to the position he now occupies.
(Translation):
My congratulations to you also, Mr. Deputy Speaker, on your appointment to the post you are now holding.
(Text):
I also wish to be associated with all the speakers who have preceded me in congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the able manner in which they discharged the responsibilities which were assigned to them.
New parliaments are invariably accompanied by new characteristics. Irrespective of political alliances, new members are greeted with the accompaniment of sincere good wishes, and former members no longer present are missed with equal sincerity. I wish to say I was particularly pleased at the opening of this new parliament to meet an old classmate of the 1934 St. Joseph's University alumni. I refer to the hon. member for lies de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Keays). To me, the hon. member is even more than a classmate; he is an old teacher. Indeed, the hon. member has the privilege of having taught me everything I know in the fine art of plain-chant. Hence, therefore, the foundation of my reputation for rendering with remarkable aptitude the so-called "silent notes" when joining in sing-songs, or otherwise. I do wish to say, however, that I am not alto-

gether disconcerted, for all that. Indeed, when such circumstances arrive, I endeavour to draw comfort from the old saying that there is always a silver lining to every cloud. And when I consider the political mantle with which the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine is now endowed, I cannot help but say: "What would have happened, had he been instead my teacher in political science". I shall not pursue further this matter, Mr. Speaker, knowing fully well that your duty would compel you to call me to order.
I have followed with deep interest, the speeches made by the different members from the maritime provinces in the course of this debate and should like to comment upon some aspects of their statements. I was particularly interested listening to the speech made on May 20 by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Creaghan). Being my first neighbour, geographically, I hope he will permit me the few observations I am about to make. I should like to note that the description he gave of his riding, if accurate in as far as it went, nevertheless was very incomplete in one other important way. While it was of significance to describe the southern and eastern boundaries of his riding, I submit that it remains of still greater significance to state that Westmorland is bounded on the north by the county of Kent, which I represent. In a facetious way, of course, might I indicate that following the result of last June 10 election in Cumberland county, Nova Scotia, and following the result of March 31 election in Westmorland county, the neighbourhood of Kent county, today is Westmorland county's greatest claim to distinction. This being said, I hasten to congratulate the hon. member for the effort and success of his maiden speech. I do hope, however, that the hon. member does not expect that I share all the views he has expressed. I would remind him, particularly, that his appraisal of the economic conditions in his area is far from depicting a true picture of the situation.
Referring to the slogan "We never had it so good," the hon. member was quite emphatic in asserting that the term during past years was not applicable to the conditions of his constituency. Following this enunciation he then proceeded to enumerate what he considers the real economic assets of his own city of Moncton. Besides the Canadian National Railways shops and offices, which are both establishments of long standing, mention was made of the other federal agencies located in his riding comprising the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Transport, the civil service commission, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the local and maritime regional offices of the unemployment insurance commission, all of which account

for a considerable number of employees contributing to the economy of his constituency. Not mentioned by the hon. member was the construction in 1951-52 of a large federal building serving as headquarters for the Post Office Department and other federal agencies, the establishment of an R.C.A.F. supply depot and of the important Lakeburn airport.
All these establishments in the Moncton district and other parts of the constituency- and this was not mentioned by the hon. gentleman-were made under the former Liberal administration and at a time when the constituency of Westmorland, according to the hon. member's own words, "Did not have it so good". In the pursuance of his speech the hon. member then referred to the present Canadian National Railways lay-offs which spelled great hardship for so many citizens of the area and he omitted to mention also that an unprecedented number of unemployed at this time were registered at the local or regional unemployment offices. The point I now wish to make is the following: In view of this recent and sudden change in the general economy of Westmorland constituency, which incidentally also affects conditions in my own county, would the hon. member be prepared to say now, "We never had it so good?"
The hon. member for Westmorland of course was not the only one to share these optimistic views concerning the maritime economy. Practically every hon. member from the maritimes who has spoken in this debate has sounded the same confident note. Confidence, of course, should not be shoved aside at any time. Some will say, and rightly so, that it is the cornerstone of success in every endeavour. And contrary to what is often said no one, I submit, wishes to be a prophet of doom; but the essence of confidence and of optimism in the future does not lie in presumption nor does it exclude true realism when realism needs to be exercised. Many resounding words were spoken during this debate, such as:
The long-awaited recognition of maritime needs.
The maritimes-a body of land submerged under the waters of Liberal indifference.
There is a new spirit abroad in the old provinces by the sea.
These are truly noble words, paying true lip service to a common cause; but how far from the true picture of the actual economic conditions in the maritimes today. In spite of all these glowing words, if ever the maritimes deserved to be described as a depressed area, it is now. The pulp industry is at a stalemate. Potato farmers are faced with faltering markets. Our labour class in increasing number is faced with the grim prospect of being unable to find work for the coming season. If hon. members opposite have any doubt as
The Address-Mr. Michaud to the accuracy of this statement I would merely refer them back to what the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne) said in this house on May 20, as reported at page 298 of Hansard:
I hasten to speak, not without sorrow, of a most urgent problem affecting most severely over 8,000 men in my riding and more than 600,000 people in Canada. There is more unemployment and more suffering due to unemployment in my riding today than at any time since the darkest days of the depression. I regard it as my duty to tell this house that if it were not for unemployment insurance, family allowances and pensions-
At this point an hon. member interjected, "Liberal measures." The hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska continued:
-many people in my constituency would be close to insurrection.
What does the present government propose to do at this time to solve the unemployment problem now crippling our national economy? We are told through the medium of the speech from the throne that a huge public works program is proposed as a remedy. Much has been said about the adequacy of this program and I shall not pursue further the discussion on this matter.
But I shall make one suggestion in regard to a project of great importance to the maritimes. I refer to the proposed Chignecto canal. May I mention that I noticed with pleasure that numerous speakers from the maritimes referred to this project in the course of their remarks. In speaking on behalf of this project today one is fortified by the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who, speaking in the city of Saint John on May 3, 1957, as reported in the Saint John Telegraph of that date, had this to say:
-a Conservative government at Ottawa would . . . carry out a complete investigation into the feasibility of the decades-old proposal for a Chignecto canal to link the bay of Fundy with Northumberland strait.
The survey would determine "whether the dream of past generations can become the reality of the future" in the Chignecto isthmus linking New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
Surely the Prime Minister will now wish to give substance to his promise made on that particular occasion by recommending, as he then said, a complete investigation into the feasibility of this proposal.
Furthermore, new developments in the industrial field of the maritimes strengthens the claim for the building now of the Chignecto canal. In this regard I wish to quote from a recent study published by the Financial Post, May 3 edition. Briefly the main points outlined in this study are as follows:
There is increasing speculation that another serious look at the costly project-estimated at more than $100 million-will be taken soon, now that work has started on the Irving Refinery

Brunswick plans to proceed with construction of a $16 million thermal power plant.
The chief advantages would be that it would shorten the water route between bay of Fundy, Atlantic and St. Lawrence ports. It would provide incentive to industrial development in the bay of Fundy region. The same study further states that the Atlantic provinces economic council takes the stand that the Chignecto canal should be regarded as part and parcel of the St. Lawrence seaway. This view was recently endorsed by the New Brunswick federation of labour which said in a brief to the federal government that the canal would be essential to the survival of the maritime shipping industry after the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway.
The proposed canal would make it possible for shipping out of any of the Fundy ports to proceed through the strait of Northumberland without having to go all the way around the elongated peninsula that is Nova Scotia.-This, it is argued, would knit the economies of the three maritime provinces more closely together. For example, it would bring Charlottetown more than 600 miles closer to Saint John; Yarmouth would be almost 500 miles closer to Newcastle, New Brunswick. Furthermore, the sea route from Prince Edward Island to Boston and other large centres of population in the New England states would be almost 500 miles shorter, and it would bring the Fundy ports of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick between 400 and '600 miles closer to Gaspe, Quebec and Montreal.
Spurred on by the approaching development of even more costly projects, businessmen and labour leaders in Saint John, Moncton, Truro, Amherst and a dozen other neighbouring towns are arguing, plotting and campaigning for the canal. For these and the other aforesaid reasons, I would urge the present government to give serious and immediate consideration to the construction of the Chignecto canal.
