Mr. Speaker, I wish now to make a few remarks on French radio and television in the maritimes provinces. First I want to pay tribute to the work accomplished by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. For the past twenty years, the C.B.C. has supplied us with a series of recreative and cultural programs of high standard; it has helped the various parts of our country to know each other better and it has been largely instrumental in the creation of a Canadian spirit. The comparison of that production with that of a number of private stations in Canada and abroad shows beyond any doubt, the high
IMr. Michaud.]

quality of our present system of government control in Canada, for radio-broadcasting as well as television.
However, criticisms are often heard from owners of private stations against the so-called monopoly of the C.B.C.; they request the establishment of a commission or a superior organization which could study their grievances. Without in any way minimizing the great usefulness and good intentions of most of those people, I think that if it is considered appropriate to adopt new measures, these measures should not in any way disturb the present system, but be based on the general and higher interests of the Canadian public rather than on particular commercial interests.
The French-speaking population of the maritime provinces is following with interest the tremendous progress made in the last few years to extend radio-broadcasting to all parts of Canada. We must pay tribute to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for having established CBAF station in Moncton, New Brunswick. During the few years it has been operating, this station has acquired a good audience. It not only broadcasts programs of the French network, but produces its own local programs and exerts a considerable influence over the whole area.
The population has also followed with equal interest the efforts made in view of developing a parallel T.V. system in the maritime provinces. Moncton, St. John, Charlottetown and Halifax are already transmitting English programs produced by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Everyone is happy about such progress. May I point out however that close to 300,000 French-speaking people in the maritime provinces are awaiting with great anxiety the establishment in their areas of some services in the field of television as well as radio on the part of the C.B.C. It is not my intention to underline the necessity of radio and television in our national life. The fact is recognized and has already been amply stressed by the report of the Massey Commission. The fundamental principles are not lacking. The first objective of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is-and I quote:
To diversify and enrich the life of Canadians of all classes in all parts of the country.
This was an extract from "The National Radio and Television Objectives of the C.B.C., February 24 1956". About the needs of the maritime provinces in particular, the report of the Massey Commission suggested:
The establishment of a French radio station to serve the French-speaking population of the maritime provinces.
The same recommendation is made for television. Elsewhere, this same report points out that:

If we want a more abundant and better cultural nourishment, we must pay the price.
As has already been said, part of the recommendations of the Massey Commission have been implemented and there is in Moncton, since a few years, a C.B.C. station linked with the French network. There is however but one radio station to serve the Frenchspeaking population of the maritimes and that gives rise to technical difficulties. The station already gives invaluable service, but it cannot reach the whole population. That is why we would be glad to see the establishment of relay stations, which would extend its coverage at low cost. Such relay stations are already numerous in Canada. In New Brunswick, there are two already serving the English-speaking population of Edmundston and Grand Sault. That is a service the utility of which nobody would question. If the principle is good in these particular cases, it is only fair to ask that it be applied to other groups which are more numerous and even more destitute. In saying this I am thinking in particular of the community of St. Mary's Bay in Nova Scotia, about 25,000 strong, whose every day language is French.
There are some less numerous, but still more isolated groups in St. John, New Brunswick for instance, where more than 7,000 French-speaking people are living, and in the mining centres of Nova Scotia, which have over 10,000 French-speaking persons. There is, too, the case of Fredericton, where the French population is not so large, but where in fact, special circumstances call for the building of a relay station. I refer to the university and to the normal school of the province and to the presence of a group of intellectuals who would benefit from French broadcasts-not to mention the establishment of an important military camp where several thousand French-Canadians will be stationed. There is no doubt that even though they may be far from their native province, they still wish to take their part of the French life of this country, a thing which they could do were they to have a French network relay station at that point.
As far as the establishment of a French language television station in the maritime provinces is concerned, that is a point which is acquiring vital significance for the Frenchspeaking people of the area. It should be recalled that the Massey commission had also recommended the establishment of a French language station in the maritimes. This has not been done to date. While recognizing the technical difficulties involved, we are still hoping that this will soon be done. The C.B.C. is so intent on repeating that its "function is to ensure that all Canadians, wherever they
The Address-Mr. Michaud may be, shall be as well served by public stations as by private stations" that we cannot bring ourselves to believe that a French language television service will not be extended to a large number of our people. The principle involved in the establishment of a basic French network radio station in Moncton applies with equal force to the establishment of a French language television station in the same area.
Mr. Speaker, I have attempted to put forward some need with regard to radio as well as to television. These are real needs and the C.B.C. is in a position to fill them. To do so, however, it will need the necessary funds. We feel that only a system like the C.B.C. is in a position to provide the Canadian people as a whole, French-speaking as well as English-speaking with a truly national radio and television service, a factor of Canadian culture. That is why any change which would make it more difficult for the C.B.C. to carry on would be highly prejudicial to the various groups in the national family.
I might add that the needs I have mentioned, which had originally been recognized by the Massey commission, were subsequently recognized by the Fowler royal commission on Broadcasting in 1957. In chapter 10 of the report published in that year, the following passage may be found:
Although the need for broadcasting in the two main Canadian languages adds to a number of facilities and programmes to be created and thus increases the complexity of the financial problem, the fundamentals of broadcasting are the same in both languages.
These are Canadian problems, rather than English-Canadian or French-Canadian problems.
And further in the same chapter, the following can be read about French television in the maritime provinces:
Another forceful and almost universal request formulated in the maritime French-language briefs was for a television station linked to the French network and the concensus pointed to Moncton, N.B., as the most favourable spot for that station. Coming from a geographical area of Canada where Canadians of French speech bulk so large-38 per cent in the case of New Brunswick-the request does not seem unreasonable. A study of the matter should be made at an early date.
Mr. Speaker, I shall conclude by a statement taken from the brief submitted to this same commission by the Conseil de la vie franpaise:
Canada is officially a bilingual and bicultural country. Indeed, one third of its population is of French origin. That third lives mainly in the province of Quebec. However, one million Frenchspeaking Canadians live in other provinces of Canada, 300,000 of them in the maritime provinces. Radio and television broadcasting, even private broadcasting, being in the service of the public must take into account this situation of right and of fact.

subtopic: GEOLOGICAL SURVEY
speechtext:
1.	When was the geological survey of Canada established?
2.	What is its purpose?
3.	How many university students were employed in this survey since its establishment, giving the number separately for each year?
4.	What are the duties of the students?
5.	How long does this work last?
6.	What remuneration do the students receive?
7.	What are the rates and allowances for 1957?
8.	Is it intended to expand the program in 1958?
9.	What is the cost of this program per year?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Comlois (Minisler of
Mines and Technical Surveys):
1.	1842.
2.	The main objectives of the survey are twofold:
(i)	To study, map and report on the geology of Canada and thereby: (a) determine the nation's potential mineral resources; (b) provide industry with the data required for the discovery and exploration of the nation's mineral deposits; (c) assist planning and development by providing fundamental data concerning engineering projects, water supply, and other factors affecting land use; and (d) contribute to the science of geology.
(ii)	To carry on other research that will contribute to the knowledge of how and when the rocks of the earth's crust and their contained mineral deposits were formed, thereby contributing to the growth of the science and enhancing the ability of geologists to map and explain the geology of Canada.
